translations.text: Of our holy and God-clad father Gregory, Archbishop of Nyssa: Commentary on the Song of Songs. I have received your zeal for the Song of Songs, as befits your honorable life and your pure soul,

concerning which you entreated us both face to face and by letter that, by a commentary suited to its subject, we should reveal the wisdom hidden in the sayings, and should clearly present the outward appearance of those words that seem easy to understand, illumined and purified by the immortality of their lofty and divinely beautiful power and meaning.

Therefore I have eagerly accepted the care of this matter, not as though you would have any need of these things, for I believe that the eyes of your heart are pure of every passionate and defiled thought, and that through the divine words they look without hindrance toward that divinely radiant grace,
but so that certain fleshly and coarse people may find some benefit for the spiritual and immaterial life,
to which this book leads by means of the wisdom hidden within it.

But since some children of the Church suppose that, apart from the simple and easily understood words of the divine books, all those that are spoken in parable, in figurative language, and in a hidden manner bring us no benefit,
I have considered it necessary first to give an answer to those who accuse us in such a matter.
For nothing in the divine Scriptures is idle and useless, if we are eager to hunt out benefit from the divinely inspired books in every way:

so that from the words in them that are easy to understand we may readily gather benefit without difficulty; but if they are hidden and obscure, spoken in parable and figure, and their force and benefit are hard to understand, we should not count them idle, but should search out such words and understand them, as the words of the Proverbs teach us and command us to know and understand -- whether as a parable,
or as a dark saying, or as a saying of the wise,

or as a discourse on natures, or as something conveyed by parable, or as figurative language, or by whatever name anyone may wish to call it; for we care nothing about names, so long as its force and meaning bring us benefit.

For the great Apostle too sets down the law as spiritual, and when he extends the name of the law more widely, he speaks also of narrative accounts, and says that all divinely inspired Scripture is law for those

who read it, and that not only through plain commandments but also through narrative accounts the Scriptures teach knowledge of the mysteries and blameless conduct to those who read with understanding;
and he uses the narrative as he sees fit, for he looks to the benefit and cares nothing about names, or how the narrative ought to be named.

But at one time he speaks of a change of voice, when he intends a change of message so as to bring understanding of the dispensation of the two covenants; and then, when he has mentioned the two sons of Abraham,
Concerning those who were born of the slave woman and of the free woman, he calls the understanding of them a parable and an allegory. And again, when he has recounted narrative events,
he says: "These things happened to them as a figure and a parable, but they were written for our instruction."
And again, when he says, "You shall not muzzle the ox that threshes," he adds and says: "It is not that God had any concern for oxen,
but it was surely written for our sake." And at times he calls partial knowledge and partial understanding a figure and a parable.
And again, he calls the change from bodily things to the spiritual a turning to the Lord, and he prescribes the stripping away of the veil.

And in all this, through every diverse figure and name and mental contemplation, he instructs and teaches us that we should not cling only to the letter and to the writings, since in many ways it harms virtuous living when the words are understood simply,

but that we should be carried over to immaterial and invisible contemplations, that we should understand bodily and coarse thoughts spiritually and divinely, and that we should shake off those coarse and bodily words like dust. For this reason he teaches us and says:
"The letter kills, but the spirit gives life."
That is to say, if we understand the force of these matters according to the simple and bare wording of the scriptures, they do not give us a pattern of good living.

For what virtue would the begetting of children by fornication teach, as is written about the prophet Hosea, or the going in of the prophet Isaiah, if someone limited the force of these sayings to the words alone? Or what kind of virtuous life does the account of David teach, in which the defilements of adultery and murder came together at once and jointly?

But when an interpretation is found that shows the telling of those deeds to be blameless, then the truth of the apostle's saying becomes clear: "The letter kills." That is, the letter presents a pattern of evil deeds. "But the spirit gives life,"
for it changes the unseemly and reproachable meaning into a divine and perfect understanding.
You know, then, that the Word himself, who is worshiped by all creatures, when he became man and taught us the divine mysteries concerning himself,

spoke thus: "The testimony of two men is true," and "I and the Father are one." And the bronze serpent, lifted up in the desert as a relief for the bites of the people, he took as a figure of the dispensation that was to be fulfilled for us through the cross.
But he trained the understanding of his holy disciples through obscure and hidden words, and set before them parables and figures and dark sayings and teachings and allegories,
which he himself interpreted and explained to them.
And when they did not understand the force of what was said, he would reproach them for the heaviness of their minds and for their lack of understanding,

as when he told them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and they did not understand, he grew angry with them and said to them: "I did not tell you to beware of bread, but of teaching," for he took leaven as a figure of teaching. And again, when they were urging him to eat, he said to them:
"I have food to eat that you do not know." And when they supposed, "Has someone perhaps brought him food?", he interpreted his saying and said to them:
"My food is this, that I fulfill the will of my Father." And many thousands of such sayings are found in the Gospel,
in which the plain surface is one thing, and the sense toward which it looks, its depth, is another, such as the water that he promised to the thirsty,
by which believers become a spring of rivers, and the bread that came down from heaven,
the destruction of the temple and its raising on the third day, and the door and the way and the stone,

despised by the builders and joined together at the head of the corner, and the two on one bed, and the mill and the women grinding, and the one taken and the one left, and the carcass and the eagles, and the fig tree whose branch has grown tender: all these and the others,

as many as are of this kind, were said for this reason: that we might seek out the force of the divine commands and pay careful attention to what we read, and that we might diligently and with all our heart investigate whether perhaps a word may be found higher and deeper than the plain surface, one that would direct the mind to understand in a divine, immaterial, and divinely radiant way.
Therefore, in keeping with this sense, we do not say that the forbidden tree was a fig or any other particular tree, as some have said,
for if the fig had then been death-bearing, surely it would not be eaten now. And besides this, we have learned from the Lord by his decree that:
"Nothing that enters by the mouth defiles a person,"

but in place of this commandment we seek some other understanding, one befitting the loftiness of the lawgiver. Even though we hear that the paradise was planted by God's labor, or that the tree of life was in the midst of paradise,

we ask to learn from him who reveals hidden mysteries what plants they are of which the Father becomes maker and planter, or how it is possible that both of those trees should be together in the middle of paradise,
that is, the tree of life and the tree of destruction.
For the exact middle is like this: when one draws a circle with a compass, the point of the compass, which was pricked on the inside by the compass, is the middle.
But if it departs from that point, in whichever direction, it is impossible, without drawing another circle, that it should still be called the middle.
And there was one paradise there, as it is written. Now then, how can it be that two separate trees were both in the middle of paradise?
And the word that called all the works of God good, and very good, teaches us that the death-bearing tree is foreign to God's labor.
And if someone does not understand all this with wisdom and find the truth, the words of truth will be regarded by the careless as unstable and as a fable.

But if we were to investigate everything said by the prophets, it would be long for us and unfitting; yet so that through these few words we may understand concerning all of it, let us add a few more and pause to consider how Micah says that in the last days the mountain of God will appear on the summit of the mountains, to destroy through faith those opposing powers.

And again the loud-voiced Isaiah says: "A rod shall spring up, and a flower shall burst forth from its roots." For thus he named the Lord's manifestation in the flesh. Or the curdled mountain proclaimed by David: what power does it have?
Or what is the plain word? Or the myriadfold chariot, and the assembly of bulls mingled among the heifers of the people?
Or the foot dyed in blood, and the tongues of dogs, and that calf of Lebanon, ground fine together with the cedars of Lebanon?
And many thousands of such things are found in the prophetic writings, which show the divinely beautiful power hidden within the manifest words.
If anyone should strip this power from them, as seems good to some, the result would be something like this:

as if someone were to lay out an unthreshed sheaf of wheat as food for people, and had neither threshed it nor winnowed it, nor separated the wheat from the chaff, nor ground it, nor baked it, as is the proper way with bread.
For just as an unthreshed sheaf is food for beasts and not for people,

so too the divinely inspired words, unless they are ground fine by subtle contemplations, and baked, and made digestible, are food for beasts rather than for rational beings. This holds not only for the words of the Old Law but also for those of the New, and above all for the teachings of the Gospel.

Such are the winnowing fan that cleanses the threshing floor, the separating of the wheat, the burning of the chaff, the unquenchable fire, the good treasure, the fruitful tree and the barren tree, and the dread of the axe,
which has spoken of cutting down, and those stones that change into the nature of men.
I have written this to your prudence on account of those who permit no one to seek in the divine words any understanding beyond the plain surface.
And because Origen showed diligence concerning this book, and we too have set our mind on writing down our labor, let no one blame us,
but let him understand the apostolic saying, for it says: "Each shall receive a reward according to his own labor."

For we do not write down these sayings to show them off to anyone, but for the sight of God alone, who is the giver of the word. Since most of these sayings were spoken by us in church, and some of the lovers of learning who were with us wrote them down in shorthand,
we took what they had written down. What ran on in proper order in those copies we wrote out from them, and the rest,

whatever needed to be added, we added ourselves. In the manner of instruction we expounded them in order, one after another, and through clear words we revealed what was hidden in those sayings, as time and occasion gave us leisure for this during the days of the holy Fast. For in these days it became urgent for us to expound the power of these words to the ears of the people.
And if Christ, the treasure of life, grants us times of life, and peace, and quiet in life, we will undertake to write down the remainder [?],
for now the power of our discourse has reached as far as the halfway point, to the glory of the Lord, whose is the glory forever and ever. Amen.

Chapter of the Song of Songs, interpreted by Saint Gregory of Nyssa. Song of Songs 1:2: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine. 1:3: And the fragrance of your ointments is beyond all fragrances. Your name is ointment poured out.
Therefore the maidens have loved you and drawn you. 1:4: We were running after the fragrance of your ointments;
The king brought me into his treasure-chamber. Let us rejoice and be glad in you.
Let us love your breasts more than wine. Uprightness has loved you. Commentary: All you who, according to the word of the Apostle, have, like a soiled garment, the old man,
stripped off with his deeds and desires, and the radiant garment of the Lord, such as he showed in his transfiguration on the mountain,

have put on through a spotless life, and still more those who have put on our Lord Jesus Christ himself together with his holy garment and have been divinely changed into impassibility: you, hear the mystery of the Song of Songs,
you, enter within that incorruptible bridal chamber, made spotless and enlightened by a pure and holy mind.
And let no one have a carnal and passionate thought, unfitting for that divine wedding,

or an unseemly garment of the mind, lest he be bound by his own thoughts and, from those incorruptible voices of the bridegroom and the bride, fall into the mire [?] of bestial and defiled passions, and through foul, impure and loathsome thoughts draw evil fancies and images in his mind, and so be thrown out of that radiant wedding feast and cast into the outer darkness, and instead of bridal joy be condemned to weeping and gnashing of teeth.
This, then, I testify to you before God, for I intend to approach the mystical visions of the Song of Songs,

for through the depths described in it the soul is adorned in the likeness of a bride and rises to the honor of that incorporeal, bodiless, spiritual and all-holy divine marriage. For he who wills that all should live and come to the knowledge of the truth shows here, by this means, the perfect and blessed form of life, which is love.
For some attain life even out of fear, when they consider the accounts of the torments of Gehenna and, from dread of them, become estranged from evil things.

And again there are others who, in hope of the good things and rewards prepared for those who have lived in the service of God, lead upright lives, not by the goodness of love but by the expectation of reward.
But the soul that is lifted up to perfection casts out fear, for such love is servile,

when one does not serve one's lord out of love, but does not flee from him out of fear of beatings. And again, it disregards even the reward, lest it reckon the reward more honorable than the giver of the gifts,
but it loves with all its heart and with all its soul and with all its strength, not for the sake of anything else made by him, but him himself, who is the fountain of good things.
Now then, he who calls us to communion with himself sets this law in the soul of those who obey him and ordains this love for them.
But the one who establishes this legislation is Solomon, whose wisdom, according to the divine testimony, has neither number nor limit,
who passed through all things that have been and that will be, evenly and without error, whom nothing among existing things escaped, and from whom nothing remained unknown. But do not suppose
that I am speaking of Solomon the son of Bathsheba, who took that Sidonian woman as his teacher of unseemly sacrifice and was ruined together with her through partnership in sin.
That Solomon who is foreshadowed by this one is another. He is another, who was also born according to the flesh from the seed of David,
who is called Peace, who is the true King of Israel and the builder of the temple of God,
who has gathered to himself all knowledge, whose wisdom is limitless, and who, even more, is himself Wisdom itself and Truth, and to whom every thought and name befitting God is fitting;

for he took that Solomon as an instrument and speaks to us through his voice and words, first through the Proverbs, then through Ecclesiastes, and now through the wisdom of this present Song of Songs, by whose order and manner he shows us, step by step through his words, the more perfect way.
For just as in this bodily life not every age can take on every work of nature,
and this life is not shared equally among the different ages, for an infant does not do the work of a grown person, and a grown person is not carried in the arms of a nurse,

but in keeping with the times of each age, a different way of life and activity suits and belongs to it, so also, in a manner resembling the ages of the body, the activities of the soul are to be seen,
through which is found the rule and order that leads people toward a life pleasing to God.
And for this reason the Proverbs instruct us in one way and Ecclesiastes teaches us in another.

And the philosophy of the Song of Songs surpasses both of them by its loftier teachings. For the teaching of the Proverbs addresses its words to those who are still infants, lays down legislation suited to their age, and says:
"Hear, my son, the laws of your father, and do not put away the rules of your mother."

Do you see from these words how infant and simple the spiritual age still is? For it still needs to look to the mother's rules and the father's laws. And so that the child may cling more warmly to its parents, it has been promised childish ornaments, which it may quickly win through learning,
for a golden necklace is the ornament of children, beautifying the neck, and likewise a crown woven of certain flowers of grace. And one must understand the force of the proverb,

for it says this in order to lead him toward what is better, and thus it depicts wisdom for him in various ways and many forms and interprets the loveliness of that ineffable goodness, so that it may rouse him to share in good things not by fear and compulsion, but by desire and longing.
For the depiction of that goodness draws the desire of the young toward sharing in the beauty set before them, and kindles their longing.
So that his desire may rise higher and be changed from love of material things to love of immaterial things, he therefore adorns the beauty of Wisdom with praise.
And not only does he display beforehand by his words the excellence of her beauty, but he also enumerates her wealth, so that if he is joined to her, he will become lord of everything.
And that wealth of hers is [?] seen in her ornaments, and the ornament of her right hand is all the ages, for he says:
"Length of days and years of life are in her right hand,"
And they have clothed her other hand with a wealth of costly virtues, which shines with the brightness of glory, for it says: "In her left hand are glory and honor."
And then it also speaks of the fragrance of righteousness from her mouth, which brings forth the beauty of ointments: "From her mouth goes forth righteousness."
And concerning her lips he speaks, in place of natural purple, of the blossoming of the law and of mercy.
And so that all beauty may be seen gathered together in the excellence of such a bride, he also praises her gait and says: "She walks in the ways of righteousness."
And he does not leave out of the praise of her beauty her height and stature, which rise like some tall and desirable tree.
And that tree to which he likens her height he designates a tree of life, which becomes food for those who are united with her in love.
And by a pillar and a firmness, immovable and unshakable, I understand the Lord, for he is life and firmness.
And the saying is this: "She is a tree of life for all who have entrusted themselves to her and who have leaned upon her,"

and so one is united to her without error, as to the Lord. And power too is mentioned along with all those adornments of hers, so that the praise and excellence of Wisdom may be filled with all good things. For he says:

"God by his wisdom founded the earth and prepared the heavens by understanding," and one by one, following the order of created things, he assigns the power of wisdom under many kinds of understanding;
for he designates the same one as wisdom and prudence and knowing and understanding and knowledge and whatever else is of this kind.
And then he begins to instruct the youth about such a marriage and union, and he commands him to contemplate that divine bridal union. For he says to him:

"Do not forsake her, and she will cling to you. Love her passionately, and she will guard you. Put a fence around her, and she will exalt you. Honor her, so that she may embrace you, so that she may place a crown of grace on your head and help you with a crown of delight."
And when with these crowns he has adorned him for the wedding as a bridegroom, he commands him to be inseparable from her and says:
"When you walk, take her along with you and let her be with you; and if you sleep, let her keep watch over you, so that when you rise she may speak with you."
By these and such words he kindled the youthfulness of the inner man to desire for the good, and by the account she gives of herself he inflamed him still more and more to love.
And along with the other things she also made this known and said: "I love those who love me."

For the hope of being loved in return for loving kindles all the more the love of the lover. And so, along with these, he also spoke those other counsels, with a certain well-ordered and beautiful teaching, and led him up to a more perfect rule of life.
And then, at the end of the Proverbs, he called this good marriage blessed, and in it he uttered that praise of the valiant woman.
And then he added that philosophy of Ecclesiastes,

for through the Proverbs he had kindled sufficient desire for the virtues, but in this book he reproves people's love of these visible things and declares vain everything unstable and passing, and he transfers all desire for what can be reached through the senses, and all the movement of our soul, into longing for those invisible beauties.

And thus, once he has purified the heart from love of these visible things, then through the Song of Songs he teaches the mind the inner, divine, inaccessible and hidden mysteries, in which what is plainly depicted is the spirit [?] of a wedding bridal chamber, but what is unseen is the blending of the human soul with God. For this reason, the one he here designates as a bride he names a son in the Proverbs, and he transfers Wisdom to the role of the bridegroom,

so that the soul may be betrothed to God and may be shown by the bridegroom to be a pure virgin, and by union with the Lord may become one spirit with him through that immortal and incorruptible blending, and so that in place of this thick and heavy flesh the mind may become pure and spotless, beholding God.
And since it is Wisdom who says: "Love as much as you are able, with all your heart and your strength, and with as much desire as your soul can hold";

but trusting in these words, I also add this: "Love her passionately as well." For this passionate love is blameless and free from passion, as Wisdom says in the Proverbs, and by it she stirs you to a passionate love of the divine beauty.
And again, this present book also commands you the same thing, and it does not introduce a bare counsel about this,

but it speaks wisdom through ineffable meanings and sets up for you an image drawn from the desirable things of this life, in order to adorn these teachings. And that image is fashioned from the customs of marriage, for whose beauty desire serves as mediator to longing. And it is not the bridegroom who makes the beginning of desire, according to human custom,
but the virgin anticipates the bridegroom, and without shame she makes her desire known openly and regards the bridegroom's kiss as the object of her prayer.
For the holy and good ones who betrothed the virgin in advance, the patriarchs, prophets and lawgivers, had sent ahead to the betrothed the divine graces, which are called bride-gifts,
that is, the gift of betrothal, which is the forgiveness of sins, the forgetting of evils, the blotting out of guilt,
the change of nature, incorruption for the corrupted, the delight of paradise, the honor of the kingdom, and endless joy.
So then, the virgin received these divine gifts from those good gift-bearers, who through prophetic teaching brought her the gift,

And she confesses her desire and confesses her longing, and she hastens toward that grace, so that she may soon delight in the beauty of the Desired One. But certain of her own people and the maidens her companions hear her,
who stir up that maiden and holy bride to still greater desire.
So the bridegroom too comes, together with a company of certain intimate, beloved ones and friends of his,

who are the ministering spirits of God, through whom people are saved, or else the holy prophets, who heard the voice of the bridegroom and who rejoice and delight because of that immortal marriage and union,
through which "the spirit that is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him," as the Apostle says.

Now I again recall those same first words. Let no one who is ruled by passion and loves the flesh, and who reeks of the stench of the old man, dare to drag these God-inspired thoughts and words, this radiant figurative speech, toward impurity through brutish and impure desires.
Instead, let each person rise above himself, go out from this material world, be lifted up to the paradise of freedom from passion, and become an imitator of God through purity.
And let such a person enter with us into the inaccessible place of the mysteries and divine teachings of this book laid out before us, and let him delight there.
But if anyone's soul is unprepared to hear such holy things as these, let him listen to Moses and learn, and let him not be so bold as to touch this spiritual mountain
until he has washed the garment of the mind and purified his soul with the sprinkling of honorable thoughts, so that, for as long as we are occupied with the interpretation of these lofty visions,
the mind may wholly forget the customs of marriage, according to the commandment of Moses, who ordered that those who were to hear the mysteries be pure from the customs of marriage.
And let us keep all the commands of the lawgiver, we who wish to ascend this spiritual mountain of the knowledge of God,
where, together with material thoughts, every fleshly possession is left below in material life,
and let every bestial and unclean intention, if it touches such a mountain, be crushed by firmer thoughts, as if by stones and rocks.
Even so, they will hardly be able to bear this voice of the trumpets, which sound loftily and terrifyingly, beyond what the hearers can endure,
so that the mist and darkness of hiddenness, in which God dwells, may be lit up for us. On such a mountain God burns up with fire every material, thorn-like passion.
Therefore, from now on let us enter within the holy of holies, which is the Song of Songs,
for just as the holy of holies has a certain greater and more surpassing holiness than the other holy things, as this very name distinctly informs us,
so too this Song of Songs promises us instruction in the mystery of lofty mysteries.
For there are many songs of truly divinely inspired teaching, through which lofty matters and thoughts about God are taught to us, spoken by the great David and Isaiah and Moses and many others.
For this superscription teaches us a meaning of this kind: that just as the praises written down by the saints are higher than outer wisdom,
so likewise are the mysteries of the Song of Songs given by the saints, whose fuller understanding human nature can neither find nor contain.
And for this reason, in the narration of these teachings, he described in figurative language the most extreme matters of desire, that is, the passion of erotic love, so that we might learn from this

that: "It is fitting that the soul which contemplates the uncontemplable beauty of the divine nature should love it as passionately as bodily love is drawn toward bodily love and passion, and that it should change passion into passionlessness, and that all
bodily love we should extinguish and be boiling with the love of the spirit, set ablaze by that fire which Christ came to the earth to spread."

Hence, as to the kind of mind with which the soul that listens to these mysterious words ought to approach them, I think that what has been said is enough. But from here on it is time for us to set forth the very words of the Song of Songs and to set our hand to the interpretation of their meaning.
But first let us consider the meaning of the title of this book,
for it is not idly that the name of Solomon is written at the beginning of this book, but so that those who read it may understand

that it relates certain great and lofty and divine words. And since the marvel of his wisdom is beyond doubt for everyone, and the testimony to him on this account is renowned throughout the whole world, for this reason, at the very beginning, by means of the name, he teaches the mind
that through this book he is relating to us something great and worthy of his wisdom.
And just as the materials of the art of painting are prepared from colours of various kinds, and then by means of them the image of the subject depicted is completed,
yet whoever contemplates that image, depicted by art and pigments, does not look with wonder at the colours laid out on the panels,
but at the image which the artist drew by means of the colours, so likewise it is fitting with regard to this book too

that we should not contemplate the material of the colouring of the words, but should look in purity, with unblemished thought, as at a kind of royal image depicted by holy minds and set up within them.
For at a quick and simple glance these words resemble a painter's colours: white, or black, or egg-yolk yellow, or red and violet, or whatever other pigments; that is to say,
kissing, and myrrh, and ointment, and wine, and a bed, and the names of the bodily members, and virgins, and a bride, and other such things.
But the image completed from these is blessedness and passionlessness and likeness to God and union with him, and estrangement from evils and assimilation to that true good and goodness.
These are the thoughts that bear witness to the wisdom of Solomon, that wisdom which surpassed the bounds of human wisdom. And what could be more marvellous than this:
that he should make nature itself the purifier of its own passions, and by means of words thought to be passionate should make a teaching and instruction in passionlessness?
For it does not say that we ought to be rid of passionate impulses of the flesh, put to death our fleshly members upon the earth, and make our mouths pure of passionate words,
but it has so changed the disposition of the soul that, through thoughts, deeds and words of the opposite kind, it may experience purity and be carried over into that endless kingdom.
But the opening of the words of this book teaches us this first of all: that we should altogether forget the human boundary and pass beyond it,
we who desire to enter into its impenetrable mysteries and to become disciples of Christ, as he testifies concerning them and says to them:
"What do men say of me, and who do you think that I am?" And so, although they were men, he himself set them apart from men.
For truly, since the plain presentation of these words makes fleshly desires something to be shunned [?], and no one stumbles because of such figures of speech, nor falls into defiled thoughts,
but instead gains divine philosophy and a spotless mind, it makes clear that such a person is no longer a man, nor mingled with flesh and blood,
but has acquired the life of the saints that is expected after the resurrection from the dead, and has become equal to the angels through freedom from passion.
For just as at the resurrection the bodies will be changed to incorruption and will be joined to the human soul, yet these passions
that now trouble us along with the body will not rise again; rather, a quiet, desirable life full of peace will be given to us, undisturbed by the flesh fighting against the spirit.

and no longer is there this inborn war within us, which through passionate impulses is arrayed against the law of the mind and, as if taking it captive, enslaves through sin the soul overcome by desires,
but the soul is made pure of all these things. Then nature and the intent of both parts, flesh and spirit, will become one, when all fleshly love has vanished from nature.
In the same way the Lord commands those obedient to him through this book that, although we live in the flesh,

So let us separate ourselves completely from the mind of the flesh, so that we look only toward the spirit. Let us offer the images that kindle desire to God, pure and undefiled, to the God who is beyond every limit of the mind, who is sweet, desirable and longed for,
from whom enjoyment forever becomes the cause of greater desire, and sharing in his good things makes longing for him grow.
Thus Moses burned with love of that immortal bridegroom, and like this bride of the Song of Songs, as one who had been given knowledge, he said:

"Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth." The one who was found worthy to see God and converse with him face to face, as Scripture testifies about him, burned with even greater desire for such a kiss. After so many visions of God, as though he had never seen him at all, he begged for that wondrous revelation.
Likewise all the saints
in whom divine love had been kindled never ceased from desire. Everything God gave them to enjoy became material for an even higher longing and made it grow. And as one who is joined to God,
Its refreshment and joy are insatiable, and the more it is filled with his beauty, the more it increases its desire.
for since the words of the Bridegroom are spirit and life, and everyone who is joined to the spirit becomes spirit,

and whoever is closely united to life passes from death to life, as the Lord said. This is why the virgin soul longs to draw near to the fountain of spiritual life. The fountain is the mouth of the Bridegroom, from which spring the words of eternal life. They fill the mouth of the one who longs for him, as the prophet did when he drew in the spirit through his mouth.
And since one who draws water from a spring puts his mouth to it and drinks and so is refreshed from it, and the Lord is the spring, who said:
"Let whoever thirsts come to me and drink." For this reason the thirsting soul longs to bring its mouth near to that mouth, the spring of life, and says: "Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth."
And he who makes life spring forth for all and wills the life of all who desire it separates no believer from such a kiss. For that kiss of his is the cleanser of all filth.
And for this reason the Lord says to Simon the leper in reproach: "You gave me no kiss," for if you had been cleansed of the disease, he would have kissed you with his mouth unto holiness.
But he was rightly without love, for in the flesh he had been altered by that disease and pain, and he was separated from divine desire and unmoved by it.
But the purified soul, which has no leprosy of the uncleanness of the flesh, always beholds that treasury of good things,
which is the divine heart, from which comes the filling of the breasts with spiritual milk, by which the soul that receives grace is nourished in proportion to its faith.
For this reason it says: "Your breasts are better than wine." According to the order and structure of the body, "breasts" signifies the heart.
And if anyone understands by "heart" that ineffable and hidden power of the Godhead, he will not err.

And by "breasts" likewise [?] those good dispensations and works of the power of God on our behalf, through which God becomes the nourisher of each person's life and bestows on those being nourished food suited to each one, according to what each is able to receive.
We also learn another teaching from the philosophy of this book: there are two kinds of senses in us, one bodily and the other spiritual and divine. The word of Proverbs speaks about this, saying:

"You will find understanding and divine knowledge." There is a certain correspondence between the movements of the spirit and the bodily senses. We learn this as follows: milk and wine are told apart by taste. When they are understood spiritually, they also give spiritual help to the soul through the firmness of their power.
And a kiss comes about through the sense of touch, for in kissing the lips touch one another.
And again there is also a certain touch of the soul, which touches the Word,
...perfected by a certain incorporeal and invisible touch, as he said who said: "And our hands ministered to the word of life."

And again, in the same way, the fragrance of the divine ointments is not something enjoyed by the nostrils, but the reception of a certain intellectual, immaterial and spiritual power, by which the fragrance of Christ is drawn in,
for thus the opening virginal praises follow one upon another: "Your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments is above all fragrances."
So by these words too there is signified, as we understand it, a meaning that is neither contemptible nor to be rejected,
for from the milk of those divine breasts and from the wine, which announces joy to us, we learn this:

that all human wisdom, and the knowledge of created things, and every power of contemplation and comprehending mind are contemptible and scarcely to be compared with the simple food of the divine teachings,
for milk springs from the breasts, and milk is the food of infants, while wine, because of its strength and heat, is given to the mature for their delight.
And likewise the mature wisdom of those outside is far lesser and inferior to the infant-like teaching of the divine word; hence those divine breasts are superior to human wine.
And the fragrance of the divine ointments is superior to the fragrance of all human ointments, which signify a power of this kind.
For by ointments we understand the virtues, which are wisdom, purity, courage,
justice, prudence and the others of this kind,

with which each person anoints himself according to his own capacity and choice, and so one becomes different from another through that fragrance and is changed into the fragrance either of wisdom, or of purity, or of justice and courage, or of some other virtue.
And a certain person has within himself a fragrance blended from all such ointments. Yet even so, all this neither befits
nor equals that perfect virtue itself, by which, the prophet Habakkuk says, the heavens are covered, saying:
"His virtue covered the heavens," which virtue is wisdom itself and justice itself and truth itself and everything else. For this reason she says:
The grace of your ointments is beyond comparison with these ointments that are known to us.

And so, step by step, that soul, the virgin and royal bride, advances toward higher wisdoms, and she proclaims the divine power that is incomprehensible and uncontainable by human thoughts, and says: "Your name is ointment poured out [?]."
And the meaning of this saying is as follows: by any name that is given it is altogether impossible to understand exactly that immeasurable nature of yours,

But the power of every act of understanding, and the figurative expression of all words and names, even if it be something lofty and divine, has no natural capacity to touch the truth itself. Rather, our speech searches it out as if from certain traces and coverings, and through attainable likenesses and figures it attempts to make it manifest.

For whatever name we may devise to make known the ointment of your divinity, we do not by that figurative speech and indication of words signify the ointment itself; rather, through the names of theology we show forth some small portion of that divine fragrance.
And just as it happens with a vessel from which ointment has been emptied out: the very nature and form of the emptied ointment, what sort of thing it is,
is unknown, but from some small vapor and fragrance left behind in the vessel we come to an understanding of what was emptied out.
And this is the force of these words: that the ointment of the divinity itself, what kind of thing it is by nature, or how it is higher than every name and conception.

But the wonders of the names of theology, spread abroad among all things, give us the material and power of understanding, by which we name and call him wise and mighty and good and holy and blessed and eternal and judge and savior.
And all this signifies only some slight quality of the divine fragrance, which all creation has gathered into itself through these visible wonders, like a perfumers' vessel.
"For this reason the maidens have loved you and have drawn you": she has stated the cause of that praiseworthy desire and longed-for love. And who would there be
who would not be passionately in love with such beauty, if only he had the eye of the soul, capable of contemplating that beauty,
whose loveliness is very great even as contemplated, but the understanding and conception of the invisible from what is manifest is many thousands of times greater.

But just as this material love does not touch one who is still an infant, for infancy cannot contain that passion, nor again are those worn out by deep old age seen in it, so too, with regard to divine beauty, one who is still an infant, tossed by waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine,
and those grown old and aged and near to corruption are found unmoved toward this divine desire.
For that invisible beauty does not touch such as these, but only such a soul as has passed through the age and condition of childhood and has grown up in spiritual stature,
to which no stain or wrinkle or blemish or any other such thing has attached, which is neither senseless through childishness nor feeble through old age, and which the word ranks as a maiden.
Such a soul obeys that great and first commandment of the law and with all its heart and strength loves that beauty whose form and image and likeness and interpretation the human mind cannot find.

Such maidens, then, grown strong through the virtues and purified by the mysteries, love the beauty of the bridegroom and are made worthy to enter within that divine bridal chamber, and in return for their love they draw him toward themselves,
for he repays love with love to those who long for him, and as was said from the mouth of Wisdom: "I love those who love me," and that:
"I will divide my possessions among those who love me, and I will fill their treasuries with good things." And this is clear: he himself is better than good things, and he himself is that possession.
So souls draw to themselves the desire for their own incorruptible Bridegroom. And such are the souls that run after the Lord our God, as it is written.
And the cause of their love for him is the fragrance of his ointments, toward which, in constant running, they forget what lies behind and reach forward to what lies ahead, as it says:
"After the fragrance of your ointments we ran." So these maidens,
Those who do not yet have the perfection of the virtues and are infants in age promise to run the race of the contestants in the stadium for the sake of the fragrance of the ointments, and they say:

"We shall run toward the fragrance of your ointments." But the perfected and advanced soul already attains its desire, for whose sake the race is run, and is made worthy of the inner treasures that are to be gained, for it says:
"The king has brought me into his treasure-house."

For she who came to desire the good through the lips also attained beauty as great as the power of her prayer shows. And this was her prayer: that through the shining forth of the Word she might be made worthy of his kiss.

The same soul, again, having attained these things and entered through inner, invisible thoughts, cries out that the race is completed not merely up to the doors of the good, but by entering the inner treasuries of the Spirit; she who first, through grace, as through a kiss,
was made worthy to search the depths of the Godhead, and entered the inaccessible inner places of paradise, like the great Paul, and speaks of seeing invisible things and hearing unutterable words.
The saying that follows reveals the ordering of the Church,
For those who were the first to become disciples of grace, and became eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word,

did not keep the good shut up within themselves, but by their teaching spread the same grace to those who came after them as well. For this reason the maidens say to the bride, who was the first to be filled with good things by kissing the mouth of the Word and was made worthy to know the hidden mysteries, that:
"Let us rejoice and be glad in you," for your joy is the common joy of us all, and they say:

As you love the breasts of the Word more than wine, so let us too imitate your breasts, by which those who are infants in Christ are suckled with milk, and we have come to love it more than human wine.

And to make this saying clearer: that is, John loved the breasts of the Word. He leaned on the breast of the Word and brought his mouth, like a sponge, close to that fountain of life, and was filled as if with certain ineffable gifts, which are the immortal mysteries stored up as treasure in the heart of the Lord.

And not only was he himself filled, but he has filled us too, with a breast filled from those breasts of the Lord, and he continually fills us with those good things of the Word and from that fountain of immortality. For he proclaims with a loud voice and, like a trumpet, sounds forth: "In the beginning was the Word";

therefore we too rightly say to him: We shall love your breasts more than wine. For we have become like the maidens, and all the more so if we do become such, and are not infants in mind like those infants joined to vanity, and there is no mire of sin in us, nor the spot and wrinkle of oldness and old age, which are close to corruption. For this reason we love the streams of your teachings, for uprightness has loved you. For it is written:
"This is the disciple whom Jesus loved," and uprightness is Jesus.
And the prophet David showed this saying more brightly and clearly when he said:
"The Lord our God is upright,"
and he appoints this as uprightness, which guides everything crooked toward uprightness and makes it upright. May he do this for us as well,

so that everything crooked may become upright for us and everything rough become straight, by the grace of our Lord, the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Heading, this saying: 1:5 I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the dwellings of Kedar and like the tent of Solomon. 1:6.
Do not look at me, for I have been blackened, because the sun has disregarded me. The sons of my mother fought against me. They set me as keeper of the vineyard; my own vineyard I did not keep. 1:7.
Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where do you pasture your flock, where do you make it lie down at noon, lest I become like someone who goes around another's flock?
1:8. If you do not know yourself, O beautiful one among women, go out in the tracks of your flocks and pasture your kids by the dwelling of the shepherds.
The beauty hidden within the divine tent of testimony was not equal to the structure on the outside.
For a woven work of linen and hair and a covering of purple skins completed it, and that outer adornment was nothing great or precious.
But within, the whole tent of testimony shone with gold and silver and the gleam of precious stones, along with the pillars and bases
and capitals and the incense altar and the altar and the ark and the lampstand and the mercy seat
and the washbasins and the curtains of the courts, whose beauty was blended from all flowery colors and dyes, and with gold thread and hyacinth blue and fine linen [?] and purple, by a certain art
and craft of weaving, woven in flowery patterns and beautifully blended and arranged, so that like the bow of heaven it gave off a certain desirable radiance.
But what I am looking toward, and why I make my beginning from this point, will be made clear to you from the words that follow,
for again the Song of Songs lies before us for the teaching of all philosophy and all knowledge of God.

For this is the true tent of testimony, whose veils and courts and materials of skin and hair are prepared from words and images of a certain erotic love, and they bring forth love for the one desired and depict beauty; the mention of bodily members,
through the display of the face and the concealment of visible veils,
but within it is truly bright and gleaming, like the lampstand and the ark full of mysteries, and the altar of fragrant incense and the mercy seat,

which cleanses from sins, and the altar of gold, and the beauty of the curtains, and that woven work skillfully adorned with the many colors of the virtues, and the unbending pillars of thoughts, and the unshakable bases of teachings, and the beauty of the capitals,
by which the ruling mind of the soul is represented,

and the washing basins of souls, and everything that looks to the way of life of the bodiless beings of heaven, of which the Law speaks figuratively through the power hidden in its words: all of this is plainly seen here and shines with divine beauty,
if only we show ourselves worthy of entering the Holy of Holies through the struggle of our life, and wash away with the washing basin of the Word every [?] of defiled thoughts.
Might we perhaps, outside the commandment of the Law, draw near to some dead thought, or touch some unclean desire, and so be made strangers to the sight of those wonders of the tabernacle?

For the law of the spirit does not permit such people to approach, unless the garment of the conscience has been washed, as Moses commanded, or if it has touched some carrion-like and loathsome thought.
Now the sequence of the words examined earlier is followed by the present saying, spoken by the bride to the maidens, that is:
"I am black and beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the dwellings of Kedar and like the tent of Solomon."
The teacher does well to begin telling those good things that it was right to tell to the souls who had become her disciples,

Those who are eager, as they promise, to count the grace flowing from those breasts of the Word as more precious than every human word, which in the parable is called wine, also speak such words to her:
"We shall love your breasts more than wine, for uprightness has loved you."
And she adds an account of her own wonders for her disciples, so that we may learn all the better the boundless love for humankind of the Bridegroom, who out of love added beauty to the one he loved.
And she says: Do not be amazed that uprightness has loved me; be amazed rather that I had been blackened by sin and made the property of darkness by my deeds.
And he made me good through love, and clothed my ugliness with his own beauty.
For he took upon himself the defilement of my sins, and bestowed on me his own purity, and made me a sharer in his own radiance.
For first he made me beautiful instead of ugly and desirable instead of loathsome, and so he loved me. And then she commands the maidens that they too should become beautiful.
And she sets before them the pattern of her own beauty, in the manner of the great Paul, who says: "Become as I am, for I was as you are." And again:

"Become imitators of me, as I am of Christ." And so she does not allow the souls obedient to her to fall into despair over beauty [?] because of that past, unseemly life. Instead, they are to look to her and take heart from her example, knowing that the present life will become a covering for the former one if they become pure.
For she says: Even though this beauty, which now blossoms upon me, was poured out upon me by uprightness in return for love,
But know this about me: formerly I was not so radiant as this, but black.
And my former life clothed me in such an image, dark and gloomy.
Nevertheless, that is how I was then, and now I am this, for that likeness of darkness was changed into an image of beauty.
And you too, O daughters of Jerusalem, look to your mother, the heavenly Jerusalem.

And although, because of the ruler from the power of darkness who has settled among you, you are the dwellings of Kedar, which is translated as "darkness," become the tent of Solomon. Now Solomon is the namesake of peace, and by the tent of Solomon she signified all the courts of that royal tent. And Paul signifies this same matter more clearly in the Epistle to the Romans, where he speaks of the love of God toward us: that we were sinners and darkened, but by the shining forth of grace he made us light-colored and desirable. For just as night darkens with its gloom everything over which it spreads, even if something is by nature among the radiant things, yet when the light rises, that gloom no longer remains upon those that were darkened, nor any appearance of darkness,
so too, when the soul turns from error to truth, the image of that dark life is changed into the light of grace.
And he says this same thing to Timothy, as the bride does to the maidens, he who was changed from blackness to radiance, namely:

"And I was made worthy of this good, I who formerly was a persecutor and a blasphemer and an insulter and black," and also: "Christ came into the world to enlighten the darkened, and not the righteous,
but to call sinners to repentance," those whom he made radiant as luminaries by the font of second birth, and whose gloomy appearance he drowned in those waters.
And the eye of David himself beheld this same thing in the heavenly city and was astonished at the wonder of it: how in that city of God, of which glorious things were spoken,
Babylon settles and Rahab the harlot is mentioned, and foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Indians enter into it,

so that no one among men should any longer reproach that city for the desolation of its inhabitants, on account of the birth of a certain man, as it is written: "And he said to Zion: A man was born in her."
For those evil tribes of foreigners become citizens of that city, and the Babylonian becomes a Jerusalemite, and the harlot a virgin, and the Ethiopians radiant, and Tyre a heavenly city.
By such things, then, the bride now also makes the daughters of Jerusalem zealous, and she recalls the goodness of the bridegroom and says: Even if he receives some darkened soul,

he makes it beautiful by communion with himself; and even if someone is a dwelling of Kedar, he becomes a dwelling place of light belonging to the true Solomon, who is the King of peace, and he himself dwells in him.
Therefore she says: "I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, so that by my example you too may become the tent of Solomon, even if you were a dwelling of Kedar."
And then she adds to these words what follows, by which she puts on guard the soul and mind of the disciples,
so that they may not ascribe to the Creator the cause of that darkened form, but to the will of each person, which becomes the beginning of such blackness. And she says:
"Do not look at me, for I have become dark"; for I was not like this at first,
for it would not have been fitting for the creation of those luminous divine hands that they should have formed me with some black and dark coloring. And she says:
I was not like this, but I became so; for I was not black by nature, but by accident, and this blemish befell me from outside, for the sun changed my image from brightness to blackness.
And she says: "The sun has disregarded me." What, then, do we learn from this? When the Lord spoke to the people in a parable about the sowing of the word,

he mentioned not only the sowing of the good heart, but also that of the rocky and thorny heart and of the one trampled by the road, and out of his love for humankind he sowed the seed of the word among them all.

And when he explained the manner of their sprouting, he spoke thus concerning the soul that is like rock: what is sown in it does not put down roots in the depths, but its immediate sprouting promises fruitfulness,
yet when the sun burns more fiercely, the moisture of its roots dries up.
And in this passage the sun is mentioned as a figure of temptations. And the teaching of the bride teaches us this same meaning:
that human nature was created as an image of that true light, and was far removed from darkness and ugliness, and shone with a brilliance in the likeness of the firstborn image;

but the trial of the scorching heat, through the snare of seduction, withered its first green shoot while it was still immature and unrooted, and dried it up before it could acquire some good habit and, through the thoughts of ascetic struggle, give strength to the roots and bring them down into the depth,
for at that very moment, by the heat of disobedience, it dried up and blackened its delightful green flowering and its shoot.
But if the temptation of the adversary is called the sun, let this seem strange to no one, for we learn this in many places of Scripture.

For in the second Psalm of Ascents it speaks thus of the one whose help has come from the Lord, the maker of heaven and earth, that he may not be burned by the sun by day; and the prophet Isaiah, when he was prophesying about the order of the Church,

depicts the brightness of that way of life in the form of praise and adorns it with his words, and he speaks of daughters being brought on shoulders and sons in chariots and shaded litters, so that they may pass by the heat unharmed,
by which he figuratively depicts a virtuous life. For by their tender age he shows new birth and innocence,
and by the shades he signifies the consolation of souls from the heat of the passions, which comes through ascetic struggle and purity,

from which we understand that the soul which is to become God's bride must be lifted on shoulders, so that it may not be trampled down by the flesh, but may instead be carried by the body of flesh; and by the shades and chariots we perceive those graces of the Holy Spirit,
through which we become children of God and no longer tread the earth with the footprints of our feet, but through them we are lifted up to the heavenly life. And our life becomes shaded and cooled
when the coolness of the virtues quenches the heat of all the passions and desires. So the scorching from the sun happens when its heat is not kept off by the cloud of the Holy Spirit,

which the Lord has not spread out over such people as a shade and a guard. And so they are burned by the sun, which is the assault of temptations, and the splendor of the body's beautiful form is blackened and becomes ugly.
And then the Bride relates where the beginning of the change of our beauty into blackness came from, and she says:
"The sons of my mother fought against me and set me as keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep."

Lend us your ears, and do not scrutinize too closely the arrangement of the words, but consider the sequence of the meaning. And if anything from the translation and arrangement is unpolished, attribute it to the weakness of the translators
who translated from Hebrew into Greek,
for to those who know the learning of the Hebrew language precisely, nothing of the kind is found that would be incongruous.
But since the rule of our speech and language does not follow the arrangement of the Hebrew language, for the sake of exact rendering it introduces a certain confusion of words into the discourse.
But as we have understood it, such is the meaning of these words set before us:
for in the beginning man was created lacking none of all the divine goods, and his task was only to keep the goods, not to acquire them. But the cunning of the enemies stripped him of those goods,
which were taken from him because he did not keep the blessedness given by God to our nature.
This, then, is the meaning of those words, and the understanding drawn from the figurative saying is expressed in this way, as it says:
"The sons of my mother fought against me and set me as keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep."
Through these few words this passage sets great teachings before us, just as the great Paul determines when he says:
"All things are created by God," and that "God and Father is one, from whom are all things," and that there is nothing among the things that exist
that does not have its being from him and through him, and that "all things were made through him, and without him not one thing was made."

but since everything that God made is good, and very good, and since he created all things in wisdom, and gave the rational nature the grace of free will and added to it a power that finds what is better,

so that doing good would be under our own authority, and not by compulsion or against our will, but would be the virtue of our will and the valor of our free will. And this freedom of self-mastery was confirming to our will
something was found in the nature of beings that misused its free will and, according to the word of the Apostle, became an inventor of evil,

He who, because he was created by God, is a brother to us, but who, because of his willful separation from communion in good things and because he was the inventor of evil things, to whose entrance he opened the door, and became the father of lies,
set himself up as a fighter and adversary against all who had the will for good, to attain what is better.
Therefore he also became the cause of the falling away from good things of those others who followed him,

which he also brought upon the nature of human beings. Hence she who was once black, but is now beautiful, rightly puts forward such sons of her mother as the cause of that darkness-clad image of hers.
And by these words she teaches us that there is one cause of the being of all things that exist, the Creator of created things being like a kind of mother.
And therefore all who are conceived among existing things are brothers to one another, but the division of wills has split nature apart into love and enmity.
For those who became estranged from the love of good things, and who by falling away from what is better acquired evil (for indeed the essence of evil is nothing other
than separation from the good), display every means and effort to make others also eager to share in and acquire an evil will and mind.
And therefore she says: "The sons of my mother." And by presenting it in the plural she makes known [?] the multitude of evil ones. And she says: "They raised up war within me," that is to say,
they do not fight from outside and externally, but they have armed the soul itself to fight against itself.
And since this war is arrayed within each and every person, the holy Apostle therefore interprets it clearly and says:
"I see another law in my members, which is arrayed against the law of my mind and takes me captive by the law of sin that is in my members."
So from this war among kin, which rose up within me from my brothers and the enemies of my life, I have become blackened,
for I was defeated by those fighting against me, and I did not guard my vineyard. And by this vineyard one should understand paradise,

for there too He appointed man as guardian of paradise, but negligence in that guarding drove him out, settled him in the west, and separated him from the east. And therefore the east appears from the west, for it says:
"Sing to the Lord, who ascended from the west," so that the light which shone forth in the darkness may change that darkness into light, and the ugly may become beautiful.

And the apparent incoherence of the words can, through this understanding that we have found, be resolved in this way. For it says: "They set me as guardian of the vineyards," which corresponds to the saying
that they made Jerusalem into a hut for guarding fruit. For it is not that they set it up as a guardian of the divine vineyard, as the plain wording appears to say,
but the one who set it up is God, while they only became defilers within it. And they made it like a fruit-watcher's hut in a fig orchard and like a tent in a vineyard;
for since she fell away from the guardianship of paradise, through disobedience she remained a useless and worthless sight, in which there was no guardian.
And since he appointed man to work and to guard paradise, for this reason the bride says that it was he who set my soul unto life, for life was that delight of paradise,
which God appointed man to work and to guard,
from which those wicked enemies drove him out and transferred him to the labor of that evil vineyard of theirs, whose cluster yields bitterness and whose grape yields gall.

Such a vineyard was Sodom, and such clusters did Gomorrah bear, which was condemned along with Sodom; their wine was the incurable wrath of dragons, which was passed down in those evil winepresses of Sodom.

And even until now many among men are seen as laborers and guardians of such vineyards, who with all diligence keep the passions within themselves, as though they were afraid that they might lose the evil.
Do you not see those evil guardians of idolatry and those workers of godlessness and lawlessness?
How they keep vigil in the furnace of evils, and have counted separation from lawlessness as hardship and loss?

And likewise a similar pattern is seen concerning the other passions, in those who have received into the depths of their souls the desire and the taste for them, namely gluttony and love of pleasure and arrogance and insolence, or anything else of the kind,
how they carefully guard and preserve those impure passions and their snares, and have counted them as gain, so that they may never purify their souls of such evils.

Concerning these things, then, the bride laments and says: "For this reason I became black, since I turned my mind to guarding and caring for the tares of the enemy and those evil stalks of his, and I did not guard my vineyard." Ah, what great compunction it stirs in those who read with understanding this word, "I did not guard my vineyard"! This cry is the equal of mourning and bitter lamentation, of such lamentation as moved the sighs of the prophets to pity and compunction, and they said:
How has the faithful city Zion, full of righteousness and judgment, become a harlot; how has the daughter of Zion been left like a tent in a vineyard;

how has the city that was multiplied with people been left alone, and the ruler of the lands become a tributary; how has the gold been corrupted and the choice silver become useless, and how has she become blackened,
she who formerly shone with the true light. Hence the bride laments and says: "All this has happened to me for this reason, because I did not guard my vineyard;
and the vineyard is immortality and likeness to God and estrangement from all evils.
And the fruits of such a vineyard are innocence and purity, these bright and beautiful clusters, which make the senses of the soul sun-colored and sweeten them;
and the [?] is the sweetness of unending life, and the shoot and the flourishing top are the height of the virtues,

which joins one to the height of the angels; and the leaf, joyful and green, moving with a smile on the branches in a gentle breeze, is the many-formed adornment of the virtues, which flourish by the grace of the Spirit.

And she says: All this I had, and I shone with the delights of such good things; and because I did not keep my vineyard, I was darkened with mourning and grief. For when I fell from purity, I put on this dark form, for such is the form of the garments of skins.
But now, because uprightness has loved me, I have become bright-colored and beautiful.
And I am afraid for this honor, lest I again destroy this beauty through ignorance of vigilance, just as formerly through lack of vigilance I became [?] and suffered loss by failing to guard it.
Therefore she leaves off her speech to the maidens and again calls upon the Bridegroom in prayer, and she makes the love she has toward him the name of this her beloved, and says:
"Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where do you pasture your flock, where do you make it lie down at noon?

Lest I become like one who wanders around another's flocks; where do you pasture your flock, you good shepherd, who carry the whole flock on your shoulders?" For all human nature is one sheep before your might, which you took up on your shoulders. Show me the green place;
make known to me the water of rest; lead me out to the fattening pasture; call me by name, so that I, your sheep, may hear your voice;
and give me eternal life through your voice. Tell me, you whom my soul has loved,
for so I name you, since your name is above all names and is incomprehensible and inexpressible to all rational nature.
Therefore the name that makes known your goodness is my soul's love for you.
For how should I not love you, who have so loved me, blackened and ugly as I am, even to the point of laying down your life for your sheep, whom you pasture?
And no greater love than this can be conceived, that you should lay down your life for my salvation.
Therefore teach me where you pasture, so that I may find that pasture of life and be filled with that heavenly food, which, if anyone does not eat it, he cannot enter into life.
And may I hasten to you, the spring of immortality, and receive the divine drink which you make to well up for the thirsty from the river of your side,
whose source the spear opened, and from which, if anyone drinks, he becomes a spring of living water flowing to eternal life.
And if you pasture me in this way, you will surely give me rest at noon, when I lie down in peace upon it and fall asleep in that shadowless light and take my rest, for noon is shadowless,
when the orb of the sun shines overhead upon all on every side,
in which you make those you have pastured lie down and give them rest, when they have received your teachings together with you upon their bed.
But no one is made worthy of that noonday rest

unless he becomes a son of light and a son of day, and separates himself equally from the darkness of dawn and of evening, that is, from the beginning and the end of evils; for such a one is given rest by that sun of righteousness. Therefore she says: Make known to me how one ought to rest and pasture and lie down.
And what is the way and the reason for the midday rest? Lest perhaps someone find me strayed from good teaching and, through ignorance of the truth, join me to a flock estranged from your flocks?
She said this about the beauty that had been given to her by God;

and she is anxious and strives and entreats to know how that beauty may remain upon her forever. But until now she has not yet been made worthy to hear the voice of the bridegroom, for God has determined beforehand something better for her,
so that by the delay of that rest he may kindle her desire to a still greater longing, and so that her longing and her joy may grow together.
But certain friends of the bridegroom counsel her and, by way of advice, tell her how to keep her good things; yet their word too is hidden in obscurity. It is this:
"If you do not know yourself, O fair one among women, go out in the tracks of the flocks and pasture your kids by the shepherds' tents."
The force of these words is clear from what follows the words spoken above, but the connection seems, as it were, disjointed. And what then is the force of what has been said?
Our unerring and careful guardian is not being ignorant of ourselves, so that no one may look at something external and suppose that he is looking at himself,
which is what happens to those who have not examined themselves, when power, or goodness, or glory, or intelligence, or the abundance of wealth, or vigor, or loftiness,
or size of body, or beauty of person and gracefulness of form, or anything else of this kind they see in themselves, and they suppose that they are looking at themselves.
Hence they are erring guardians of themselves, who through love of alien things despise themselves in their own folly. For how could anyone protect what he does not know?
And therefore I say that the unerring guardian of our good things is not being ignorant of ourselves;

And so that each person may know himself, what he is, and may wisely tell himself apart from the things that are not his own, so that he does not unknowingly guard what belongs to others in place of himself. For whoever is nailed to the means of living of this world and considers some passing honour worth guarding carefully,
does not know how to distinguish what is his own from what is alien.

For nothing among passing things is ours, and how indeed could anyone hold on to these passing and unstable things? Since, then, only the invisible and immaterial nature stands forever in the same state, whereas matter passes away through a kind of change and flow, ever being altered.
And this is indisputable: whoever parts from what is firm has undoubtedly been joined to what is unstable, and flows and turns along with it.

And whoever pursues this passing thing and abandons that which does not pass undoubtedly falls away from both: from the one by [?] abandoning it, and from the other because holding on to it is impossible.
For this reason the counsel of the friends says to the bride these words: "If you do not know yourself, O fair one among women,
go out in the track of the flocks and pasture your kids at the dwelling of the shepherds." And this means something like the following:
Whoever does not know himself falls away from the flock of sheep and is joined to the herd of goats,
whose place has been appointed among the unworthy.

For thus the good shepherd set the sheep on the right, but to the goats he assigned the portion on the left. And this we learn from the counsel of the friends to the bride: that one must examine the very nature of things, and not imagine finding the places of truth by erring tracks. But it is proper that we tell you more clearly about this matter.
Many people do not understand things as the nature of things truly is,
but they look to the custom of those who went before and stray from the right understanding of things, for they take as judge of the good not rational thought but brutish custom.
Hence they acquire rulerships and authorities for themselves, and they reckon the distinction of this world and material abundance to be gain,

for them it is unknown what kind of end each of them will reach after this life. For habit is an untrustworthy guarantor of things to come, and its outcome often turns out to be a flock of kids, not of sheep;
Understand this saying from the words of the Gospel.
But whoever examines what belongs to his own human nature, that is, reason, let him despise brutish custom, and let him reckon nothing good that is not a gain for the soul.
Therefore I say that one must not look to the track of the flocks, who by their tracks point to the earthly life of those who passed before and have departed from life,
for it is impossible to know how to distinguish what is more honorable from what is conspicuous until we depart from this life. And then we shall understand whom we have followed.
Now then, whoever does not make the distinction between good and evil from the things themselves,

but follows the track of those who passed before and presents the custom of a past life as the teacher of his own life, will be found at the time of God's righteous judgment to be a goat instead of a sheep. Hence the friends say such words to her:
"You, O soul, have become beautiful from blackness, and if you wish the grace of beauty to remain with you forever,
do not go astray by the tracks of those who lived unworthily and who passed through this world before you, for the track of goats is unknowable, pathless and incomplete.

If you follow their track, through ignorance and through inability to comprehend their tracks, then when you depart from this life and are placed in the fold of death, you may be joined to the herd of those goats whose track you ignorantly followed in this world.
For if you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out in the track of the flocks and pasture your kids at the dwelling of the shepherds." This another translator has set out more clearly,
and through him no discord of words is seen in what is said, for he says:

"If you do not know yourself, beautiful among women, go out from the track of the flocks and pasture kids instead of the dwellings of the shepherds," so that even the hidden sense of the meaning of these words agrees well with the words we have written down.

Now therefore, so that this may not befall you, take heed to yourself, for this is the unerring guardian of good things. Understand how much more you are honored by your Creator than the flocks and the cattle.
For it was not the heavens that were made in the image of God, nor the sun, nor the moon, nor the beauty of the stars, nor anything else at all among created things,

but you alone of all creatures were made in the image and likeness of that nature exalted above all minds and of that incorruptible beauty, a seal of the true divinity, a dwelling place of that blessed life, and a receiver and mirror of that divinely radiant light,
looking toward which you also became just as it is, an imitator of the one who shines forth in you, through the radiance of your purity and spotlessness.
For nothing among beings is so great that it could equal your greatness,
for the expanse of the heavens is measured by the divine span, and the earth and the sea are measured in the hollow of the hand.

Yet the one who is so great and of such a kind, who holds all creatures in his will, is wholly contained within you and dwells within you, and is not confined by your nature as he walks within you, as it says: "I will dwell and walk among them."
And if you look upon this, you will turn your eye to nothing of the earth.
And what is this that I am saying? Rather, let not even the heaven seem marvellous to you. For how could you marvel at the heavens,
O man, when you see that you yourself are firmer than the heavens? For they pass away, but you abide for ever with Him who eternally is;

Do not marvel at the vastness of the seas, nor at the breadth of the earth. You were created to have authority over them, as over two yoked chariot teams, to drive and to race them. They obey your will and serve your authority.
For the earth sets before you the things needed for life, and the sea, like an obedient steed, takes you up on its shoulders and back and carries you on your journey over it.
If you know yourself, O fair one among women, you will despise the whole world, and by forever contemplating immaterial goods you will pass by the deceptions of the paths of this life.
