Therefore always take heed to yourself, and you will not stray into joining that herd of kids, nor become a kid instead of a sheep at the time of judgment, nor be cast out from standing at the right hand, but you will hear that sweet and longed-for voice
which says to the meek and innocent sheep: "Come, you blessed of my Father, and inherit the kingdom prepared for you" before the creation of the world,
of which may we too be made worthy through Christ Jesus, our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter. This is the saying: 1:9 To my horse among the chariots of Pharaoh I have likened you, my close one. 1:10 How beautiful your cheeks have become, like those of a turtledove;
your neck is like a necklace of beads [?]. 1:11 We will liken you to the form of gold and to finely inlaid silver. 1:12 Until the king laid his hands upon her, my nard gave forth its fragrance.
1:13 A bound bundle of myrrh is my kinsman to me; he shall rest between your breasts. 1:14 A budding cluster is my kinsman to me, among the vineyards of Gadi.
All that we read and examined earlier, in the beginning of this Song of Songs, before the portion now read, is like the dawn that comes after the night,
for it is not the light itself, but the beginning of the light.
And those sayings too are of this kind, for they announce to us the rising of the true light, but they do not have the brilliance of the sun manifest in themselves.
For in them it is the bride who speaks, and the friends and the maidens; but now the voice of the Bridegroom himself, like the disk and eye of the sun,

It rises and with the brilliance of its own rays covers all the brilliance of the stars and the light of dawn. And all these words mentioned above also have a certain power of cleansing and sprinkling, and they also teach,
and through them the cleansed soul is made ready to receive divine graces.
But the word now spoken reveals communion with God himself, which the Word of God gives to the hearer by his own command, and makes him worthy to share in that incorruptible power.
And just as at Mount Sinai Israel was first prepared for two days by that purification, and on the third day, at dawn, was made worthy of the vision of God,
when it was no longer occupied with the washing of garments, but with the vision of the Godhead and converse with it,

for the sake of which it had washed away the stain of the soul through those earlier purifications, so too now the beginning of the Song of Songs, spoken above, together with these two past days, has been of such benefit to us that in them we might be washed and purified of the stain of flesh and mind.
But the Word of God himself today, on this third day, after the first and second purification,
appears to us not with mist and cloud and the blast of trumpets and flames of fire terribly kindled, which enveloped the summit of that mountain and made known [?] the glory of his coming,
but sweetly and mercifully, changed from that terrifying vision into bridal joy. For when the bride had entreated
to learn the places of rest in which that good shepherd dwells,
so that nothing unseemly might befall her through ignorance, and when the friends had then set before her a careful and true judgment and counseled her to take heed to herself and to know herself,
for they determined that ignorance of oneself is the beginning of all passions, and that whoever does not know himself

cannot understand anything else that is good either; and since the Word saw through these things the due purification of her soul and mind, he shines forth upon his beloved and, in regard of her zeal, arms her for more perfect virtues,
for praise of good deeds successfully accomplished gives those who have advanced an even greater zeal to advance toward the good.
And what is the saying uttered by that Word to the true virgin: "To my horse among the chariots of Pharaoh I have likened you, my near one"?
But since the meaning and power hidden within this saying are not understood from the word as simply spoken, its power must be investigated diligently and with effort, as far as is possible.

For we have learned from Scripture of a different power that was arrayed against the steeds of Pharaoh, that is, the cloud and the rod and the fierce wind, and the abyss split in two, and the dried-up deep, and the walls of waves, and the floor of the abysses laid bare of water,
and those strange paths between the walls of water, through which came the deliverance of the Israelites and the drowning and destruction of Pharaoh with his chariots and horsemen and all his host.
Now therefore, since no cavalry force attacked Pharaoh and that host of the Egyptians, it is hard to understand
to what steed, appearing among the chariots of Pharaoh and destroying the chariots of the Egyptians, the bride is now likened by the word, for it says:
"To my steed, which won the victory over the chariots of Pharaoh, I have likened you, my close one."

Or is it clear and evident that, just as there can be no victory of those who fight in ships unless those who fight in ships are arrayed against them and defeated, and no victory of cavalry without the charge of armed warriors,
so also, since the strength of the Egyptian cavalry lay in horses and steeds, that power which came upon them invisibly,
by which they were defeated and their camps fell, the word has named a steed.
For they too perceived the one fighting against them, and said: "The Lord is fighting against the Egyptians," and: "Let us flee from the face of the Lord."
And this is clear, for the true commander armed his own power in a manner resembling their armament.
Hence there was a certain invisible power, which through those wonders of the Red Sea accomplished the destruction of the Egyptians, and which was depicted in the form of a steed,
which are the hosts of the angels, concerning which the prophet says: "You will mount upon your chariots, and your cavalry is salvation."
And again David mentions the chariots of God and says: "The chariots of God are ten-thousandfold," which the guiding thousands have yoked together.

And again, the power that took the prophet Elijah up to the height of the ether is called by the name of horses in the Scriptures, and Scripture calls the prophet himself the chariot of Israel and its horseman.
And those who go about all the world, through whom the earth is brought to rest and governed, the prophet Zechariah names horses,
speaking to the man standing between the two mountains. Now therefore it has been made known that there are also certain divine horses,

those which took up the prophet, and those which govern the world, and those which are yoked to chariots, and others on which God mounts for the salvation of human beings, and another which drowns the host of the Egyptians.

And since the powers exercised by the divine horses are of many kinds, the soul that has been brought close to God through the race of the virtues is likened to that steed which overthrew the host of the Egyptians. For thus the word says to her:
"To my horse among the chariots of Pharaoh I have likened you, my close one."
But this word has gathered within itself many great praises, and this likeness of the mare is an ordered array of her virtues,
for all the evil that is recorded as having befallen the Israelites during their sojourn in, and slavery to, the Egyptians,

and likewise, in turn, those saving powers of theirs, are all images of the adornment of such a soul as has become God's own. That is: the slavery, the burning, the clay, the brick, and every earthly labor, and those wicked overseers and tormentors who exacted from them the tribute of brick, on account of whom blood was changed into water, and the light was darkened, and houses were filled with frogs, and the soot of the furnace made bursting boils seethe up from the flesh, and everything in succession: the locust,
the fly, the gnat, the dog-fly and the hail, that slaughter of the firstborn, and this and everything else of the kind, and those astounding powers,
for it would not have been likened to that power which overthrew the wicked Egyptians, by which Israel was delivered from their wicked tyranny,
had not all this, which demolishes Egypt and prepares for the going to God, been set in motion on behalf of those who were being led into the land of promise out of Egyptian matter and clay.
And since, according to the word of the Apostle, "all things were written for our instruction," as many as are written in the divinely inspired books,
this word, spoken to the bride, counsels us nothing other

than that we too should accept the Word riding upon the shoulders of our soul, and should set ourselves against the horses and chariots of Egypt with their horsemen, and drown all their evil and devilish power in the waters of repentance and of the baptismal font.
But so that we may learn more clearly what has been said: the likeness of that mare by which the chariots of the Egyptians were drowned cannot be attained in any other way,

unless through that water of the mystery one escapes from slavery to the adversaries, and leaves in the waters every Egyptian mind and every foreign-born evil and sin, and comes up pure, and has no stain of the Egyptian mind, and brings up nothing that would muddy and defile the life that follows.
For whoever is completely and without defect purified of all those Egyptian plagues, which are blood and frogs and boils and darkness and locust and fly and hail and rain of fire and the others
which the book records, that person becomes worthy to be an imitator of that power upon which the Word rides, and, as I suppose,
we are not ignorant of the meaning indicated by the plagues, how the blood of the Egyptians comes about,
the plague and the stench of frogs and the changing of light into darkness, and everything in succession.
For who would not know by what kind of life a person has his drink, instead of water, changed into corrupting blood, and by what deed one becomes, in his own house, a begetter of the stench of frogs,
and how he exchanges the life of light for love of the deeds of darkness and gloom,
on account of which that furnace of Gehenna kindles the bursting coals of punishment for the wicked,

In the same way, each of those evils of Egypt can also easily be turned into instruction, into a source of wisdom, and into teaching of the good life for the hearers and for whoever wishes. But to prolong the discourse about matters so evident and plain is superfluous.
If, then, we show ourselves superior to these and such things and draw near to God, we too will without doubt hear these words:
"To my steed among Pharaoh's chariots I have likened you, my close one." But let the comparison to a horse not trouble anyone among those who strive for a holy and spotless life,
since many of the prophets reproach us for likeness to a horse; for Jeremiah depicts the lust of adultery under the name of the horse and says:

"They became lustful [?] horses, [?]; each one of them neighed after his neighbour's wife." And the great David decrees an even harsher rebuke if anyone resembles the senselessness of the horse and the mule, and he commands that their jaws be turned with bit and bridle.
Therefore he comforts such a mind through the following words and says:

"Although I have called you a horse, your cheeks are not such that bit and bridle would be needed to turn them; rather, because of your purity the cheeks of the turtledove adorn you." And he says to her: "How beautiful your cheeks have become, like those of a turtledove."

It is attested of this bird by those who investigate such matters that, if it is parted from its mate, it no longer accepts union with another mate from then on, for this love of purity is sown in it by nature.
Hence, by the figure of this bird, the word composed its praise, so that before the bridles the likeness of the turtledove might become an adornment for the cheeks of that divine steed,

by which it signifies the beautifying of such a steed through a holy life. Therefore it says this to her in amazement: "How beautiful your cheeks have become, like those of a turtledove," and at once it adds another praise similar to this one and says:
"Your neck is like hanging beads."
For since he once undertook a parable of praises, he has composed the praise of the bride through images of a steed,

for he praises her neck, adorned in the likeness of necklaces and [?]pendants, as is seen on spirited and praised mares. By mentioning necklaces he depicts the roundness and beauty that make the form and build of the mare appear more beautiful.
Now there is also another kind of "neck,"

which is seen on the shores of the sea, when a cliff of the dry land turns and bends like a neck into the depth of the sea, receives the sea's depth into its bosom, and by that turning, by the neck-like bend of the cliff, turns back the waves and the assault of the sea.
Such a place is called a refuge and a haven, which gives rest to those who travel on the sea and are beaten by storms.
The word likens such a neck at one time to hanging beads and at another to a refuge and haven for the storm-beaten, and both these figures become occasions for great praises of the bride,
for when a mare, with her curving and finely shaped neck, turns her neck to and fro,
carefully examines the going of his feet, and runs his course without stumbling and without error, and neither strikes his foot against a stone nor is caught down in a pit.

And this is no small praise of the soul, when it examines itself and with all reverence toward God directs its course, and crosses over every stumbling block that comes upon it from temptations, passes by it, and rises above it.

And then again, that first name of the beads itself, by the likeness of its figure (it is the ornament of the neck and is called "pharghel" [?]), is a figure of certain great praises of excellence, when the neck is likened to beads.
And what are those praises made known to us through those images? Let us set forth all of them together, but first let us speak about the harbour.
So the harbour is sweet and saving for sailors. And after seeing disaster at sea, taking refuge in some calm shelter,

in which they forget the hardships of the sea, and all turn to rest and are comforted by quiet after their long labours, when there is no longer among them any fear of sinking, nor concern about hidden rocks, nor anxiety about robbers, nor the buffeting of winds,
nor the boiling up of the deeps; rather, those beaten by the waves become free of all such troubles once they have taken refuge in a harbor amid the abysses.
Now, if someone so moors his soul that he himself is in a waveless calm, and is neither stirred up by evil spirits nor agitated by pride,

and it is not [?] by the raging of the waves, nor is it tossed by any other passion and carried this way and that by every wind that stirs up the various groanings of the passions. It would also calm, by itself, the others who are tossed in the abyss of life by the threefold and various waves of wickedness, and would lay open to them a calm and waveless life, fortified by the virtues,
so that those who take refuge in it may become free from the fear of drowning in evils.
such a person is fittingly likened, by the word of praise, to jeweled beads, which through their many beads signify the fullness of the various virtues.
For if he were likened to only one bead, his praise would indeed be incomplete, since he would not have the same testimony concerning the other virtues as well.
But as it is, the likening to many beads gathers together in its word the testimony of all the virtues at once.
And this is the force of this teaching: it gives general counsel to the body of the Church, saying that it is not right to acquire some one virtue and neglect the others.
But if you have acquired purity, and with a spotless life, as with pearls, you make your neck shine, acquire other beads as well,
in which the precious stones of the commandments are set, which will adorn the ornament of your neck all the more.
And again, let the ornament of piety and of right faith not be lacking from the nape of your neck, for this is that golden collar,
which is fashioned from the gold of holy piety and makes the neck radiant with God's light,
concerning which it says in Proverbs: "A crown of grace has been placed on your head, and a necklace of gold on your neck." Such, then, is the meaning regarding the beads.
But from here on it is time for us to add the next saying as well, with its interpretation, which the friends of the bridegroom speak to the virgin. It is this:
"We shall liken you to a form of gold and to finely sprinkled silver, until the king lays his hands on it."

But if someone should examine this in light of our previously stated consideration, it may perhaps seem to harmonize with it and to follow in its sequence; yet these words are concealed under the form of figurative speech and become hard to understand because they are expressed in parables.
For since the beauty of the soul was likened to the horse that overthrew the chariots of the Egyptians,
that is, to the angelic cavalry, and concerning that horse the one who rides well upon it says that its bridle is purity,
This he signified by the comparison with the cheeks of a turtledove, and again he portrayed its beauty as an ornament of the neck, made of various beads shining with virtue.

So the friends also wish to add some beauty of their own to the beauty of the horse, and they adorn its head with likenesses of gold, on which they also stud the purity of silver, so that the beauty of that ornament may shine all the more, when the brightness of the silver,
interwoven with the gleam of the gold, makes it shine more brightly.
However, it is necessary for us to leave aside figurative words and not to remove our discourse from a profitable understanding.

Such a soul, purified by the virtues, has thus been likened to that royal horse. But the Word has not yet [?] it, nor has it yet borne upon itself him who mounts such chariots and horses for the salvation of humankind.
First, then, it is fitting that the horse be adorned on every side, and only then receive the king as its rider.

But whether the king mounts such a horse and rides for our salvation, or whether he takes up his dwelling and walks among us and enlightens the depths of our soul, there is no form of difference in power,
for whichever of these two comes about, with it everything is brought to perfection,
for when a person has God dwelling within himself, or carries him as a rider, both of these are blessed, longed for, and desirable!
Hence the king intends to rest upon that horse and, as we said,
to sit and to lie down, and whichever of the two comes about in us, the grace is equal,

And since the king's preparers and servants are making that horse ready to receive him, and the divine mounting and the divine indwelling are one and the same, the preparers set aside the figurative language about its adornment, called the horse a couch, and said
that: "It is fitting for us to make a likeness of gold, finely studded with silver, and so to adorn the head and forehead of the horse,"
so that the king may rest upon it, not by sitting but by lying down.
So the sequence of the discourse has this kind of connection, as the discourse has just shown. But we ought not to pass over without inquiry why it is not gold itself that is prepared as an ornament,

but a likeness of gold, and not silver itself, but a sprinkling for that thing prepared from the material in the likeness of gold. According to our understanding, then, the force of this saying is as follows.
All teaching spoken about that inexpressible nature, however much it may present a divinely radiant and lofty power,
is a likeness of gold and not gold itself, for it is not possible to present exactly that good which surpasses minds;
even if it be Paul, who heard those unspeakable words in paradise, the understanding of the divine nature still remains inexpressible, as he testifies by means of those unspeakable words.
For even if some good thoughts have been sown in our minds for understanding the divine mysteries concerning that inexpressible nature, they are unable to express anything,

for as "radiance of glory" and "image of power" and "image of God" and "Word without beginning and from the first" and "Word of God" and "God" — all these are reckoned by us as the gold of those invisible treasures.
But for those who are able to contemplate the truth, it is a likeness of gold and not gold, but sprinkled with finely scattered silver.
For silver represents the words of truth, as Scripture says: "The tongue of the righteous is refined silver."
Now what is made known by these things is this: that the divine nature is exalted above every reach of minds,
while the understanding of it revealed to us is a likeness of what is being sought. And they do not present and make visible that image itself, which no one has seen and no one is able to see,
but by a mirror and a figure they depict a certain region [?] and likeness of what is sought, formed in our souls through mind and parable.

And every word that expresses such a power shows the force of a certain sprinkled, dividing and finely scattered silver. For what the mind intends, it cannot reveal, and so every mind is weak and incapable of understanding and contemplating the divine power.
And again, every interpretation in speech resembles some minute and invisible form, which is unable to reveal and serve that breadth of the mind;

Therefore the soul, helped and strengthened by such understandings for contemplating those unreachable things, and without searching them out, understands by faith alone that nature which surpasses every mind.
And these words are spoken by the friends: We will make for you, O soul, who have been well likened to a steed, certain forms and images of the truth,
for the words expressed through silver have this power: as if through sparks, they give off the light of understanding, though they cannot reveal precisely the power and meaning.

But you, if you receive this, will become his horse and his dwelling through faith, since he intends to recline in you by dwelling with you; for you will be shown to be both his temple and his throne.
And if anyone should say that the soul of Paul, or of someone else like him, is worthy of such words,

he would not stray from the truth. For Paul became a chosen vessel, and he both had the Lord within himself and carried him. By bearing His name aloft before kings and rulers, he was a royal horse. And since he himself no longer lived,

but Christ lived in him, who spoke of Christ, he became a temple of rest for that uncircumscribed nature. This, then, is what the friends of the bridegroom bestow on the holy and spotless soul of the virgin,
that is, they are ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for those
who are to inherit life. Therefore the bride becomes more perfect and more radiant through the addition of those graces, and she draws nearer to the one she desires,
on her; and before seeing his beauty with her eyes, she touches what she seeks through the sense of smell
and perceives its fragrance through the sense of smell, and acknowledges the knowledge of it through that ointment and myrrh,
which is called nard, and she gives this answer to the friends, saying to them: "My nard has given forth its fragrance."
That is to say, just as you did not grant the very gold of the Godhead itself,

but granted a likeness of gold, of an understanding that we can contain, and did not reveal its radiance by a plain revelation, but by some invisible fineness [?] and by the sparks and filings of the silver of eloquence gave us a kind of figurative speech about the one sought,
so too have I received the scent of his fragrance.

Now what is said here has this meaning: since from many and various ointments, of different and distinct fragrances, a certain skillful and measured blending prepares such a perfume with one particular fragrant flower that gives them their scent,
which is called nard.

It gives its own name to the whole perfume of those various blended fragrances, and the fragrance gathered together from all those spiced ointments represents the fragrance of the bridegroom, which the purified sense of the soul smells.
And the force of these words teaches us this: that the Creator of created things himself, whatever he is by nature, is unattainable, exceeds all thoughts, and is beyond scrutiny and without limit,

but through the purity within us, what is blended with virtues in the manner of ointments becomes for us a fragrance in place of that perfume, and by purity it comes to resemble the one who is holy by nature, by goodness the good one, by incorruption the incorruptible one, by immutability the immutable one, and through all the virtues accomplished in us, that true virtue
about which the prophet Habakkuk speaks as the covering of the heavens. Therefore, through these words which the bride says to the friends of the bridegroom, namely:
"My nard grants me his fragrance,"
Such wisdom he teaches us: that whoever gathers every fragrant flower,

or the perfume of the various kinds of virtue, from the gardens of paradise, and prepares his whole life through each of the struggles and labors into a single fragrance and myrrh, and becomes perfect in every part, and just as
it is not in nature to perceive the disk of the sun by looking at it directly, so also looking upon and perceiving the Word of God is impossible.
But just as we see the sun by means of itself and by means of a mirror, so also the flashes of that true and divine virtue, through the rays of impassibility, in a purified life
shine forth, and they make that invisible one visible to us, and the untouchable touchable, and that Sun of Righteousness perceptible through the mirror of our minds.
Now both of these are one for understanding, whether one speaks of the rays of the sun, or the brightness of the virtues, or the fragrance of perfumes.
For whichever of these we make the starting point of our discourse, one understanding is given to us by all of them, namely the understanding that comes through the virtues,
granted to us by that good which is above all minds, just as understanding and likeness of beauty come about through the firstborn image,

just as the bride did, that is, the holy soul of Paul. Through the virtues it was made like the Bridegroom, and through its own life it portrayed within itself that incorruptible beauty. From the fruits of the Spirit, love, joy and peace, and from other such flowers, it made that ointment of nard fragrant.
He called himself the fragrance of Christ, and he smelled within himself that divine, divinely radiant, royal grace.

And again he gave himself to others like a kind of free incense, whose fragrance, as lay in the power of those who received it, perfumed and illuminated according to the will of each person, those whom it either gave life or else put to death.

For if someone applies the same ointment to a beetle and to a dove, it does not have one and the same effect on each of them; rather, the dove becomes more alert and stronger through the fragrance of the ointment, while the beetle perishes.
Likewise the great Paul set that divine incense before everyone, and if someone was a dove,
like Titus and Silvanus and Timothy, he smelled the fragrance of that myrrh and advanced in all good things by becoming like him.
But if someone was a Demas or an Alexander or a Hermogenes, they could not bear to smell that incense of fasting and purity, and like beetles they were driven away from that fragrance.
For this reason he who breathed such fragrances said: "We are the fragrance of Christ among those being saved and among those perishing,
to some a scent from death to death, and to others a scent from life to life."
But if the nard of the Gospel also has some agreement with this bridal fragrance, let whoever wishes understand from what is written
what that "faithful, very costly nard" was, "which was poured on the head of the Lord and filled the whole house with fragrance."

And, as I suppose, the ointment is not separate from the ointment: the one that spreads the Bridegroom's fragrance over the bride, and the one in the Gospel that is poured on the Lord's head and fills with fragrance the house in which the Lord was dining.
For, as I suppose, by some spirit of prophecy that woman announced beforehand the mystery of his death, as the Lord testified when he said: "She has done it for my burial."
And the filling of the house with fragrance was a figure of the fragrance of the whole world and all the earth, as the Lord declared:
"Wherever this gospel is preached in the whole world, the fragrance of this myrrh will also be told along with it, and this will be done as a memorial of her."
Now therefore, since in the Song of Songs the nard spreads the fragrance of the Bridegroom over the bride,

while the ointment of the Gospel, which then filled the house, makes the whole body of the Church fragrant throughout all the earth and all the world, one fragrance is signified by both of these, and a shared unity is found.
The following saying presents the image of repose in the bridal chamber,
but in its interpretation and meaning it introduces a higher and more perfect philosophy and wisdom, the attainment of which is possible only for the perfect, for it says:
"A bound bundle of stacte is my kinsman to me; he shall rest between my breasts." They say
that worldly women are so eager that it is not only by outward [?] and adornments that they make themselves desirable and longed for by their husbands,
but they find another device as well, and make themselves fragrant by anointing themselves with certain perfumes and ointments,
so as to draw their husbands' desire all the more; and they hide certain bundles of perfumes inside their garments, which give off vapor and smoke full of fragrance and make the whole body fragrant.
For this reason this all-wise virgin says: My bundle, by which I make my body fragrant, hangs down from my neck to my breast.
And it is not any other of the perfumes, but the Lord himself, who became stacte; he lies in the bundle of my mind, and he rests in my heart, for the place,
the dwelling of the heart, is set between the breasts,

as those who know this by experience say; for this reason the bride says that she keeps her bundle where good things are treasured. And they also say that the "spring of heat," by which the constitution of our body is governed, is the heart, from which, in the manner of streams, the heat spreads through the veins and channels and is distributed through the whole extent of the body, and by this all the members of the body are warmed and enlivened, that is,
by that fire of the heart.

Now therefore, whoever receives the fragrance of God into the ruling part of his mind and shows his heart to be a [?] of such incense warms all the affairs of this world, as if they were limbs of a body, by the spirit dwelling in his heart. He lets not one of the limbs grow cold toward divine love, and he does not allow any defiled and impure stench of unseemly thoughts or deeds to touch that divine fragrance.
But let us go on to the words that follow and hear what that fruitful vine says about her fruits,
which are spread out to all the sides of the house of God and hang by the tendrils of love from that divine and immortal life, for she says:
"My kinsman is to me a budding cluster in the vineyards of Gaddi."
Who is so blessed? Or rather, who is so far beyond all blessedness as to look upon his own fruit and to see, in the cluster of his own soul, the Lord of the vineyard?

For behold how greatly she has grown, she who in her own nard recognized the fragrance of the Lord, who bound him on her conscience as a sweet-smelling stacte and enfolded him with her heart, so that the good ointment might remain with her forever without departing.
She becomes the mother of the divine cluster, which before the Passion was budding, that is, blossoming, but at the time of the Passion brought forth wine;
for the wine that gladdens our hearts was, after the dispensation of the Passion, called the blood of the grape, and truly became so.

And the delight of the cluster is understood in two ways: the one is seen in the flower, when it gladdens the sense of smell with fragrance, and the other in the fullness of the fruit, when through ripeness it gives the means to delight in eating or to brighten banquets with wine. Here the bride as yet brings forth only a flowering cluster, and she gives the name "budded" to its coming out, just now, from the flowering.
For the child who was born to us, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, "advanced in wisdom and stature and grace" in different ways among those who receive him,
for he is not seen equally in all, but according to the measure of the one into whom he enters and as that one who receives him has the power to contain him;
and this is shown by the tender infancy, the growth and the maturity that accord with the nature of the cluster, which is by no means seen in one form in the vineyard,
but from time to time changes its form, into flower, budding, ripeness and wine.
The vine therefore gives a promise through its fruit, which is not yet ready for pressing. It awaits the fullness of the times, yet it is not lacking in delight,
for instead of through eating, it gladdens the sense of smell with fragrance, and through the expectation of good things and the fragrance of hope it sweetens the senses of the soul.
For the undoubting and trustworthy hope of the graces to come becomes a divinely radiant delight to those who await them with patience.
So also is the budded cluster, for it promises us wine, yet it has not yet become wine, but through the flower, which is hope,
makes the grace to come trustworthy; and that "the increase of Gadi" signifies a fertile land, in which the vine that has been planted makes its fruit fair and sweet.
For this is what those who have experience of that region of Gadi say: that it is well-tempered and suited to the rearing of vines and clusters.
Therefore whoever has his own will united to the law of the Lord and exercises himself in it day and night becomes forever a tree of gladness, always in delight,
made rich by the streams of waters and bringing forth its fruit in its season.

Likewise the vineyard of the Bridegroom, planted in the place of Engedi, that is, planted in a rich place, means one watered and made to flourish in the depth of the mind by divine teachings. It brings forth that ripe cluster with beautiful blossoms, and it looks to its husbandman and planter. How blessed is such a cultivated work, whose fruit is made like the image of the Bridegroom!
For he himself is true light and true life and true righteousness, as Wisdom says, and everything else of this kind.

And when someone by his own deeds comes to resemble him who truly is, such a person beholds the cluster of his own mind and sees the bridegroom himself in it, through a radiant and undefiled life, and is seen in the light of truth.
Therefore that fruitful vine says: "My cluster, which blossoms and buds." He himself is the true cluster, who was hung upon the wood of the cross,
whose blood becomes drink and gives life to those who are saved and who rejoice,
through the same Christ Jesus himself, our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Heading text: 1:15 Behold, you are beautiful, my close one. Behold, you are beautiful. Your eyes are doves. 1:16 Behold, you are good, my kinsman, and beautiful;
over our bed is a shade. 1:17 The beams of our house are of fir, and our rafters are of cypress. 2:1 I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. 2:2
And as a lily among thorns, so is my close one among the daughters. 2:3. As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman among the sons.
Under his shade I longed and sat down; and his fruit is sweet to my palate. 2:4.
Bring me into the house of wine; set love in order upon me. 2:5.

Strengthen me with ointments. Surround me with apples, for I am wounded by love. 2:6. His left hand is upon my head, and his right hand shall embrace me. 2:7. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and the strengths of the field,
if you should rise and awaken love, until it pleases.

Now, it is said of those who refine gold by their craft that, if some corrupting matter has mixed with it and darkened the beauty of its brightness, they separate out the foulness by melting it in fire; and they do this not once but many times.

At each smelting they examine how much better than its first appearance the gold has become through one smelting after another. They do not stop purifying it from the harmful matter in the furnace until the very appearance of the gold itself testifies to its purity, spotlessness and brilliance.
But as for the reason why we have mentioned this before examining what has now been read, you will understand the force of these words from the words that follow.
Human nature was golden in color and pure in the beginning, and it shone with the likeness of that incorruptible good, but through the admixture of evil it became corrupted and blackened.
After this, as we heard from the bride at the beginning of the Song,
that it was blackened by faintheartedness in keeping the vineyard. To heal its ugliness, God, who governs all things in wisdom, did not contrive for it some new beauty that it did not have before,
but restored it to that original grace by melting it and by consuming that evil blackness in the furnace, and changed it to incorruption,
just as those skilled goldsmiths do: after the first melting they examine how much the beauty of the gold has increased and how much of the stain has been consumed by the fire.
And when they melt it again a second time, if its beauty is not perfected,
they perceive this and melt it again, until, by the keenness of their art and from experience, they recognize that it has reached sufficient loveliness.

So too here, the one who labors over that blackened gold of souls purified the soul and made it shine by healing remedies, as if by a kind of furnace, and above, as we read, he bore witness on its behalf to the beauty of a steed.
But now he reckons her goodness and loveliness as the beauty of a maiden, and says:
"Behold, you are beautiful, my close one. Behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves."

By these sayings the word teaches that the beginning and starting point of her goodness is this: that she has come close to the source of good things, as it says: "Behold, you are beautiful, my close one."
That is to say: You were not beautiful before for this reason, that you became estranged from that original beauty, and by drawing close to that wicked evil you were changed to ugliness.
And the meaning is this: since human nature was created free and self-governing, it is changed toward whichever side the inclination of its will turns.

For when it takes on the passion of anger, it becomes angry, and when desire overcomes it, desire bends it toward love of pleasure. Likewise fear and fearlessness, and the assault of all the passions, clothe it in the form of each particular passion.
Likewise with good deeds, such as long-suffering, purity, peace, freedom from anger, freedom from distress, courage and fortitude: when it has taken all of these into itself,

the tranquillity, imperturbability and calm of the soul show the form of each of them. And since nothing stands between virtue and vice except the will, the two cannot both be gathered together at once in one and the same thing,
For whoever separates himself from holiness will surely come to delight in an impure life.

And whoever has come to loathe the impure life has, by turning away from evil, set purity on its course. The same holds for all the others: the humble person has cast off arrogance, and the one who puffs himself up with insolence has put humility far from himself.

And what need is there to state each one individually, how, among things opposed in nature, separation from the one becomes the beginning and the essence of the other, since such was our will and it had the power to put on whatever form it might wish, from whatever source it might wish? The word speaks well to that adorned virgin, saying:
By separating from evil you have drawn near to me.
And when you drew near to that primal goodness, you too became good, and as from a mirror, you were adorned with my likeness.
For human nature is truly like a mirror because of its self-governing will, and it is changed according to whatever it wishes.

For if it wishes to be changed into gold, it becomes gold and shows the colour of that material through its form. And if it wishes to be made like some ugly thing, it takes on that thing's filthy and loathsome form as well,
that is, it depicts within itself the form of the frog, the toad, the centipede and other such ugly and loathsome things, if it sets one of them before itself as its model.

Therefore, since that purified soul has thrown evil behind its back, it has, according to the word, received the eye of the sun into itself, and has shone together with the light that shines forth within it.
For this reason the word says to her: Behold, you have become beautiful by drawing near to my light, and through that drawing near you have drawn to yourself the beauty of communion with me.
"Behold, you are beautiful, my close one." When he looked in this way and saw her goodness advanced and increased in beauty, he repeated the same word again and said: "Behold, you are beautiful."
But in the first instance he gave her the name "close one," whereas here he made her known by the form of her eyes and said: "Your eyes are doves."

Earlier, when she was likened to a mare, she received praise for her cheeks and neck, but now, when her own beauty has appeared, the grace of her eyes has become worthy of praise. And the praise of the eyes is that "your eyes are those of a dove," and the force of this saying is as follows:
In the pupils of pure eyes the faces of those looking at them are seen, and as those experienced in such matters say, whoever looks at any radiant and shining forms becomes wholly fastened upon them.
For this is how the eye accomplishes seeing, and therefore, as a figure of praise for the eyes and their beauty, the word gives them the name of doves.
For whatever form one looks at, one receives its likeness into oneself,
and whoever does not gaze upon flesh and blood, such a person gazes upon the spiritual life, as the Apostle says:
Whoever lives by the Spirit, and abides in the Spirit, and puts to death the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, such a person has become altogether and entirely spiritual, and not soulish or fleshly.

And thus the soul freed from carnal love is called to have the form of a dove in her eyes, which is the image of the spiritual life, shining forth in the eyes of the soul. Since, then, that pure eye of hers became receptive of the form of the dove, she was for this reason able to perceive the beauty of the bridegroom.

For behold, this is the virgin's first look toward the bridegroom, and now she perceives his form and his voice, once she has acquired the eyes of the dove and the very innocence of the dove and of its form,
"for no one can say 'Lord Jesus' except by the Holy Spirit," and she says: "Behold, you are good, my brother's son, and beautiful,"
for since I have reckoned nothing else as good, but have held in contempt all that I formerly thought to be good, no longer does the choosing of the good lead me astray,
as it did before, so that I would consider anything apart from you to be good: neither human praise, nor glory, nor distinction, nor worldly power.
For all these things, for those who are nailed to these visible things, are smeared over with an illusion of good, and they are not such as they make them imagine.

For how could that be good whose being is altogether invisible? For all the things honored in this world have their being only from the weakness and suddenness of those who possess them, and even that being is invisible and insubstantial and wholly foreign to truth.
But you are truly good, and not merely good, but the very essence of the good, you who always are, and are such

as you are. You neither blossom in seasons nor shed your flower in season, but with the endlessness of life that boundless beauty of yours increases along with you, whose name is love of humankind, you who have shone forth for us from Judah.
And that one, the Judean, is brother to the Gentiles gathered by you; hence she who longs for your glory rightly calls the manifestation of your divinity in the flesh "brother's son."

And then she added and said: "Upon our bed a shade," that is to say: I have known you, as far as human nature is able to know, you who became shady and a cool shade through the dispensation of the incarnation,
for you came, O good brother's son, and became a beautiful and shady covering for our bed;
for if you yourself had not overshadowed yourself and had not concealed those rays of divinity, which the eyes cannot bear, with that form of a servant, who could have endured your appearing,

"for there is no one who has seen the face of God and lived." You came to us, you who are beautiful in goodness, but in such a way as we were able to receive. You came and overshadowed the rays of divinity by clothing yourself with flesh.

For how could mortal and weak nature have contained the joining of union with you, who are unbearable to the eyes and unapproachable, if for these who sit in darkness and shadows that shadow of your flesh had not been made a mediator for the sake of the light of your incorporeal divinity?
And the bride calls "bed," and interprets figuratively, the mingling of human nature with divinity,
just as the great apostle betroths us to Christ as a holy virgin and becomes steward to the soul

And the joining of the two together and their becoming one flesh he names a great mystery, and he brings his discourse to completion with reference to the union of Christ and the Church, for when he had said that:
"The two shall be one flesh," he immediately added: "This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church." And likewise that virgin soul gave the name "bed" to the mystery,
This is the divine communion, and it could not have been brought about in any other way had the Lord not come to us under the shady covering of the flesh. He is not only the Bridegroom

but also the Builder. For he himself built a house among us, and he himself became the material of that building. He builds the roof of the structure and adorns the building with incorruptible materials.

For such are the cypress and the cedar, and the strength of their firmness is beyond all rotting: time does not overcome it, worms do not destroy it, and devouring creatures do not corrupt it. And of these, the cedar timbers make firm the span of the house.
And the cypress timbers, under the name of "rafters," beautify the built interior of the structure by being fitted onto it.
And their words are these: "The beams of our house are of cedar, and our rafters of cypress."
And the figure indicated by these trees is clear and evident to those

who understand the force of the composition of the words. In the Gospel the Lord gives the name "rain" to the onslaught of temptations of many kinds, and he says of the one who built his house well upon the rock that:
The rain came down and the winds blew and the rivers rose, and that house stood unharmed by their onslaught.
Because of this rain of evils, then, such beams are necessary for us,

which are the virtues, which because of their firmness and strength do not let the flow of temptations into themselves, and which rescue those who have fallen into temptations, leaving them untouched by evils.
And if we wish, let us learn this word more clearly in Ecclesiastes, for there it says that:
"Through sloth the building will sink low, and through idleness of hands houses will leak."
For just as, if the timbers that bear the roof are weak and thin,
And when the master of a house is negligent in building it, the roof is of no use to him when the rain drips down through it and soaks it,
for under the weight of the rain and the earth the roof is forced to sag. The weak timbers cannot hold out against it, and they cannot bear the weight of the roof.

so that it breaks down, and the water collected in the sagging part becomes the mother of a violent dripping, and the drips, according to the word of the Proverbs, drive a man out of his house on a day of rain.

And thus, through the figurative language of the proverbs, he commands us to remain unbent by the weight of temptations through the firmness of the virtues, lest we break down under the onslaught of the passions, and receive the drippings of such torrents into the depths of our soul, and destroy the treasure of our soul.
But these cedars of Lebanon, which the Lord planted, on which the birds raise their young and the nest of the heron is prepared,

These firs, then, which are the virtues, make firm that bridal house of rest. Upon them souls make their nests, like birds and sparrows that have flown up from the snares of the enemy and have been raised higher. Among them are counted also the nests of the herons, as Scripture testifies.

It is said of these birds that they loathe coupling. When, by the compulsion of nature, coupling is about to take place so that their seed may not be wiped out, they perform that hateful and forced union with a kind of distaste and turning away [?].
And, as I think, by the name of these birds the word figuratively teaches us purity. The bride, then, sees the coming of these birds in the ceiling of that undefiled bridal chamber.
She also sees the adornment of cypress, finely planed, joined together by firm fitting, and beautifying the bridal chamber, for she says:

"And our panels are of cypress." Now "panelling" is the name not only for the fitting together of coffers, but for the fastening of a whole ceiling with incorruptible, finely planed boards firmly joined together, which by various kinds of cutting and carving make that ceiling flowery.
What, then, do we learn from this? The cypress is by nature fragrant and incorruptible, and suited to every skill of craftsmen,
that is, to smoothing, fitting, cutting, carving and planing.
And, as I think, its interpretation teaches us this: that we should not carry out the virtues only inwardly in the soul, hidden and unseen,
but also that we should not neglect outward and visible good order. For it is right to purpose what is good before God and before men, and before God there is to be manifestation,
and toward men obedience, having a good testimony from those outside, shining with light by works before men, and walking becomingly toward those outside.

And these are those panels, made fragrant by Christ, of whom the cypress is a figure, carved by a beautiful way of life. Their fitting and joining, done well and with godly beauty, are known to that wise master builder Paul, as he says:
"Let all things be done among you in order and decently."
When this is carried out in this way, a growth of good comes about among us, and the fields of our nature bring forth that fragrant and pure flower,
which is the lily, whose natural brightness signifies the radiance of purity.
For the bride declares this about herself and says: After the shading of our bed by the bridegroom,

He who has overshadowed me with the shadow of the flesh, built me as his own house, fitted my roof with the cedars of the virtues and adorned my panelled ceiling with the fragrance of cypress — through him I have become a flower of the fields of nature,
surpassing in colour and fragrance those flowers that are so named, and I have sprung up as a flower of the valleys.
And the saying is this: "I am a flower of the field, a lily of the valleys."
True, then, truly, was our first consideration, for the soul, ordered from the breadth of the mind, was called the field of human nature. And we have understood it as a field for this reason,
For it is broad, able to receive many, various and countless understandings, deeds and teachings.

Therefore, according to the figure spoken of earlier, the soul cultivated by that Husbandman of our nature springs up as a fragrant, radiant and pure flower from the plains of our life; and this plain, even though, when compared
with the height of heaven and of the divine governance, it is called a valley, is still a plain, and the beauty planted in it is not prevented from being called a flower.
For this plant rises from the valley to a height, like the lily.
For when the shoot of the lily has risen from the root to a height over a long time, only then does the flower spring up at the top of the stem,
at no small distance from the earth, so that in that height it may remain pure of earthly matter.

Therefore the righteous eye has seen her either as already in bloom or as longing to bloom. The first saying points to both of these. Either she boasts that she has already blossomed, which is what she longs for, or she says that it is right
that she should become a flower through the wisdom of the Chief Husbandman and rise up beautifully, like a lily, from the valleys of human life. Or else she is about to do so,

to become, or indeed has become, that for which it longed. Well then did that righteous eye of the Bridegroom look upon that good desire which gazes toward him, and he judged it fitting that she should become a lily not choked by the thorns of the world,
which he named daughters, thereby silently indicating, as I suppose, those powers hostile to human life, whose father is given the name of inventor of evils; for he says:
"As a lily among thorns, so is my close one among the daughters."

But some have translated it thus, for in place of "close one" they wrote "sister." But you, consider to what height the God-loving soul of the virgin ascends. For her first ascent and height is likeness to that mare which overthrew the might of the Egyptians; and the second ascent is being close to him and acquiring the eyes of a dove; and now the third ascent is to be called no longer close one, but sister of the King, as he says:
"Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven, this is my brother and my sister and my mother." For since she became a flower, and no harm befell her from those thorny trials,
so that she became a lily, and since she forgot her people and her father's house and looked to the true Father,

she through whom she was also called the Bridegroom's sister. Through the Spirit of adoption she gained this divine kinship and was set free from fellowship with the daughters of the father of lies. She again rises higher than herself and sees certain mysteries with the eyes of a dove,
that is, with the eye of prophecy. And what she sees is this:
"As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my brother's son among the sons." What then is this that she has seen?
That is, following the usual way of the Scriptures, she gives the name "forest" to human life with its many material things, which has made the manifold materials of the passions spring up.
In it the destroying beasts make their lairs and hide. By their nature they are inactive in the light and the sun,

but in their darkness they show their wickedness. As the prophet says: after the sun has set and night has come on, the beasts of the forest come out of their dens. And since the boar of the forest has ravaged the good vineyard of human nature, as the prophet says:

"The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the fierce wild beast has grazed upon it." For this reason the apple tree springs up in the forest. Because it is a tree, it signifies participation in human nature,
for he was tested in every way, in complete likeness [to us], except for sin.

But by bringing forth such fruit, by which the senses of the soul are sweetened, it surpasses the order of the forest by its difference, even more than the lily does in relation to thorns; for the lily offers delight only of sight and fragrance,
but the apple gladdens three senses, that is, the eyes by the beauty of its appearance, the sense of smell by the fragrance of its scent, and the taste by the sweetness of its flavor.
So the bride did well to see the portion allotted to her by the King. For he becomes light for us who see, fragrance for those who smell, and life for those who eat, as the Gospel says:
"Whoever eats shall live." But human nature, made perfect by virtue, becomes only a flower. It does not feed the one who tends it, but only adorns itself,
for it is not that he lacks our good things, but we are in need of his, as the prophet says: "You have no need of my good things."

For this reason the purified soul sees the Bridegroom as an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so that he may graft onto himself all those wild branches of the forest and, by their bringing forth the same kind of fruit, make them transformed.

And just as we say of those daughters who were likened to thorns, as daughters of the deceitful father, who sprang up together with that flower, that they will at some time be changed into lilies, so also here concerning those sons
whom it likens to the trees of the forest: it is not speaking of friends of the Bridegroom,
but of adversaries, who were sons of darkness and children of wrath, and whom, through that sharing in the fruit, he has shown forth as sons of light and children of peace.
For this reason that soul trained in its senses says: "His fruit is sweet to my palate." And understand the fruit to mean teaching, as the prophet says,
for "Your words are sweet to my palate, more than honey to my mouth." "As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman among the sons.
Under his shade I desired, and I sat down; and his fruit is sweet to my palate." For truly the senses of the soul are sweetened by the Word at that time,
when the shade of the apple tree shields us from the heat of trials, and the burning of the sun, blazing upon our bare heads, can no longer scorch us.
Otherwise it is impossible to find rest under the shade of that tree of life, unless desire directs our soul toward it.
Do you see why the power of desire has been implanted in you? It is so that it may kindle in you the longing for that apple, whose delight becomes manifold for those who draw near to it.

For it refreshes the eyes with the goodness of its beauty, the sense of smell with the fragrance of its scent, the body with nourishment, and the mouth with sweetness; and it gives relief from the heat and a seat of shade, on which the soul sits that has rejected the seat of the lawless." And then it says:
"Bring me into the house of wine; set love in order over me.
Strengthen me with ointments. Surround me with apples, for I am wounded by love."

Ah, how the soul that has been likened to a horse runs on this divine racecourse! How, with fine and orderly steps, it advances forward and does not turn back, however many good things it has met with on the way up!

And it is still thirsty, and the burning of its thirst is so great that the mixing bowl of wisdom is not enough for it, nor has it considered pouring that whole bowl into its mouth to be enough to satisfy its thirst,
but it seeks to be brought into the very house of wine and to put its mouth to the very winepresses
that produce that sweet wine, and to see the cluster of grapes that is pressed in those winepresses, and the vine that makes such a cluster grow, and the worker of that true vine,
who so cultivates that sweet and beautiful cluster. To interpret each of these is superfluous, since their figurative application is clear and evident.

And undoubtedly it wishes to see that mystery as well: how the bridegroom's garment is made crimson by the pressing of the winepress, concerning which the prophet says: "Why is your garment crimson, and your tunic like those of the treaders of the winepress?"
For these and such things it longs to enter inside that house in which the mystery of the wine is seen.
And when it has thus entered inside, it is renewed still more, for it seeks the setting in order of love.
"But love is God," as John testifies, and David declared the soul's submission to him to be life. Therefore,
since it has entered the house of wine, it says: Make me submit to love; that is to say: "Set love in order over me."

For however one takes this turn of phrase, the same meaning is found both ways, whether someone submits to love or love subjects him and is set over him. Or else this saying teaches us some other, deeper sense: how we ought to love God, and how others.
For if, according to the word of the Apostle, everything must be done in an orderly and beautiful manner, must this not all the more be done in an orderly way?
For Cain would not have been condemned for dividing wrongly if, along with offering rightly, he had also kept the proper order,

which is to set aside what is for one's own use and to offer to God. For he ought to have offered the sacrifice to God from the first fruits and to have been nourished himself from what remained; but he sated himself from the most valuable portions and entertained God with the remainder.
It is necessary, then, to know the order of love,
which the Law teaches us: how one ought to love God, and how one's neighbor, and how one's spouse, and how an enemy, so that the order of love may not be carried out in disorder and perversion.
For God must be loved with all the heart and with all the strength and with all the soul and with all the mind and understanding,

and the neighbor as oneself; and the spouse, if she is pure in soul, as Christ loved the Church, but if she is inferior and subject to passion, as one's own flesh, as the teacher Paul commands in these matters;
and as for the enemy, one should not repay evil for evil, but should cover injustice with good deeds.
But now among most people love is seen mixed up and disordered, and through an unfitting exchange it is practiced in error.
If such people attain possessions and spouses and honors, they are kindled toward them like fire and love them with all their soul and all their strength,
so that, if anything should be required, they would give up even their own life for them; but God they love only as they see fit,
and to the neighbor they would hardly show even the love prescribed for enemies, and their love for those who hate them is this: that they repay evil with a worse evil.
So she says: "Set love in order upon me," that is: offer to God as much as you have, and toward all others do not depart from the proper measure. Or else this saying gives us to understand this:
that since I was made beloved in that first creation, and through disobedience was counted among the enemies,
and now I stand once more in that same grace and through love have been united to the King, confirm upon me the ordering of this grace unchangeably, you,
you friends of the Bridegroom, and through reverence and striving make the inclination of my mind toward the good firmer and more zealous.
And having said this, she again hastens toward the higher part, and seeks her establishment in good firmness by means of ointments, and says:
"Establish me with ointments." Oh, these marvelous pillars and new supports and foundations! For how can ointments become the pillars of a house,
or how can the floor of a house be made firm by fragrance?

or else it is plain and evident that the substance of the virtues, which takes many forms among us, is called and named according to the different kinds of struggle. For virtue is not only seeing the good and sharing in what is better, but also steadfastness and constancy in good things. So whoever wishes to be sustained with ointments
is seeking the steadfastness that comes from the virtues. For virtue is called an ointment for this reason:

because it is far removed from all the stench of sins. It would not be surprising if someone marveled at how these sayings fit together, and at what kind of materials she seeks to strew her house with:
not brambles, thorns, [?] and reeds. Or rather, as the Apostle says, not wood, reeds and straw, the materials from which perishable and decaying houses are built.

Instead, the apple becomes what this house is strewn and bedded with, as she says: "Bed me with apples," or else, "Surround me with apples," so that this fruit may be everything to her in every way: beauty, fragrance, sweetness,
food, coolness through its shade, a seat of rest, a pillar of strength, and a covering for the roof,

For as beauty is perceived through desire, and as ointment perfumes the sense of smell, and as food fattens the flesh and sweetens the taste, and as shade cools the heat, and as a seat gives rest to the weary, and as the roof
of a house becomes a covering for those who are in it, and as a pillar keeps a thing from falling, and as a shining apple adorns the roof.

And what sight more beautiful and more fragrant could anyone devise than the apple, when they are laid out one beside another on some level place and, blooming with color and whiteness, adorn the sight?
And if it were possible for it to rise above green fields and be viewed by looking down from above, what would be more splendid than such a sight,
which is not impossible for the desire of the virtues,
for the composition of this fruit is not heavy, nor does it drag down to the earth, but its impulse rises by nature toward the height.
For virtue is from above and looks toward heaven; hence the bride has desired the beauty of such an apple, so that with it she may adorn the roof of her house.
And as I suppose, the aim of this saying is not to display its coloring as a desirable sight by means of that roofing with apples,
for what progress toward virtue would come from this, if its figurative language did not convey to us some understanding of spiritual benefit? What, then, is it that we understand?
It is this: he who sprang up in the forest of our nature out of love for humankind became an apple by taking on flesh and blood,
for the coloring of that fruit resembles both of these,
for by its whiteness it presents the appearance of flesh, and by its color it displays the likeness of blood.
Hence, when the soul delighted by divine graces desires to see the roof of the house, its parable gives us this understanding.
For looking toward the height and beholding the apples is advancement, through the teachings of the Gospel, toward the heavenly way of life, which he who comes from above,
and who is above all,

showed us by his incarnation, and he gave himself to us as the model of all good ways of life, as he says: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart." And the apostle presents this same aspect of humility and teaches us,
for it is possible through a single understanding to confirm all the teachings of truth, for to those who look toward heaven he speaks thus:

"Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus." Being the image of God, he did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself and took the form of a servant. He came into the world in flesh and blood, and instead of the joy set before him, sharing in our lowliness, he willingly endured crucifixion and death. That is why the bride says:
"Bed me with apples," so that I may always look on high and contemplate the forms of good things that the immortal Bridegroom revealed.

These are meekness and freedom from anger; bearing no grudge against enemies; love toward those who cause distress; kindness toward the ungrateful; and fasting, purity and long-suffering, untainted by any vainglory or worldly temptation.
Having said this, she goes on to praise the archer's skill and how well he aimed his arrow at her, and she says: "I am wounded by love."
With these words she shows that the arrow is fixed in the depths of her heart, and the one who shot the arrow is love.
And love is God, as the divine Scriptures teach us. He sends his chosen arrow, the Only-begotten God, to those who are being saved, armed with the life-giving Spirit as its three-edged arrowhead.
Understand faith as the arrow, so that in whomever it is fixed, it may bring in the archer along with the arrow, as the Lord says: "I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him."
So the soul, lifted up by divine ascents, sees within herself that sweet arrow of love which wounded her heart, and she boasts of such a wound and says:
"I am wounded by love." O this good injury and sweet wound, through which life comes to dwell within, and the cut made by the arrow opens itself as a kind of door and entrance,
for as soon as she received the arrow of love, the archery was immediately changed into the joy of a wedding.
This is clear from practice: how the hands use the bow and how they divide the work between them. The left holds the bow,
while the right draws the bowstring together with the arrow, and the grip of the left directs the arrow toward the target.

Therefore she who a little earlier became [?] of the arrow now sees herself in the archer's hands in place of the arrow. One part of this arrow is held by the right hand and the other part by the left. But since the bridal order has changed the spectacle to its own order and form,
the left hand no longer holds the arrowhead, nor does the right hand hold the other part,
so that her soul would be in the hands of the Mighty One, directed toward the heavenly target,

but in place of the arrowhead the left hand touches the head, and the right hand the remaining limbs. And as I think, through the twofold figures of those divine ascents this teaching at once sets before us a twofold philosophy and shows us that the same one is both our Bridegroom and our archer.

He uses that purified soul both as a bride and as an arrow: as an arrow, he sends it toward the good target, and as a bride, he receives it into communion with eternal incorruption, and with his right hand he grants it length of days and years of life,
but by the left hand he bestows the riches of the eternal good things and the kingdom in his presence, from which those who seek the glory of this world are justly cast out. Therefore she says:
"His left hand is upon my head, and his right hand shall receive me."

That is to say: his left hand is upon my head, for by it the arrow is directed toward the target; but may his right hand draw me to himself and lead me, and make me light of spirit [?] to run the heavenly course, so that I may also ascend there and not be separated from the archer, so that I may at once be ready for the target and also rest inseparably in the hands of the archer.
The book of Proverbs clearly tells us the character and work of these hands, and says: "Length of times and years of life are in his right hand, and in his left hand are glory and riches."
And then she turns her word to the daughters of the heavenly Jerusalem.

That word is a supplication spoken with an adjuration, that they should always increase and multiply love, until he fulfills in deed his own will, he who wills the life of all people and their coming to the knowledge of the truth. And the word is as follows:
"I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field, if you should arise and awaken love until he wills."
Swearing is a word that confirms the truth by means of oneself. And the matter of an oath is twofold:
when someone either himself assures his hearers of the truth, or by putting others under oath compels them to do nothing falsely. That is to say:
"The Lord swore to David in truth, and he will not slight him." Here, then, he confirms the trustworthiness of the promise with an oath.
But when Abraham was concerned about a wife for his only-begotten son, he commanded his servant
not to join to Isaac in marriage any of the Canaanites, who had been condemned to servitude, so that mixture with the tribes of servitude should not corrupt the nobility of the lineage,

but that he should take a wife for his son from the land of his fathers, from his kindred and tribe. So that the servant would not neglect his command, he bound him with an oath, so that he would carry out his every command concerning his son.

The matter of the oath is therefore twofold, as we said. In this place, the soul that has reached such a great height, as great as we described above, tells the souls it has taught about progress toward perfection,

not to persuade those it has met of its own truthfulness by the oath, but to direct them by the adjuration toward a virtuous life, so that until that time they may keep their love wakeful and unsleeping,
until that good will of his is accomplished,
that is, the life of all and their coming to the knowledge of the truth.
And just as the swearing there was done by the loins [?] of the patriarch, so here it is done by the powers and strengths of the field, for she says:
"I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field, if you should arise and awaken love, until it pleases."

Among these words, then, we must inquire and examine first what the field is, and next what the power and strength of the field are, and whether these differ from one another, or whether both signify one and the same power.
And again, what is the arising, and what is the awakening of love? For the meaning of "until it pleases" has been made clear to us by what was said above.
This, then, is known to all: that by the field the Lord signifies this world in the Gospel. But that "the form of this world is passing away,"
and that nothing is firm in this unstable nature, is clear from the loud proclamation of Ecclesiastes,
who gave the name of vanity to everything visible and transient. What, then, is the power of such a field, which is this world?
Or what is the strength, the mention of which makes the commandment inviolable through the adjuration of the daughters of Jerusalem?
For if we look to the simple words and suppose that there is some power or strength in such things, Ecclesiastes does not accept it,
but refutes such a supposition, since he declares everything visible and perishable to be vain; for what is vain is without being, and what is without being has by nature no power.

But perhaps, from the plural expression of "powers," some sense may be found that reveals the meaning of these sayings? For we have learned such a distinction from the holy Scriptures concerning names of this kind: when they speak of power in the singular,
the understanding of such a word is raised up to the Lord, but when they speak of it in the plural, they indicate the nature of the angels.
And understand it in this way: "Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God." In this place it has told us in the singular concerning God. "Bless the Lord, all his powers."
Here, by speaking of "powers" in the plural, it signified the intelligent natures of the angels,

while the mention of "powers and strengths" is a reinforcement of the expression and has the same force. For such is the custom of the Scriptures: by joining together two words whose force is one, to show more firmly and to confirm that of which they are speaking; as when it says, "Lord, my power, Lord and my strengthener,"
the meaning of these two words is one, but by this extension it, as it were, reinforces and adorns the structure of the speech.
Now, then, the mention of "powers" in the plural and the addition of "strengths" lead the minds of the hearers to examine the nature of the angels.
Therefore this adjuration, which confirms the words and is performed by the teacher toward the souls, was not made with respect to this transient world,

but with respect to that world which does not pass away and to the nature of the angels, to whom he commands them to look, so that by that model he may establish in them the steadfastness and firmness of virtuous conduct.
for since a life like that of the angels has been promised to human beings after the resurrection, and the one who promised does not lie, it is fitting and just
that we should also change our life in this world to be like the life we await, and not be conformed to this world, but even though we are alive in the flesh and live in this field of the world,
we should not live carnally or be nailed to the material things of the world; rather, let this life of the world be for us a training for that life which does not pass away.
Therefore the bride, by an oath, confirms the souls who have become disciples, so that their way of life, conducted in this world,
may look toward the incorporeal powers and, through freedom from passion, may become like the purity of the angels.
for in this way love is awakened, and in this way it is raised up,

which means being lifted up, always increasing, and advancing toward what is higher, and carrying out that good will of God on earth as it is in heaven; that is, the angels' freedom from passion being brought about among us as well. This is what we have understood from this saying, that:
"I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and the strengths of the field, if you should rise up and awaken love, until it pleases."

But if some other explanation should be found that comes closer to the truth we are seeking, let us accept that grace and give thanks to the one who reveals hidden mysteries by the Holy Spirit through Christ Jesus
our Lord, to whom glory is fitting forever and ever. Amen.

The heading of this discourse: 2:8. The voice of my kinsman! Behold, he comes leaping on the mountains and running on the hills. 2:9. My kinsman is like a gazelle or a young deer on the mountains of Bethel.
Behold, he stands behind our wall, and he looks through the window and looks down through the lattices. 2:10.
My kinsman answers and says to me: Arise, come, my close one, my beautiful one, my dove. 2:11. For behold, the winter has passed, the rain has ceased and gone its way. 2:12.
And the flower has appeared in our land. The time of pruning has come. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. 2:13.

The fig tree has put forth its blossom; the vines are in flower, they have given their fragrance. Arise, come, my close one, my beautiful one, my dove. 2:14. Come, you yourself, my dove, under the shelter of the rock, near the wall.
Show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful. 2:15.
Catch for us the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, for our vineyards are in flower. 2:16.
My kinsman is mine and I am his, he who shepherds among the lilies. 2:17. Until the day passes and the shadows draw on,
turn back and be like, my kinsman, a gazelle or a young deer on the mountains full of ravines.

Now, what has been set before us from this reading of the wise words of the Song of Songs both leads us to desire the understanding of those surpassing good things and spreads sorrow over our souls, because we despair of attaining the understanding of things that cannot be attained.

For who would not be distressed on seeing that the soul, exalted by so many ascents of love and purified by participation in good things, according to the word of the Apostle no longer thinks that she has attained what is sought, even though we were contemplating those former heights which we mentioned above, and were calling her blessed for that exaltation,
