when she discerned that sweet apple and distinguished it from the unfruitfulness of the forest trees, and desired its shade, and was made glad by tasting it, and entered into the treasuries of joy.
And he calls joy wine,

which gladdens the heart of those who receive it. And as one made subject to love, she was strengthened by ointments and surrounded with apples, and she received that arrow of love into her heart; and again, in the hands of the archer she herself became that arrow, and by the hands of the mighty one she was directed toward that target of truth.
Seeing this and things like it, I supposed that through such great heights she had reached the summit of blessedness. But now, as I see, those former advances are only the beginnings of the ascent.
For she gives to all those heights the name, not of open vision and attainment of the good and the truth, but of the voice of the Desired One,
represented through the forms of hearing, and not known through contemplation and making glad.
And if she was so greatly exalted, as we hear of the great Paul's exaltation up to the third heaven,

and still has not reckoned herself to have openly attained what is sought, what then shall we do, or where shall we place ourselves, we who have not even drawn near to the courtyard of inaccessible understandings? But it is fitting
that from her very own words we should see how difficult it is to attain what is sought, for she says:
"The voice of my kinsman!" She presents neither form, nor image, nor face that would make known the one sought,
but a voice, which suggests doubt about the speaker rather than confirmation of who he is. And that this saying resembles a likeness, and not undoubting full assurance and attainment,
is clear from this: she does not establish her word upon one thought,

nor does she contemplate one form, but she shifts toward many visions and supposes that she sees now one form, now another. And that she does not remain fixed at all on one face, her words make known, for she says:
"Behold, this one comes", not standing, nor waiting, so that by standing he might be revealed to the one contemplating him,
but he snatches the sight of himself away from the beholder before she has fully contemplated him, as she says: "Leaping upon the mountains and running over the hills."
And at one time he is taken to be a gazelle and at another a fawn, for she says: "My kinsman is like a gazelle and a fawn of the deer on the mountains of Bethel."
In this way, always being tested, it changes from one form into another. And this is
what cuts off my hope of understanding it clearly, because of the simple way it is spoken and the depth of its meaning, and it confines my mind. Yet through hope in God, who gives the word
to those who preach by the power of God, let us not be negligent, but let us connect the arrangement and ordering of the passages now read with those examined before.
For it says: "The voice of my brother's son!" And immediately it added: "Behold, here he comes."
And what is it that we understand from these words, except that these sayings foresee the dispensation of God the Word made manifest through the Gospel,
which was first preached by the prophets, but was revealed by the coming of the Lord in the flesh?
For the divine voice bears witness through deeds, and the fulfillment follows the word of the promise, as the prophet testifies: "As we have heard, so also have we seen."
And here it says: "The voice of my brother's son!" This is what we have heard. And again: "Behold, here he comes." And this is what we have seen with the eye.
"In many parts and in many ways God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets." This is the hearing of that voice. "But in the last days he spoke to us through the Son."
And this is what is said: "Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains and running upon the hills."

Fittingly and suitably, by a certain appropriate reasoning, he is likened to a gazelle and to a young hart. Likewise, in another way again, the gazelle signifies the swift sight of the All-Seeing One,

for they speak of the exceedingly swift sight of this animal, from which fact it has received its name. For "gazelle" is interpreted as "swift-seeing," and likewise God is called All-Seeing because he beholds and sees all things.
And "seeing all things" is the interpretation of "God."
And since God, who came into the world to overthrow the opposing powers, appeared in the flesh, he is for this reason likened to a gazelle, who looked down from heaven to earth, and to a fawn,
who takes hold of mountains and hills by running; that is, he trampled and destroyed the heights of the wickedness of the demons.
And he calls "mountain" that which is shaken by his strength and cast into the heart of the seas, concerning which the Lord said to the disciples:
"If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain" (and by this word he indicated that evil spirit

which they were not able to cast out) "'Be uprooted from here and fall into the sea.'" And since it is a property of the nature of fawns to destroy reptiles and snakes, and to drive them away by their snorting breath and the vapor of their sweat,

for this reason he is likened to a gazelle because of his seeing all things, and to a young hart as the trampler and destroyer of venomous and opposing things, which figurative speech has named mountain and hill.
So then the voice of the Bridegroom came through the prophets, in whom God spoke. And after the voice came the Word, and he trampled the opposing mountains and crushed those assailing hills,
which are the apostate powers, and he ground them fine like dust,

That is, those who are greater than them in evil and those who are lesser. This is what the distinction between mountains and hills signifies, for both the more evil and the lesser are equally trampled by the power and authority of the one who walks on the asp and the viper and tramples the lion and the dragon, and likewise snakes and scorpions,
which apparently signify the lesser ones. It is as if someone were to say that, among the people who followed the Lord, the most evil demons were counted as mountains,
as happened in the country of the Gerasenes, and other such demons who rose up and exalted themselves against human nature,
among whom there were mountains and hills, lesser and greater. But the fawn of the deer, the one who confirms [?] natures,
when he gave the disciples authority to trample on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy,

trampled all of these alike and ran upon them in godly beauty, as upon mountains and hills, so that through this the wealth of those exalted by the virtues might be revealed, and so that they might no longer be darkened by the hills and heights of wickedness.
For the mountains of Bethel, by the interpretation of this name, signify a lofty life that imitates the heavens,
for this word is translated from the Hebrew language as "house of God"; hence it says: "upon the mountains of Bethel."
This was seen by the purified and foreseeing eye of the spirit, which accompanied those divine leapings accomplished upon the opposing hills.

And concerning what was to come in the last times, it speaks thus as of something already accomplished, and it contemplates in hope, as something already done, that grace which is awaited as trustworthy and undoubted.
For it says that he who with that beautiful haste "was leaping upon the mountains and running upon the hills"

shows himself to us standing, having arrived inside the wall, and he converses with her through the windows of the lattices. And the saying is this: "Behold, this one stands behind our wall, and looks through the window, and peers down through the lattices."

Now the coarse and bodily form of what has been said is this: the one who is outside converses through the window with the bride who is inside the house, and although a wall separates the two, the communion of speech becomes unhindered,

for the head looks down through the window, and from the viewing-place of the lattices the eye gazes inward through the narrowness of the windows. But the figurative contemplation accords with the sense of the things examined earlier.
For this word, by a certain way and sequence, brings human nature into intimacy with God, for first it enlightens it through the prophets and then through the commandments of the law,

For by the window that lets in the light we understand the prophets, and by the lattice, the composition of the commandments of the Law. And through both of these the radiance of the true light enters among us. And after this comes the shining forth of the perfect light, when that true light appears to those sitting in darkness and shadow, by its mingling with our nature. First, then, the lights of the prophetic and legal commandments, which we have understood as the window and the lattice, illuminate the soul and bring us desire and longing to see the Sun of righteousness openly, and after this that longing is fulfilled in deed. Let us hear, then, what kind of words he speaks to the Church, he who for the moment has not yet come within the wall but still converses with her through the windows that admit the light, for he says:
"My kinsman answers and says to me: Arise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove.
For behold, the winter has passed, the rain has ceased and gone.
The flower has appeared in our land, the time of pruning has arrived. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.

The fig tree has put forth its blossom. The vines are in flower, they have given their fragrance." Oh, how brilliantly the creator of spring depicts for us the grace of spring, he to whom David says: "Summer and spring you created,"

he who dispels the gloom of winter and says that the [?] of winter and the unpleasantness of the rains have passed, and who displays the beauty of the gardens and of the fields overspread with flowers.
And about the flowers it says that, along with it, they have reached the time of pruning,

so as to stir up the desire of garland-makers, perfume-mixers, and all who gather flowers, and so that at that time the word [?] may be made sweet by the voices and songs of the birds that call from the woods, when the sweet voice of the turtledove coos and delights the ears.

And he mentions the fig tree and the vine and points to the delight that is to come from them, so that by their flowering he may gladden the sense of smell. Thus, then, the discourse is adorned with the depiction of spring and is graceful, for it casts away gloomy things and is made beautiful by those desirable descriptions.

But, as I think, it is right that our discourse should not be spent among these brilliant images, but that by these words, simply set forth, our understanding should be directed toward the power of the mystery, and that the treasure of those mighty mysteries should be revealed,
which is hidden in these words. And what, then, is this of which we speak?
Human nature was once frozen with the ice of idolatry, and from the changeable motion of human beings it had been changed into the nature of those motionless objects of worship, as it has been said:
"Those who make them shall become like them, and all who trust in them."
And this befell it fittingly, for just as those who look toward the true God receive within themselves the likeness of the divine nature, so too those who were nailed to the vanity of idols
become like that vanity of theirs and are changed into stone and wood instead of human beings.
And since it had turned to stone through the service of idols, and was frozen and motionless,

for this reason the Sun of righteousness dawned in that evil winter, and springtime spread abroad with the blowing of the Spirit, which melted such ice, and by spreading its rays it warmed the whole world,

so that humanity, which had been turned to stone by ice, when warmed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, might thaw, and by the heat of the Word might once again become living water and flow to eternal life, as it says:
"His wind shall blow and the waters shall flow," "who turned the rock into a pool of waters and the uncut rock into springs of waters,"
which the Baptist indicated still more clearly when, preaching to the Jews, he said:
"God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham," and to make them his imitators through the virtues.

This, then, the Church hears from the Word, and through the prophetic windows and the lattices of the law she receives the light of truth, while that figurative wall of teaching, I mean of the law, still stands,
which had a shadow of things to come and of those good things, and not the very image of the realities, and behind which the truth stood close to the figure,

the truth which first, through the prophets, made the light of the Word shine upon the Church, but afterward, by the revelation of the Gospel, made the whole illusion of the shadows of the figure vanish,
and through which the dividing wall was dissolved and the air of the house was joined with the light of the ether, so that illumination through windows would no longer be needed,

but so that the very light of truth itself, by the lights of the Gospel, might illuminate everything within her. For this reason the Word, who raises up the fallen, calls out to the Church through those luminaries and says to her: "Arise," that is, from your fall,
you who fell through the bitterness of sin, you who stumbled because of the serpent, were struck to the ground, and plunged into the fall of disobedience.

"Arise," as I command you; yet it is not enough for you merely to be raised from the fall, but come to me as well, by progress in good and by living virtuously and without blemish, as we have learned concerning the paralytic.

For the Word not only raised up that paralyzed burden of the bed, but also commanded him to walk, which signified advancing toward what is better and growing through the movement of good deeds, as it says here too:
Arise and come. O the power of the command!
Truly the voice of God is a voice of power, as the Psalmist says: "Behold, he will give forth his voice, a voice of power," and:
"He spoke and they came to be; he himself commanded and they were created."
Behold, now too he said to her who lay prostrate: "Arise!" and "Come!"

And at once the command became deed, for swiftly, as she received the power of the word, she both rose and came forward and drew near to the light, as she is attested by the very one who calls her, for he says: "Arise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove."
What is this orderliness of the discourse, and how one thing follows upon another, and how are the sense and force of the sequence of these words fitted together and linked like a golden chain?
For it hears the divine command and is strengthened by the word, and it rises and comes forward and draws near, and is given the names "beautiful" and "dove."
For how is it possible for an image in a mirror to become beautiful unless it receives the form of some beautiful image?

Therefore the mirror of human nature also could not become good at first, but only when it drew near to the good and was changed into the image of the divine beauty. For just as it had the form of the serpent as long as it lay upon the earth and gazed at it,
in the same way, once it rose up and set itself face to face with that good and kindly countenance and cast evil behind its back,
it becomes the image of whatever it sees.

But he sees that firstborn beauty, and that beauty is a dove; so as soon as it drew near to the light, it became light. By that light I mean the one through which it was changed into the beauty of the dove, that dove whose form revealed the coming of the Holy Spirit.

This, then, is what the Word called her, and this is the name he gave her: fair because of her nearness, and a dove because of her beauty. After this he goes on to tell her that the winter that chills souls is no more, for frost cannot hold out against brightness, nor cold against heat.
For behold, the winter has passed; the rain has ceased and gone.
For it presents evils under many names and, in keeping with their many deeds, also the name that fits the lawless one,
for the same thing is winter and rain and dripping, and the form, activity and name proper to every kind of trial are found in it.
For in winter the flourishing beauty of the trees, with which they were naturally adorned through their leaves and fruit, withers, for it casts this off and mingles it with the soil.
And the song [?] of the sweet-speaking birds falls silent. The swallow flees, the nightingale withdraws and grows quiet, and the turtledove becomes a stranger to its nests.
And everything comes to resemble the gloom of death. The meadow dies, the shoot falls asleep, the vine is stripped bare, and like bones
stripped of flesh, so the branches, stripped of leaves, become ugly and unpleasant to look at in place of their former beauty.
And what could anyone say of the violent sufferings that occur in the sea in the winter season, how it boils up from the depths and raises its waves on high in the likeness of mountains and hills?
And how it charges at the dry land [?] like a warrior, and falls upon the cliffs and beats the shores, and with wave upon wave, as with the blows of siege engines, shatters the rocks.
But you, understand these sufferings of winter, and transform all such things into divine figurative interpretation.

What is signified by the withering of the flowers in winter, the falling of fruit and leaf from the trees, the silencing of the sweet-voiced birds, the roaring of the sea from its waves, its moaning and its exultation, and the rain and the dripping and the departure of the rain?

Indeed, through all these things the figures of these matters depict for us the voluntary and spiritual winter, and even if the word does not interpret them one by one, the force and meaning of each of them is not unknown to the hearers.

And how human nature blossomed in the beginning, while it was in paradise and was nourished by the water of its spring and blossomed, when, instead of leaves, the fruit of immortality adorned humanity!
But when the winter of disobedience dried up its root,
that flower fell and was mingled with the earth, and it was stripped of its immortal beauty, and that flower and meadow of the virtues of the love of God withered through the increase of lawlessness.
From this, the various passions of the opposing spirits rose up among us like fierce waves, and through them that evil ruin of souls comes about. But when the Creator of the spring of souls came,
he who saw that sea stirred up at that time by the evil wind,
he rebuked the unclean spirits as well, and commanded the sea: "Be silent and shut your mouth!"

And he changed everything to calm, and our nature began to blossom again and to be made beautiful again by its own flowers. The flowers of our life are the virtues, which blossom now and will yield fruit in their own time.

And for this reason the Word says: "The winter has passed, the rain has ceased and gone, the flower has appeared in our land. The time of plucking has come." So it is saying: Do you see this paradise, blossoming with virtues?
Do you see purity, which is that radiant and fragrant lily?
Do you see the rose of modesty and reverence? Do you see the violet of the fragrant ointments of Christ? Why then do you not weave a crown from these?
This is the time in which it is fitting to pluck and weave spiritual crowns and to be adorned, for the time of their gathering has come.
To this the voice of the turtledove bears witness to you, that is, "the voice of one crying in the wilderness," who is John, that turtledove of the wilderness,
for he is the forerunner of this radiant spring, who showed people those good flowers of virtue, and to those who wished to gather them
he pointed out beforehand the flower that came up from the roots of Jesse, the Lamb of God

who takes away the sins of the world, and he taught repentance of sins and virtuous conduct. For it says: "The voice of the turtledove was heard in our land." Perhaps it gives the name "land" to those brought up in evil, whom the Gospel calls tax collectors and prostitutes,
among whom the voice of John was heard and who received his preaching; but among those who did not receive it, it was not even heard.

As for what is said of the fig tree, that "it has put forth its early figs," let us understand that saying in this way: the fig tree, by its heat, draws up to an exceptional degree the moisture that lies in the depths, and since its core is filled with abundant sap,

the nature of the plant, by necessity, through the melting of the moisture within it, pours out that useless, thick sap from its tips, and it does this many times, until in its season it produces purified fruit, fit for food, separated from that useless richness.
So what the fig tree puts forth before that sweet and complete fruit, in the likeness of fruit, is given the name "early fig." If anyone ever wishes,
it can even be eaten; yet it is not itself the fruit, but becomes the beginning of the fruit.
And whoever sees it will undoubtedly also expect fruit at some time, for those green figs, whose putting forth it speaks of concerning the fig tree, become harbingers of the sweet figs.

Since the Word has depicted a spiritual spring for the bride, and this season stands between two seasons, the winter of grief and the summer of receiving fruits, it therefore openly announces the good news of the departure of evils,
but it shows the fruits of virtue as not yet perfected, and instead keeps silent about them until the proper time, when summer and the autumn harvest arrive.

And I know that you are not ignorant of the Lord's saying that was foreshadowed by summer, for summer is the end of this world, and to the one flowering with virtue it already now shows the good hope of the rewards to come.

Since human nature, in the manner of the fig tree mentioned above and of the winter spoken of before it, in which the evil moisture gathered, [?] the one who has favorably spread the spiritual summer over us and tended us with godly husbandry,

first scatters from nature everything superfluous and useless, in place of the tips of the shoots, through confession, and then through the divine life plants in the world a certain image of those blessed hopes,
as through the blossoms of the fig tree, by which it gladdens us with the sweetness to come.
And such is the saying: "The fig tree has put forth its blossom." In the same way understand also the blossom of the vines,
by which the wine that gladdens hearts will at some time fill the bowl of wisdom and offer the drinkers, by lofty proclamation, the freedom to draw up that good and watchful drunkenness.
And I mean the drunkenness by which human beings are brought in ecstasy from material things to immaterial ones.
But for now such a vine only blossoms and gives off a sweet and pleasant breath of fragrance,
mingled with the grace of the Spirit, which it prepares for those who are saved, as the Apostle says.

This is what the Word shows the bride, foretelling that good spring of souls, and it urges her on and rouses her toward the delights prepared, and says to her: "Arise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove."

How many teachings and instructions the Word sets before us through these few words! For the divinely inspired teaching does not speak excessively in such words as these for anything vain or idle. Far from it!
Rather, by this twofold speaking it shows us a great and godly understanding, and what I mean is this:
That blessed and eternal nature, which surpasses all minds, holds all being within itself, is bounded by nothing, and is not contained at all,
for nothing delineates or contains it: neither time, nor place,

nor form, nor color, nor likeness, nor extent, nor quantity, nor quality, nor any other encompassing name, or thing, or concept. Rather, the multitude of its good things in every way exceeds all these ten-thousandfold and a thousandfold, innumerably and incomprehensibly,
for where evil has no place, there is no end of good things.

For in this changeable nature, since we have equal power and capacity of will and of inclining in both opposite directions, that is, toward good and evil, which by succeeding one another either come to an end in us or grow, and the limit of the good becomes its opposite, evil,
and all the actions of our souls, as many as are opposed to one another, bring one another to an end and take each other's place.
But that simple and pure and sole and unchanging and unalterable nature stands forever in one state and is never changed from itself, for this reason:
because it does not admit any participation in evil, and it stands without limit in the good, and sees no end at all within itself, because it does not admit evil.
So when it draws the human soul to participation in itself, as much as that soul advances toward greater good things, by so much that divine glory continually becomes higher and higher in measure,
for the soul, by that participation in what is more excellent, continually rises above itself and does not cease from growing.
But the good in which it participates remains always in one state, and always, to the same degree, becomes more and more excellent than that soul.

For this reason we also see that holy bride, as if led by the hand up the steps of the virtues, raised higher and higher by the Word, she whom first through the prophetic windows and then through the lattices of the law,
which are the commandments, the Word enlightened, and whom he now also commands to draw near to the light, and to become beautiful, and to be changed into the form of a dove and of light.

And then, when she has received beauty, as much as she could contain, she is drawn again, as if from the beginning, as though she were still without any share in good things, to participation in a more excellent beauty,

so that in keeping with her advance and constant ascent she may also increase her desire and longing, and by the surpassing greatness of those more excellent good things she seems as if she has only now learned how to approach the ascent. For this reason, to her who has been awakened and set in order, the Word again says:
"Arise!" and to her who is coming: "Come!"
For one who has thus risen will never lack a constant rising, nor will the extent of the divine racecourse ever be shortened for one who is running toward the Lord.

For this reason, as many times as he says to her, "Arise and come," so many times he gives her power and eagerness for the ascent toward what is more excellent. Understand the next saying in the same way as well,
for he who commanded her to be changed from beauty into beauty commands her, according to the apostolic saying, to be changed from glory into glory,

so that, however great and lofty the things already reached and found may be, what has not yet been reached may always be reckoned greater and higher. Therefore, although she was a dove in those first advances, nothing prevents the word from calling her a dove once again on account of higher advances. And when she has become so, the word, by means of this name, again shows her a higher way, one step after another, as it says: "Come of yourself, my dove, under the shelter of the rock, near the wall." What elevation to a greater perfection now appears in these words? It is this: that she should no longer look to the eagerness of the one who urges and draws her, but should have her own desire and zeal as her guide toward what is better. For it says:

Come of yourself, not with grief and under compulsion, but of yourself, through your own thoughts, kindle the desire for the good, and do not follow compulsion; for virtue has no master and no lord, and is voluntary and free of all compulsion.
Such was David, who prayed that only what he did voluntarily might be pleasing to God, and who promised a voluntary offering.
Such was each of the saints, for they offered themselves to God of their own will and were not dragged by compulsion.
And you too, then, show perfect advance and rising up of your own accord; acquire zeal for what is better, and if you become such,
you will come to the shelter of the rock, near the wall. And this saying means the following:

O soul, if you have been shepherded by the commandments of the law, if you have seen within your mind the light of the prophetic windows, do not remain any longer under the shadow of the wall of the law,
for such a wall casts a shadow of the good things to come, and is not itself the image of the realities. Instead, cross over to the rock, near the wall,

for that rock is close to the wall, since the law was made an outer wall for the faith of the gospel, and the force of the commandments of the law and that of the teachings of the gospel are close to one another.
And what could be closer than this? For the law says, "You shall not commit adultery," and the gospel commands, "Do not lust."

And the one says, "You shall not kill," but the other, "Do not even become angry." And since the shelter of the rock is close to that outer wall, it is not difficult for you to move from the wall to the rock and to remain there without separation. The wall has circumcision and the rock has circumcision,
sheep and sheep, blood and blood, Passover and Passover; and almost everything is likewise, and thus close to one another.
Except only this: that the rock is spiritual, whereas the wall is fleshly and built of earth and coarseness.
But the rock of the gospel has no clay of fleshly thoughts,
but a person receives circumcision and yet remains entirely whole and living, and inflicts no wound or severing of the body on nature.
and he also keeps the Sabbath by resting from evil things, but does not accept resting from good things,
since he has learned that it is right to do good on the Sabbath. He takes food without doubting, and he does not touch what is unclean, for he has learned from the Rock that:
"What goes into the mouth does not defile a person."

And in this way he removes from himself on every side the fleshly scruples of the Law, and spiritually and intelligently receives the understanding of what is said, as Paul said: "The Law is spiritual."
And whoever keeps the Law in this way enters beneath the shelter of the rock of the Gospel, close to that fleshly wall.

When the Word has told her all this through the windows, the dove, illumined by the light of understanding, who has intelligently recognized the rock and understood that it is Christ himself, answers well and says:
"Show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful."

What is said here means this: Speak to me no longer through prophetic and legal parables, but as much as I am able to see, so much show yourself to me openly, so that I may enter within the rock of the Gospel and leave behind the wall of the Law.
And as much as my hearing can contain, so much grant the hearing of your voice to my ears.
For if the voice from the windows is so pleasant before the appearing of your face, how many times greater would its sweetness be?

This and the like the bride says, having understood the mystery of the Gospel, toward which the Word, appearing at the windows in many parts and in many ways, has guided her; and she is stirred with longing for God's appearing in the flesh,
so that the Word might become flesh and God might appear in the flesh and let our ears hear those divine words, by which he would promise the worthy that eternal blessedness.
And see how the words of Simeon agree with this prayer of the bride, the words which he spoke:
"Now let your servant depart, Master, according to your word, in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation," for he saw, as he had longed to.
But the very sweetness of his voice is known to those who received the grace of the Gospel, and who confessed and said: "You have the words of eternal life."

So the all-holy and good Bridegroom of souls accepts the bride's prayer as just and fitting. When he was about to show himself openly, he first sends out hunters to hunt the foxes, so that by their cunning they may no longer keep the divine vineyard from flowering and budding, and he says to them:
"Catch us the little foxes." That is, they are little, but they destroy the vineyards, for the vineyards will flower once there are no more destroyers.
"Catch us the little foxes, the destroyers of the vineyards, and our vineyards are in blossom."
Is it then possible to attain worthily to the height of the understanding of these sayings?
And how great a wonder of the divine glory this saying displays, and how great a surpassing of God's power the hiddenness of these words reveals!
And how can it be that the one about whom such things have been said—that murderer, mighty in wickedness, whose tongue is sharpened like a razor, about whom the prophet says:
"The arrows of the mighty one, sharpened, with coals of desolation," and:

"He lies in wait like a lion in his den," and "that great and apostate dragon," and "Hell, which has opened wide its mouth," and "the world-ruler of the power of this darkness," who holds the power of death—

and so much that prophecy declares from his own mouth: he who would take for himself the boundaries of the nations, which the Most High established according to the number of his angels; who would seize the world like a nest and gather its people up like abandoned eggs; who spoke of setting his thrones above the clouds and being like the Most High; and all the terrible and fearsome things the word says about him in Job,
whose "sides are bronze and his back cast iron," and "his innards a hardened stone," and everything else of this kind—
by which this word depicts his terrible nature. So then, this commander of the hosts of demons, so great and of such a kind: see how he is called a little fox by the only and true Power.
And all those hosts that follow him, all alike and all together, become despised and contemptible by him who sends out his hunters to hunt them,
who perhaps were also the angelic powers, the forerunners and ministers of the royal coming to earth, who brought the King of glory into the world, who showed him to the ignorant and said to them:
"Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty in battle," and the others, the "ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit life."
And if anyone should call the holy apostles hunters, sent out to hunt these beasts, he would not stray from the truth,
to whom the Lord said: "I will make you fishers of men,"

for such a hunt could not have succeeded—the hunting of bodies and the life of souls, which they carried out with the snare and net of words—unless they had first driven the little foxes out of the holes of the hearts where they had made their nests, and made those hearts ready as a place for the Son of God, where he may lay his head.
Therefore, whichever of those we have mentioned one may reckon as the hunter, by all of them his divine power is displayed, for he did not say:
Hunt the boar of the forest, which ravaged the vineyard of God, or the raging beast [?], or the roaring lion, or the great dragon of the abyss, or the crooked serpent,
for if he had said anything of the kind, the hunters might perhaps have supposed that some power is to be seen among the adversaries. For this reason he says to them:
All those worldly tyrannies against which the struggle of men is waged, that is, the principalities and powers of darkness and the spirits of wickedness,
are little foxes, though cunning and crafty; if they come up against our power and if you overcome them, your vineyard will receive its proper beauty and grace;
which is human nature, and the ripening of the clusters from the flower, which is virtuous conduct, it makes manifest:
"Catch for us the little foxes, the destroyers of the vineyards, for our vineyards are in bloom." So the divine command was heard by that vine of which David said:
"Your wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house."

And she saw herself cleansed, by the power of the one who gave the command, from the ravaging of these beasts, and at once she gave herself to the laborer who had broken down the dividing wall of the fence.
For she is no longer separated by that fence of the Law from communion with her beloved; therefore she says:
"My kinsman is mine and I am his, who pastures among the lilies,
until the day breaks and the shadows move away." She says this: this is the face-to-face vision, which abides forever, as it is;
but for my sake he shone forth in the flesh from my sister, who is the synagogue, and in him I take my rest and become his dwelling place.
For this is the good shepherd, who does not prepare hay as pasture for his flock, but feeds his sheep on pure lilies.

For truly, one who would no longer feed grass with grass — for grass is the food of brute nature, but rational man is nourished by the word of truth. If he is nourished with grass, he too becomes grass, for it says, "All flesh is grass," as long as it remains flesh.
But if someone is born of the Spirit and becomes spirit,
he will no longer graze on a life resembling hay; rather, the Spirit will be his food, which the purity and fragrance of the lilies signify.
He too will be a pure and fragrant lily, changed into the nature of his food.

And this is the day that follows the rays, which breaks forth, as the divine word named it, which through the Spirit comes to spread out the rays, which it named breaking forth and dawning, whence the shadows of this life pass away, the shadows that are eagerly gazed upon by those whose soul's eyes have not yet been illumined by that true light,
who look upon shadows and vanities as things that somehow endure, and despise the true truth as something that does not exist.
But those nourished by the lilies, that is, those who fatten their souls with pure, fragrant and divine food,

will remove from themselves every deceptive and shadow-like illusion of the affairs of the world and will perceive the firmness of the true realities, and such people will truly become sons of light and sons of the day.

The bride sees this and hastens the word, so that the hope of good things may swiftly be fulfilled in deed and the onslaught of evils be undone. Therefore she says: "O my kinsman, be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains full of ravines." That is to say: as a gazelle,
look, you who see the mind of men, who read the thoughts of hearts,
make the existence of evil things vanish, as the young of the stags, the slayer of venomous serpents, does.
Do you see these gully-ridden mountains of human life, whose ruggedness consists not of mountain peaks but of gullies and pits and ravines? So the Word runs swiftly over the gully-ridden mountains,
for every height raised up against the truth is a pit and not a mountain, a gully and not a hill. Therefore the bride says to him: "If you run over such things,
every such ravine will be filled up and every such mountain will be brought low."
Such things are said by the soul whom the Word shepherds and nourishes, not with any thorns and hay, but with the fragrance of the lilies of good conduct,
by which may we too be nourished, shepherded by the Word, by Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and might forever and ever. Amen.
The heading of this discourse: 3:1. On my beds by night I sought him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me. 3:2.
I will arise and go about the city, the marketplaces and the streets, and I will seek him whom my soul loved;
I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me. 3:3. The watchmen who went about the city found me.
Have you perhaps seen him whom my soul loved? 3:4. Scarcely had I passed from them when I found him whom my soul loved;
I took hold of him and did not let him go until I had brought him into the house of my mother and into the chambers of her who bore me. 3:5. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the powers and strengths of the field, if you rouse and awaken love until it pleases. 3:6.
Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like a branch of the smoke of incense, of myrrh and frankincense, from all the powders of the perfumer?
3:7. Behold, the couch of Solomon, and sixty mighty men around it, from the mighty men of Israel. 3:8.

All of them hold a sword, trained in battle. Each man has his sword on his loins, because of fear and terror in the night. Once more we learn great and lofty teachings from this, from the Song of Songs now read aloud,
for this lofty account of the bride is philosophy, through which she speaks about herself and teaches the lovers of that divine and surpassing beauty what kind of love they ought to have toward it.
What we learn from these present words is this. For I think it is necessary
that we first set out the meaning contained in these words, and then join what has been examined to the divinely inspired words. To put it briefly, these words set before us the following teaching:
The nature of beings is divided in two by the highest division: one part of it is visible and material, and the other invisible and immaterial.
We call visible whatever is examined and understood through the senses, and invisible whatever surpasses the examination of the senses.
Of these, the one is endless and unbounded, while the other, by some reach of comprehension, is undoubtedly finite. For everything visible, being encompassed by quantity and quality,
is examined and understood in size and shape and color and kind, and is brought to a limit.

And whoever investigates anything material will be able to devise no form or conception higher than these. But the invisible and immaterial is foreign to such circumscriptions as these. For this reason it escapes the boundaries of limit by its limitlessness.
And again, the invisible nature is divided in two. One part is uncreated. It is the creator of created things and the giver of being to all that exists, and it exists eternally
as it is, and remains wholly the same, above all increase and diminution.

And since it alone is the treasury of all good things, it cannot acquire further goods. But the part brought into being by creation looks always toward the first cause of all that exists. By sharing in what is higher, it remains always in the good. In some incomprehensible way it is always being created, changed toward the higher as it grows in good things,

so that in this way it too becomes unending, limitless and uncircumscribed in its progress toward the higher. The goods it gains, wholly and always, however high and exalted they may be, become only a beginning of higher and greater ones, according to the word of the Apostle:
"And by reaching the things that lie ahead, I come to forget the things before."
For the continual finding of some higher and surpassing good things does not allow the desire of the one acquiring them to dwell upon the good things that have passed,
for delight in the higher things hides the honor of the lesser ones. Hence such is the philosophy of the Lord's teachings, as we suppose.
And it is fitting that we first recall the divinely inspired words themselves and then add the understanding of what has been said, for it says:
"On my beds by night I sought him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me.
I will arise and go about the city, the markets and the streets, that I may seek him whom my soul loved.
I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me. The watchmen who go about the city found me: Have you perhaps seen him whom my soul loved?
Scarcely had I passed from them when I found him whom my soul loved; I seized him and did not let him go,
until I brought him into the house of my mother and the treasuries of her who bore me." See how through these sayings we find the pattern of the teachings stated earlier,
which we mentioned above.

For the soul of that spotless virgin continually rises higher than the heights she has already ascended, and she never stops among the good things she has acquired, nor is she satisfied. For at one time she is likened to a mare, the overthrower of the tyranny of the Egyptians, and again to beads and a turtledove, by the ornament of the neck.
And then, as though these were not enough, she rose up toward higher things and by the fragrance of nard received the divine fragrance.

And she did not stop here either, but again she fastened her beloved upon herself, like some fragrant ointment, between her rational breasts, from which she brings forth the divine teachings, and she fixed him in the expanse of her heart.
And after this, she made the planter of good things her own fruit, and called him a cluster, full of sweet and desirable fragrance, with the beauty of a flower.
And when she had advanced in this way, she came near and was called beautiful, and the beauty of her eyes was likened to doves.

And then she grew higher still and became a seer of invisible things. She beheld the beauty of the Word and marveled at how that beautiful shade comes down as the bed of our life and is overshadowed by the material flesh of human nature.

Along with these, the word describes the height of the virtues. It becomes timber for the roof, cedar and cypress, which are free from rot and decay. By these the word signifies the firmness and unchangeableness of the love of the good. Then again it makes known her change toward the higher, and she is called a lily among thorns.
And again the beauty of the Bridegroom, set apart from others, is contemplated by her.

For she names him an apple tree among the fruitless trees, and she adorns herself with the color of its fruit and rests in its shade. She enters the house of wine, is strengthened by ointments, and is surrounded and entwined with apples.
And through that sweet wound she receives the chosen arrow into her heart, and then she herself becomes an arrow
in the hands of the archer: by the left hand her head is aimed at the target of heaven, and by the right hand she is drawn by the archer toward his own head, like an arrow.
And after this, as one who has attained perfection, she also becomes one who urges others to zeal, and by a kind of oath she rouses them to eagerness for love.
And who would not say that she has reached so great a height?
Yet the end of those earlier advances becomes for her the beginning of progress toward higher things.
For all of that was reckoned as the voice of the Word, turning the soul toward mystical visions. From there she begins to see the Desired One, and she presents the sight of him in another form,
for she likens him to a gazelle and compares him to a fawn, and the one who appeared did not remain in any one vision or in any one place,
but leaps upon the mountains and runs upon the summit of the hills.
And the bride again rises to a higher rank by hearing a second voice,
By this she was commanded to leave the shadow of the wall, to come out into the light, and to rest in the shelter of the rock

near the wall, and to rest in the beauty of the [?]. She was to gather colourful and beautiful flowers, ready to be shared, along with all the other delights that entice lovers of pleasure with the voices of singing birds. Through these the bride becomes more perfect still.
And she entreats that she may see plainly the image of the Speaker himself and be made worthy to hear his word,
and that she may no longer converse with him through others. Therefore this soul should be called blessed, which was made worthy of such heights that she reached the summit of her desires.
For what greater blessedness could anyone imagine than the sight of God?
Yet this too is only the end of the good things already passed through, and it becomes the beginning of higher hopes.
For behold, again she hears a voice commanding the hunters, for the preservation of the rational vines, to hunt the beasts that harm the fruit, which are the little foxes.
And when this has come about, the two are united into one and blended with each other, for God comes to dwell in the soul, and in turn the soul becomes a co-dweller with God, as she says:
"My kinsman is mine and I am his, who pastures among the lilies," so that he may change human life from shadowy fantasies truly into truth.
Do you see to what a height the soul has ascended, going, according to the word of the prophet, from strength to strength,

until it can be thought that she has been raised to the summit of good hopes? For what could be higher than that the desired one should dwell in her and she in the desired one? Yet even this has come about. And again, as though deprived of good things, she mourns, and as though she did not have the fulfillment of her desire, she grieves and is sorrowful; and she makes this grief of the soul public by her narrative, and through her words she shows how she found her desired one and how she did not find him.
And from all this we learn from these present teachings that the glory of the divine nature is not bounded by any end,

Nor does the measure of understanding already reached become a limit to the understanding still sought, a point at which someone who longs for the heights would have to stop going forward. Rather, the mind that runs toward the height and attains exalted understandings must hold that every perfection of understanding
that human nature can attain becomes for it a beginning of desire and longing for higher things.

Consider carefully the force of these present words. For the bodily picture in this word is drawn with the joy of the bridal chamber and the wedding, and it becomes material for an understanding of this kind, which the philosophy contained in them [leads] toward the immaterial and holy allegorical meanings
It presents the teachings in altered form through figurative interpretations, in order to reveal lofty and surpassing things to the initiated [?].
For since the word has depicted the soul as a bride,
and the one loved by her with all her heart and with all her soul and strength and with all her mind has been given the name of bridegroom,

fittingly, then, when she thought she had attained the summit of hopes and had been blended with the desired one, she gives the name of bed to the perfect communion in good things, and she appoints night as the time of the bed; and by the name of night she indicates the seeing of invisible things, like Moses,
who entered into the cloud where God was, who, according to the word of the prophet, "made darkness his covering."

And when she has reached such a measure, only then does she understand that she is as far removed from perfection as those who have not even made a beginning. For she says: When I thought that I had attained perfection, and I was resting myself as if on a bed through the understandings and attainment I had come to know,

When I left behind the things perceived by the senses and entered within the invisible things, and when I was seized by that divine night and sought in that hidden cloud, then I had a burning love for the Desired One. But the Beloved himself flew away from the grasp of my thoughts.
And I sought him by night upon my beds, so that I might know what his nature is, or from where it begins, or where it ends, or in what it has its being, but I did not find him;
I called him by name, as far as it was possible for me to find a name for the Incorporeal One,
but no form of speech was found that could convey his name.
For how could he who is above every name be found by any name that is given? For this reason she says: "I called him, and he did not answer me."
And then I understood that of the magnificence of his glory and holiness there is no limit and no end.

Therefore she rose up again and went about with her mind through the intelligible and invisible nature above the world, which she names a city, in which dominions and principalities and authorities and thrones and the assembly of the countless heavenly powers are established,
which she names marketplaces and streets, in the hope that perhaps the Beloved might be found among them.
And as she went to and fro and searched through all the adornment and the host of the angels, and as she did not see the one she sought among the good things found there,
she reasoned within herself thus: Can my Beloved, then, be attained by them?

And she said to them: "Perhaps you at least know, or have seen, him whom my soul has loved?" But they kept silent at such a question, and by their silence made known that the one she sought is unattainable to them as well.

And when, with her much-searching mind, she had gone through the whole supramundane city, and did not see among the intelligible and invisible powers the one for whom she longed, then she left behind everything that can be found and every object of search that is found, and so she found

the one she was seeking. He is grasped only by being beyond grasp, and only in this way is the one who cannot be found found, as to what he is: when his total incomprehensibility is confessed. For the seekers, every investigation that tries to grasp him becomes an obstacle that opposes and hinders finding him.

Therefore she says, "Scarcely had I passed by them." That is: when I had left all created things, passed by all formed things and all invisible and visible beings, and left behind every investigation that thinks it can grasp him,
by faith I found the beloved, and I will no longer let him go from the hands of faith, with which I took hold of the one I found,

until he comes into my inner treasure-chambers. And the treasure-chamber is without doubt the heart. It becomes able to receive the divine indwelling when it reaches the original order and calm it had when it was created by its Begetter.
And if anyone understands by "mother" the first cause of our being, he will not sin.

But now it is time to join to these words those divinely inspired words and divine utterances, so that those words may be blended with and fitted to the sense of what has been examined here. For it says:
"On my beds by night I sought him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me.
I will rise, then, and go about the city and the marketplaces and the streets, and I will seek him whom my soul loved.
I sought him and did not find him. I called him and he did not answer. The watchmen who went about the city found me.
Have you perhaps seen him whom my soul loved? And when I had gone on a little way from them, until I found him whom my soul loved,
I seized him and did not let him go, until I had brought him into the house of my mother and into the chambers of her who bore me."
After this, again out of love for humankind, she addresses the daughters of Jerusalem as well,

whom the text earlier likened to thorns, when the beauty of the bride was compared to the loveliness of lilies; and with an oath by the powers of the earth she commands them to the same measure of love as her own,
so that the will of the bridegroom may be accomplished in deed among them. And on this account, since it has been said above what the world is,

or what those powers and strengths of the field are, and what the will is, or what it is to love with the whole heart, it is now superfluous to repeat the same words and to prolong the discourse, for the same account suffices for the explanation of this question as well.

Therefore let us go on to the words that follow, if only it may become possible for us too to fly up to the height with that divine dove and to hear the voice of the friends of the bridegroom, who are amazed at her coming up from the wilderness,

which all the more increases the astonishment of those who behold it, that a wilderness should be able to bring forth such a thing, resembling a tree of beauty, which in the wilderness is formed from the fragrance of the smoke of incense.
Now those incenses are myrrh and frankincense. And again, from the fragrance of these a certain fine dust, perfumed from the ointments, burst up along with it
and went up along with it, so that in place of dust the air might be blended by it, that is, by the pouring out and spreading of those finely ground ointments,

By these the powder was truly perfected and raised up [?]. The saying is this: "Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like a column of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, from all the powders of the perfumer?" If anyone examines this carefully, he will find the truth of what we discussed earlier.

For in the entertainments of the theaters, the actors stay the same people, yet when they take on the role assigned to them they are thought to be different people. Through the change of role they even change their appearance. One who is a slave and lowly becomes valiant and a commander. Again, the slave leaves behind the appearance of slavery and puts on the appearance of nobles, or even of the king himself.

In the same way, those who advance in virtues do not stay fixed in a single form. Through lofty desires they are changed from glory to glory. In keeping with their virtues and their constant advance toward good things and perfection, they shine out and give light, even if they were slaves or lowly. Through that growth in good things they become one person instead of another and are seen as such.
And for this reason, as I think, this sight of the virgin seems strange to the friends of the bridegroom,
who before this beautifully, and after it with the likeness of gold and silver, adorned her beauty.
But now, since they saw in her none of those wonders seen earlier, they therefore depict her in higher forms, and they marvel not only at her ascent but also at the place from which she ascended.
For this is what increases that amazement:
she who ascends is seen all at once, and she resembles a dense thicket of tall trees and is taken for a branch, grown to its full height and flourishing.
Yet what nurtures that branch and tree turns out to be no rich and moist land, but parched and thirsty desert.

On what, then, is this branch planted, and from where does it grow? Its root is the dust of perfumed ointments, and its nourishment is the vapor of incense, which through its fragrance [?] such a grove.

And through so many testimonies of this kind, what great encomia and what praises does the text present? For the question they put to one another about her who has appeared, and the seeing of her not in the former form but in another image, is an increase in the praise of the soul that has advanced to perfection through the virtues,
which bears great witness to her growth and advance toward what is better and more excellent.

For this is the cry of people who are amazed, as they are when, contrary to what is usual, they see an image blossoming with such beauty: "This one who comes up from the wilderness was once seen by us as black, and now how that darkened image has been washed,

and it shines like snow with beauty!" And this is wonderful: the cause of such form and beauty is the wilderness, which raised her up in this way and adorned her with beauty and goodness like a fir tree [?].
For it was not by some chance or haphazardly that she was raised to such a height,
but through her own labors and struggles she acquired such beauty.
And so too the soul of the prophet once thirsted for that divine spring, when his flesh became desert, trackless and thirsty, and he received that divine thirst into himself.
Hence this ascent from the desert testifies that she ascended to such a height through reverent restraint and struggle, until she became a marvel even to the friends of the bridegroom,
who interpret her beauty through many forms,
since it was impossible to encompass everything by means of one; for first they compare her appearance to a tree, and not to a tree of one kind,
but to a grove of tall trees, so that through the many colors of that grove they may display the manifold variety of her virtues.
And then, as a figure of her goodness, they bring in the smoke of incense, and not this released in simple form, but mixed with myrrh and frankincense,

so that the fragrance of the incense may be joined from both, and thus by these mixtures of ointments the beauty of the bride is shown to be still greater. Of these, myrrh serves for the embalming of bodies prepared for burial, while frankincense is set apart for offering to God.

And whoever wishes to dedicate himself as a servant of God cannot become incense and divine fragrance in any other way unless he first becomes myrrh. That is, unless he puts to death his members that are upon the earth and is buried with him

who endured death for our sake and took upon himself the anointing of his dead body with myrrh. And if a person is adorned in this way, he gathers every ointment of the virtues around his life, like that fragrant powder of ointments. Whoever smells it becomes full of the Holy Spirit, a seer of hidden things and a prophet.
And after the testimony to her beauty, the friends of the bridegroom, the stewards of that undefiled bridal chamber and those who betroth that holy bride, show her the beauty of the royal bed,

so that they may lead the bride to a greater desire for that divine and incorruptible union. And the form of that royal bed is such as they make her see through clear words, plainly depicting and recounting it to her, and they say to her: "Behold, the bed of Solomon, and sixty mighty men around it, from the mighty men of Israel. All of them hold a sword, trained in battle, each man with his sword at his loins, because of fear and alarm in the night." But since this account of the bed does not come from a narration of historical reports, let it be recognized by all and made known from what is written in bodily terms about Solomon, whose kingdom and table and the rest of the ordering of his reign the text has depicted with all exactness, yet about the bed it has said nothing new or different. Hence it is right and obligatory that this narrative not be left idle, as a mere record of that kind,
but that by some diligent inquiry we should change what is said here into spiritual contemplation and draw its meaning away from material figures.
For how could sixty mighty men be an adornment for a bridal bed? Their training is the terror of battle, their ornament a sword girded at the loins, and their marvel the alarm and fear of the night,
that is, some terrible and frightening sound and alarm in the night, which comes about for those armed men.
Therefore we must by all means seek from these sayings some understanding that follows from what was considered earlier. And what might that understanding be?
That is, the divine beauty holds desirability within its awe, which is the opposite of bodily beauty,
for here, what increases desire is softness (literally "wateriness") and delicacy [?] of form, far removed from anything fearsome or stern in love.
But that divine and incorruptible beauty and goodness is at once desirable and terrible and fearsome.

And since the passionate and defiled desire of the flesh, settled in the bodily members like some troop and camp of robbers, lies in wait for the mind, and many times plunders it and carries it off according to its own will and purpose, and this thing is enmity against God, as the Apostle says:

"The thinking of the flesh is enmity against God." For this reason I say that divine love comes into being as the opposite of fleshly desires. And since pleasure, ease, looseness and unseemly love go before the one, there the material of divine love comes to be fear, trembling and courage. For when, with valiant courage and wrath, they have terrified and driven off the robbers of desire,
then that holy beauty of the soul appears, which no desire of the passion of the flesh defiles. For this reason also the bridal bed of the King is fittingly surrounded by armed men,
who, in the art of war, have the sword ready upon their loins, and scatter and terrify those thoughts of darkness
which in the night and the gloom plunder and oppress the upright in heart.

And that the armor of those warriors surrounding the bed destroys and kills foul desires is clear and evident also from the description in the following words, for it says: "All of them trained in war, each man with his thigh-sword at his loins."
Truly, it belongs to those who are trained and knowledgeable to know how one ought to set oneself against flesh and blood, holding the thigh-sword upon the loins.

And I know that if anyone is not ignorant of the figurative language of the Scriptures, he will without doubt understand, from the mention of the sword and the loins and the thigh-piece, what they signify, and that the sword is God the Word. Hence whoever girds on that fearful weapon, which is the sword of purity,
he is the one who longs for and loves that incorruptible bed, one of the mighty men of Israel, worthy to be joined to that number of sixty, and a guardian of that God-radiant place of rest.
And that this number has some mystical force we do not doubt, but it is known only to those to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit reveals hidden mysteries.

But for us it is good to be satisfied with the manifest force of this saying, just as Moses commanded concerning the Passover those who eat the manifest flesh, that they remain without touching what lies hidden and unrevealed in the bones.
But if anyone desires those hidden marrows of the word, let him seek them from the one who reveals hidden things to those who are worthy of him.
But so that we may not be guilty of passing over the passage entirely unexamined, and may not grow lazy in fulfilling the divine command that tells us to search the divine Scriptures,
let us examine the passage about the number sixty in this way. By divine command Moses took twelve rods, according to the number of the twelve tribes,
but he honoured only one of them out of all, by its budding and bearing fruit. And again, Joshua son of Nun set up twelve stones in the Jordan, also according to the number of the twelve tribes,

as a testimony to the mystery that took place then. Not one of these stones was despised, but all were accepted. And what sequence does this account show? It portrays the people's advance toward what is more perfect: at the beginning of the giving of the Law only one rod was found living and budding, while the others, being fruitless and withered,

were cast aside. But when long periods of time had passed and the people had gained more experience of the commandments of the Law, until the second circumcision was performed by Joshua, and when everything superfluous and unclean was cast away with knives of stone,
and I know that the attentive listener is not ignorant of what is likened to those knives of stone, from which it was fittingly done,

for after that lawful and pleasing way of life he cast away not one of those stones which were taken as a figure of the tribes of Israel; and since it is necessary always to seek the increase of good things,
when the times had passed and the strength of the Israelites had grown still greater, as this passage before us informs us, for it says: "of the mighty of Israel,"
then no longer is one stone or one rod taken from a tribe, but instead of the stone and the rod five men are chosen from each tribe, men of war,
trained in battle, bearers of the sword, from the mighty of Israel, as guards of that divine bed, of whom for this reason no one is cast aside,
for the firstborn of every tribe are five, and their number, multiplied by twelve, completes the number sixty.
Therefore it is necessary that from each tribe there be five armed men, fearsome guards of the royal bed, for if the number five is lacking, those who remain become unacceptable.
Now then, may I venture to say what I have in mind: how five from every tribe are armed so as to become guards of the royal bed,
and how each one of the five becomes dreadful to his adversaries by reason of his armor and draws the sword at his waist?
Or is it clear that in place of that one stone these five are armed, who, to the terror of their adversaries, draw a sword suited to each sense?
So the sword of the eyes is always to look toward the Lord and to see rightly, and not to be defiled by any stained sight.
And likewise, the weapon of the ears is the hearing of divine teachings and never admitting a vain word.

Likewise the arming of taste, touch and smell is accomplished by the sword of ascetic struggle and fasting; the ascetic arms each sense in the manner suited to it, and by these arms he becomes terrifying and dismaying to those powers of darkness,
for whom the time of battle and of the harming and destruction of souls is night and darkness.
For it was in this darkness, the prophet said, that the beasts of the forest seek their evil food from the flocks of God. For he says: "You set darkness, and it became night.
In it all the beasts of the forest went about, the lions' whelps roaring." Now then, since all Israel is to be saved,
For not all who are of Israel are Israel, but those who with their mind see God through good deeds are the ones who truly become worthy of this name.
But for one who looks to God, this is his task and his property: that he does not perceive sin with any one of his senses. For no one can serve two masters,
but by loving the one he will hate the other, especially if they are opposed to each other. This is why everyone who is saved becomes the King's litter.
For if all the saints see God with the heart, then they are rightly called Israel, which means the mind that sees God, being spotless and holy in mind and soul and heart.
And by some hidden power this name is divided into twelve tribes, and the fullness of the saved is fittingly completed by this number of sixty,
for one is brought from each tribe, and according to the number of the senses that one is divided into five armed men. Hence all
who put on the full armor of God surround one royal bed, and all of them become one Israel, and through the twelve tribes, divided into fives of warriors, they complete the number sixty.

And through the perfection of such valiant men they become one battle line and one army and one bed and one faith and one church and one people and one bride, all under one commander and gatherer of the people and bridegroom, and united in the communion of one body.
And that the rest of the saved is called a bed, the word of the Lord also confirms and teaches us, for he says to the one who was asking shamelessly,
"Behold, my door is shut, and my children are with me in bed."
For those who by the armor of righteousness have gained freedom from passion for themselves, the word fittingly ranks as children, and by this it teaches us the doctrine
that the good things we have gained through struggle are not foreign to us, but were sown in our nature from the beginning.

And he who has girded the sword on his loins has, by virtuous living and reverence, cast out those impure passions and has become an infant. And an infant in age is ignorant of impure passions, for passions cannot find room in him because of his infancy. Hence the standing of the armed men around the bed and the rest of the children on the couch are one and the same,
for the freedom from passion is one for both, for those who did not admit passion and for those who removed it from themselves. For the former did not even know the taste of the passions,

while the latter raised themselves to the same state, for they turned and became children through freedom from passion. And blessed is he who is found among these, so that he may become either a child, or an armed man, or a true Israelite,
so that as an Israelite he may see God with a pure heart,

and as an armed man he may, with freedom from passion and with purity, guard the King's bed, that is, his own heart, and as a child he may rest on that blessed couch of innocence, through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
The heading of this discourse: 3:9. King Solomon made a litter from the trees of Lebanon. 3:10.
He made its pillars of silver and its arched vault of gold; its ascent is of porphyry, its floor is paved: love from the daughters of Jerusalem. 3:11.
Come out and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding and on the day of the gladness of his heart. 4:1.
Behold, you are beautiful, my close one. Behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves, apart from your silence. Your hair is like flocks of goats that have appeared from Gilead. 4:2.

Your teeth are like flocks of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing. All of them bear twins, and there is none barren among them. 4:3. Your lips are like a scarlet cord, and your speech is beautiful. Your cheeks are like a slice of pomegranate, apart from your silence. 4:4.
Your neck is like the tower of David, which is built in Thalpioth. A thousand shields are hung upon it, and all the arrows of the mighty. 4:5.
Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies. 4:6.
Until the day breathes and the shadows move, I myself will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. 4:7. You are all beautiful, my close one, and there is no blemish in you.
In many places and in many ways King Solomon is named as a type of the true King. And I say that frequently in the holy Scriptures the account of him is given on the better side,
for he is called Peace, and he builds the temple, and he has countless wisdom, and he reigns over Israel, and he judges the peoples with righteousness, and he is of the seed of David.
Moreover, the queen of Ethiopia also came to him. This and other such things are said of him in parable and figurative speech, but in truth they signify the grace of the Gospel.

For who could be so truly peace and peacemaker as he who put enmity to death and nailed to the cross both us, these enemies, and indeed the whole world, laying it upon himself, and who broke down the dividing wall of enmity,
so that by himself he might create the two into one new man, making peace; he who proclaimed peace to those far off and peace to those near, through those evangelists of peace?
And who is such a builder of the temple as the one who laid his foundations in the holy mountains, that is, of the prophets and apostles?
And he builds, as Paul says, upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with those living and spiritual stones
which of their own accord, according to the prophetic word, roll toward the wall to be joined to it,
so that they may be united by the unity of faith and the bond of peace, and may make themselves grow into a holy temple, to become a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.
And that by his wisdom Solomon signifies the true Wisdom, no one who is able to discern type and truth will dispute with us, for Scripture testifies concerning him
that he passed beyond the bounds of human wisdom and gathered all knowledge within the breadth of his heart, so that he surpassed all those before him and became unattainable by those after him;
But God by his very nature is wisdom and truth and power, and the creator of all wisdom.
For this reason too the Apostle interprets that saying of David, "In wisdom you have made all things," and says, "By him all things were created."
And that the Lord is king of Israel is attested even by his enemies,

who wrote upon the cross the confession of his kingship, that he is the king of the Jews. For we accept this testimony, even though confining his universal sovereignty within kingship over Israel seems, as it were, to diminish the glory of his kingship,
That is not so. Rather, the inscription written on the cross in a twofold manner [?] declares his rule over all, since it does not add:
"He is King of Israel only": for the statement plainly testified to his rule over the Jews, and through this statement it silently joined to it the confession of his dominion over all.

For the king of the whole earth undoubtedly also holds kingship over a part of it. But Solomon's zeal for judging justly points to that true Judge of the whole world, for he says: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son," and:

"I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just." For this is the highest standard of just judgment: when one judges those who are to be judged not on one's own authority, and not out of any leniency or favour,
but first hears the case of those on trial, and only then gives sentence on them.
For this reason the power of God admits, about a certain matter: "I cannot do it," because truth cannot pervert judgment apart from justice.

And that the Lord is of the seed of David according to the flesh, as was confessed from the beginning through the promise made to David. Let us now leave aside the many other figures and move our discourse along.

And the mystery of this Indian queen will become plain to anyone of understanding: that it proclaims the wonders of the Gospel, how she left the kingdom of India, crossed such great lands and distances, and came to Solomon out of love for his wisdom, and honored the king with precious stones and gold and fragrant ointments. Understand this as follows:

For who would not know that formerly, because of idol worship, the church of the Gentiles was black and Indian, before it had yet become the Church, and was far removed, by the distance of ignorance, from the knowledge of the true God?

But when "the grace of God appeared" and wisdom shone forth, and that true light spread its rays over those sitting in darkness and the shadows of death, then the Israelites, when it came to beholding the light,

closed their eyes and became strangers to the sharing of good things. But the Indians from among the Gentiles came to faith, and those who were once far off became near, and they washed away that Indianness with the water of the mystery. Thus India was first to stretch out its hand to God and to offer gifts to the King,
These gifts are the fragrant spices of devotion to God, the gold of knowledge of God, and the precious stones of fulfilling the commandments and the virtues.
From here on it is time for us to set our hand to the interpretation of these divinely inspired words that lie before us and to reveal what is hidden in them. For it says:
"King Solomon made a litter of the wood of Lebanon. He made its pillars of silver and its curved vault of gold, its ascent of purple,
its floor a stone pavement, love from the daughters of Jerusalem," as the discourse has found from those who examined this before,
for those deeds of Solomon depict divine mysteries. Likewise, by the preparation of this litter too, the Lord's dispensation accomplished for our sake is foreshadowed,
For among those worthy of him God changes in many forms, and as each one is able and is worthy, so he comes to be in each one,
for one becomes a place of God, another a temple, another a throne, another a footstool, and another a chariot,
or else a steed and horse, which obediently accepts the mounting of that good rider, and wherever he himself directs it, in that direction it steers its course.
And as we now learn, someone also becomes his litter, which, in accordance with that wisdom of his, is prepared not only from the timbers of Lebanon,
