but is also prepared with gold and silver and purple and the brilliance of stones, as befits each part, and through these his love is perfected in deed,
the power of which love is not contained by all, but only by the one who through virtuous living has become free-born and a daughter of the heavenly Jerusalem.
Now the one who carries God within himself, for he is a litter of the one dwelling in him, this is clear even from our earlier discourse, for the one who,
in accordance with Saint Paul, no longer lives himself,
but has Christ living within himself and gives proof by deed of Christ speaking in him, such a one truly becomes and is called a litter of the one borne by him.
However, this is not what we are seeking; rather, we must strive to understand what the variety and diversity of that material signifies:
how along with gold there are also taken silver and purple and stones and the material of wood for preparing that litter, and all the more so,
since the wise master builder Paul cast out wood, together with wood [?] and reed, from the building of the temple, as something to be burned and consumed by that power which tests deeds by fire.
Yet we also know a certain nature of wood that does not remain as it is, but changes itself into gold and silver and some other precious material,
as the same apostle says: "In the great house of God some vessels are by nature of gold and silver."

And by these, as I think, he signifies the incorporeal and intelligent powers; and some are of wood and earthenware, and perhaps he says this about us, whom disobedience made earth and likened to earthenware,
and the sin that came from the tree changed us into wooden vessels instead of gold. And according to the order of the materials the use of the vessels is also divided,
for the use of those of precious materials is appointed as honorable, and that of the dishonorable ones is assigned to dishonorable services. But what does Paul say about such vessels?
That the vessel has the power, of its own will and mind, to change from wood into gold, or from earthenware into silver. For he says:
"If anyone cleanses himself, he will be a precious vessel, useful to his Lord, prepared for every good work." And as I think,
through these things that have been said we draw near to the meaning of this present passage,
for Mount Lebanon is mentioned in many places of the holy Scriptures as a figure of the opposing power, as when he says through the prophet:
The Lord shattered those cedars of Lebanon and ground them fine, and Lebanon too,
like that calf which was ground up in the wilderness by Moses and through that grinding became a drink for the Israelites.
And this prophecy sets forth a meaning of this kind: that not only those evils which sprang up from the opposing power,
but also that very mountain of Lebanon itself, the beginning and root of evils, which nourishes the material of such cedars, will be made to vanish and will perish.
Hence we indeed were those trees of Lebanon, as long as we stood and were planted on it through an evil life and the error of idols,

but since we were cut down from there by that rational axe and were taken into the hands of that skilled master builder, he made us into his own litter, and through the second birth he changed the nature of wood into gold and silver, into flowered purple and the brilliance of stones.
And as the Apostle says, according to the zeal of each person God has distributed the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and to one he gives mercy, in proportion to his faith,

and to another, some other one of the helping gifts, whose grace has the power to sustain each one. Such a person may become an eye to the body of the Church, or be appointed as a hand, or strengthen it in the place of a foot.
Likewise, in the construction of this litter, one becomes a pillar, another a step, and another the part at the head, which he called a curved vault.
And there are some set within as a floor, whose material the master of all craftsmen uses not merely for adornment,
but he procures their brilliance as that which beautifies all the adornment.
The pillars of the litter, then, are of silver, and its step is of purple.
And the curved vault, in which the Bridegroom reclines his head, is of gold, while the whole interior is adorned with precious stones.
By pillar we understand those pillars of the Church, whose "word is pure silver,

refined and tested." And since purple is understood above all as a royal adornment, this means that by that lofty way of life one becomes king over the passions, and they reign with Christ. And their ruling mind, where he reclines his head,
he, the builder of the litter, is the gold of their holy teachings.
And all that is hidden and invisible is beautified by the precious stones of a spotless and pure mind, and through all this the love of the daughters of Jerusalem is brought to perfection.
But if someone should wish to call the whole Church a litter as well, and should divide the parts of the litter according to the division of the helps, as we said above,
even so the discourse would show great fittingness, when they assign the materials of the litter to the individual orders according to the word of the Apostle:
"God has appointed in the churches first apostles, second prophets, third teachers," and then all the others, each one in turn,

As it says, "for the establishing of the saints," so that through these names the preparation of the litter may be completed by priests and teachers and honorable virgins, who make the floor of the litter gleam with the purity of the virtues, as with the brilliance of precious stones. And let this suffice up to this point.
The next saying presents the bride's invitation to the daughters of Jerusalem,
for just as the great Paul counted it a loss if not everyone were to share in his own good things, and so said to those who listened to him:
"Become as I am, for I too was once as you are," so too this bride, who loves humankind,
since she has been made worthy to know the divine mysteries of the bridegroom, and has seen the couch, and the royal resting place has been revealed, cries out to the virgins,
who are the souls of those being saved, saying: How long will you stay shut up in the cave of this transient world?
Come out from the coverings of nature and see a wondrous sight. Become daughters of Zion and see the crown
that adorns the royal head, which his mother set upon him, according to the word of the prophet: "He set on his head a crown of precious stones."
But no one who knows the meaning of the divine words would scrutinize the difference of the names, for "mother" is mentioned in place of "father," and one meaning is shown by both,
For the Godhead is neither male nor female.

For how could any such notion exist in the Godhead, when not even among us humans does such a thing last forever? When through Christ we all become one, then we shall strip off these marks of division together with the whole old man. And for this reason every name that is found shows equally the power
of that ineffable nature, and neither a female nor a male name defiles that incorruptible nature.
For this reason too, in the Gospel the Father is said to be the one who holds the wedding for his son. And the prophet says with reference to God
that he set on his head a crown of precious stone, while here it speaks of the crown being set on the bridegroom by the mother.
Therefore, since there is one wedding and one bride, and the crown is set on the bridegroom by one, no difference enters in at all, whether the Only-begotten God be called Son of God
or son of his love, as Paul says, since one power is signified by both names, and by the name of bridegroom and bride his dwelling among us and his union with us becomes [?].

For this reason the bride says to the virgins: Come out and become daughters of Zion, so that as from a high watchtower (for this is how Zion is translated) you may be able to see this wondrous spectacle, which is the crowning of the bridegroom.
And the Church becomes crowned, and with those spiritual carbuncles it encircles the divine head. The maker of such a crown is love,
and whoever calls it either mother or love will not be mistaken,
"for God is love," as John says, and through this crown,

As with a bridal adornment, the bride proclaims his gladness, for he truly rejoices, he who revealed the Church as his fellow-dweller and was crowned by her with the splendor of the virtues, which are the lives of the saints.
But it is more beautiful that we should recall those divine utterances themselves, which are composed in words such as these: "Go forth and see, O daughters of Zion,
King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding and on the day of the joy of his heart."

Such love of humankind on the part of the bride, then, the Bridegroom and Word accepted; and since, like the Lord, she too "desires the salvation of all and that they should come to the knowledge of the truth," he therefore shows her to be more honorable and more glorious, and he becomes the herald and painter of her beauty,
for the praise of her goodness does not come about in a simple way,

but a certain extended encomium of her beauty is set forth, and he praises her with a likeness fitted to each member, figuratively and truly, and says: "Behold, you are beautiful, my near one; behold, you are beautiful,"

for she became like that loving will of the Lord toward humankind, and, as with Abraham, she commanded each of the virgins to go forth from her own land and from her kindred of these visible senses, so that they might see her holy Bridegroom crowned with the crown of the Church.
For this reason she truly became near to the goodness of the Lord, and through love of neighbor she was shown to be a friend of God,
and so the Word says to her: "You are beautiful, you who by that good will of yours have drawn near to the Good." And the second repetition of the praise shows the infallibility of the testimony,
for the divine command establishes the confirmation of truth by a double testimony; hence it says: "Behold, you are beautiful, my near one; behold, you are beautiful."
But since the whole Church is of one flesh with Christ and in one body, as the Apostle says,

there are many members, and all those members do not have one function; rather, God created one as an eye in the body, and another was planted as an ear, and some are a hand for the accomplishing of mighty works.

And those by whom the weight of the body is carried are called the foot, and others serve for taste and smell, and one after another they complete the structure of all the members, through which humanity is portrayed.
And it is possible to find also a tongue in that common body of the Church, and lips and teeth and breasts and belly and neck and, as Paul says,

also those parts that are thought unseemly in the body. Therefore he who minutely examines and tests the beauty of the members of the whole body brings forth fitting and suitable praise of those that pleased him,
and he begins the encomium from the chief members.

And what among our members could be more honorable than the eyes, through which we receive the aid of light, and through which the meeting with enemies and friends takes place, and one's own is distinguished from what is foreign, which become the guide and teacher of every art and the director toward walking without stumbling,
Those joined and inseparable ones, whose structure, surpassing the other senses, displays the supreme benefit to our life that is produced by them.
and I think it is clear to all who hear it which members of the Church that praise of the eyes refers to. Samuel was an eye, who saw, and who was also called the Seer.
Ezekiel was an eye, who was appointed by God as a watchman for the life of those under his watch.
And again, the seer Micah was an eye, and the deified Moses, who for this reason was even called a god.
All those appointed as leaders of the people were eyes, whom the people of that time called seers. And now those who fill their place in the body of the Church are rightly named eyes,
if they look straight toward the Sun of Righteousness and do not blind their eyes by works of darkness,

And if they distinguish what is their own from what is alien, that is, so that they know that everything visible and transient is alien to our nature, while what is our own is those good things that are awaited in hope and prepared beforehand,
whose possession is everlasting and cannot be taken away.
It is therefore also the work of the eyes to recognize friend and enemy, to love the true friend with all the heart and soul and mind,

and if they show perfect hatred toward the enemy of our life. And again, the spotless and holy eyes become guides of action, teachers of what is better, and leaders toward God, and all such things are their work,

like these bodily eyes. Through a lofty way of life [they are] higher than the rest of the virtues [?]. Therefore, from this point the discourse begins to praise the beauty of the bride and says: "Your eyes are doves,"

for he saw simplicity and innocence in her in the form of eyes, and was pleased with this and accepted it. For this reason he also named them doves, because innocence is proper to doves. And perhaps the word also testifies to something of this kind through the praise of the eyes,
for since the images of all visible things, received by a pure and cleansed eye,
bring the power of sight to completion, for it is impossible that it should see anything unless the organ of sight has received its image and, in the manner of a mirror, perceived its likeness.
And when this power of vision is directed toward the Church and contemplates nothing material and bodily, an immaterial and spiritual life advances within her.
And such a life is formed by the grace of the Holy Spirit and advances through it.
Therefore the most perfect of all praises is the praise of the eyes, so that the form of such a life may be shaped by the graces of the Holy Spirit.
And since the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, and since two eyes are praised, that is, so that both the visible and the invisible man may fully attain to praise,
Therefore he added to that praise another, higher praise, and said: "apart from your silence,"
For part of a good life is manifest, so that it becomes known even to people, but part is hidden and ineffable and seen by God alone,

Therefore he who contemplates what has not yet come to be and sees hidden things testifies concerning that praised face that what is kept silent is greater than what is seen. Concerning the eye also he says:
"Your eyes are doves apart from your silence." For the wonder of the silence lies beyond the form that was praised,
and then, step by step, he directs his course in that manner of praise and says:
"Your hair is like flocks of goats that have appeared from Gilead." First, then, we must understand the nature of hair, and afterward consider the praise
that the word bestows on the bride by means of the hair.
Paul calls hair the glory of a woman's head, and says that this hair was given to her as an adornment.
For this reason he says that women ought to adorn their heads modestly and honorably, and he describes what is fitting for women who profess the service of God,
they are to adorn themselves with modesty and purity.
Thus by the hair of the head, with which a woman is adorned, modesty and purity are signified by Paul.
And indeed, nothing else ought to be given the name of glory for the soul that professes the service of God except modesty and purity,
which has also been given the name of hair; and whoever does not have it shames his own head, according to the word of the apostle.
And if Paul spoke thus wisely about hair, we must attend to that praise and apply the force of that saying to the church, for it says:
"Your hair is like flocks of goats that have appeared from Gilead."
For by this the word depicts and praises a virtuous way of life. And to this discussion of hair this too should be added,
that hair is foreign to all conscious sensation, and indeed this is no small enhancement of the praise,
that in the sensation of hair there is neither pain nor relief.

For the flesh from which the hairs grow feels pain when they are pulled, but the hairs themselves, whether they are cut or burned or pampered by some care, receive no sensation at all, and lack of sensation is the property of the dead. Now, then, whoever receives no sensation from the busy concerns of this world,
who is neither puffed up by glory and honor nor pained on account of [?] and contempt,

but that in both of these matters that arise they should keep themselves evenly balanced. Such is that praised hair of the bride, for she is unmoved toward the affairs of this world, like a dead person. Whether you understand it this way or that way, as we said above,

it would not be foreign to the truth. But as for how the growth and the praise of the hair resemble the flock of goats that appeared from Gilead, as it must be understood precisely, on this point we have not been able to arrive at it.
But we suppose that, just as the King changed the trees of Lebanon into gold and silver and purple and made them into a litter for himself,
Likewise the good Shepherd is able to change even a flock of goats into a flock of sheep, those that graze on the mountain of Gilead.

This is the name of a mountain of the foreigners, which has shown forth such grace: the Gentiles who followed the good Shepherd were changed by him into hair that adorns the bride's beauty. By them, according to our word examined earlier, modesty, purity, ascetic striving and the mortification of the flesh are signified. And perhaps Elijah too may be included in this figurative interpretation of the goats. He struggled for a long time on that mountain of Gilead and, still more, by his striving appeared as a leader of the ascetic life; he was sallow in color and shaggy-haired, and instead of soft garments he was covered with goatskin. Therefore all who conduct their life as he did become an adornment of the Church, which now holds, as a flock, the pattern of ascetic striving: those who strive together for virtue. And the appearing of such flocks from Gilead heightens all the more and surpasses all the more in wonder, because our change to the ascetic striving of the service of God came from a pagan way of life.
For it was not Zion, his holy mountain, that became the leader in such a life as this,
but that race which had been enslaved to idols was changed by such a good change, so that through progress in the virtues it became the adornment of that bridal head.

After this the discourse passed over the mouth and lips and presented the praise of the teeth. We must not pass over without examination why, in the praise, the teeth are mentioned before the lips. And perhaps someone might say

that it is so that, through the smile that shows the teeth, it might display the beauty of the mouth and lips as more radiant, since the whiteness and orderly arrangement of the teeth subtly enhance the redness of the lips. And for this reason it kept silent about the mouth and lips.
But besides this I also perceive another meaning, by which it becomes fitting that the praise of the beauty of the teeth should come before the mouth. For neither did it leave the lips unpraised,
but it called her lips dyed purple and her speech beautiful. And what is it that I perceive? It is the good order in learning:
that one should first learn and then utter what has been learned, or that one should first be taught and then teach.
And if someone calls spiritual teachings the food of souls, he does not stray from the truth. And just as we grind fine the food of the body with the teeth and change it into what benefits the body,

so likewise there is also in the soul a grinding power, by which spiritual instruction and teaching are changed into benefit for those who receive them. Hence those teachers who examine, distinguish, and finely grind instruction,

through whom the power of teaching and instruction becomes understandable, comprehensible, and beneficial to us, the word figuratively names teeth. Because of this grace the praise of the teeth goes first, and the praise of the lips follows afterward.
For how would the beauty of those speaking lips have blossomed, if those teeth had not clothed the lips with the grace of words from teachings examined with diligent effort?
Therefore, within the arrangement of the praises, understand this to be the reason for the praise of the teeth.

Now it is time for us to examine the praise itself as well: how it compares the beauty of the teeth to shorn flocks that have just come up from the washing, all of which rejoice together over twin offspring. The very words of the praise are these:
"Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing. All of them bear twins, and there is no barren one among them."
But if we were to consider these words in a bodily sense, I do not know how an image for praising teeth could be found in the image of prolific, shorn flocks,
for what is praised in teeth is firmness and whiteness and a well-fitted structure, and a setting arranged evenly and smoothly on the gums.
But flocks coming up from the washing, bearing twins, scattered over the pastures and marked with purple: what sort of beauty of teeth they depict by their appearance, I do not know.
The former stand together, fitted, joined and set in order,
as is the way of teeth, whereas the latter are separated from one another and scattered over the pastures.

And again, teeth are by nature bare and unsuited to comparison with wool-growing creatures. So it must be asked how the one who adorns the arrangement of the teeth with praise can liken their goodness to twin-bearing flocks,
shorn and washed. And what is it that we are to understand about this passage?
Those who by their interpretation openly break down the divine mysteries into fine pieces, so that the spiritual food may become beneficial and suitable for the body of the Church,

such people perform the work of the teeth, for they take the coarse and hard bread of the word into their own mouth, and by fine contemplation change it into beneficial food for the souls that receive it.
And I think it better that we make the meaning of this statement clear by an illustration. Blessed Paul at one time, simply and without preparation,
as if it were some unchewed bread,

He sets before us the commandments of the law and says: "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain." And again at times he softens the intent of the law by interpretation and makes it acceptable, and says: "Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Rather, it was written for our sake." And he does much else in the same way, as when he says [2?]:
"Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman." And this is the unground bread.

But see how he grinds it and makes it food for those who receive it, when he interprets their pairing as a figure of the two laws, and shows that the one was born into slavery and the other into freedom.

So too with everything in the law, that I may not speak of each item singly and prolong the discourse: he takes the coarse flesh, breaks it down finely by interpretation, changes it from bodily to spiritual, and says: "We know that the law is spiritual."
Now therefore, what we have understood concerning Paul, that he performed the work of the Church's teeth by breaking down finely and revealing the teachings,
the same we say of all those who, like him, interpret the mysteries for us,
Hence they are the teeth of the Church who grind fine for us the unchewed herbage of the divine words and chew it thoroughly,

just as the holy apostle writes concerning the bishop, that: "Whoever desires this office desires a good work." Then he depicts his life, how it must be for him to be a high priest, and when he has set forth each of his works one by one, he adds this as well: and that he should have the grace of teaching.
So likewise here the word wishes those who fulfil the office of service of the teeth of the Church
first to be purified of all material heaviness, and then to be washed with that washing of the mind from all defilement of flesh and spirit, and then
to rise ever upward by progress and never to turn back to the downward slope [?] of laxity, and then
to rejoice in the many-coloured virtues with the twin offspring of good thoughts, and not to be barren of any offspring of good works.
The bearing of twins becomes a figure of the two-sided progress of our mind, and these are those twin-bearing teeth,
so that in the soul they may give birth to impassibility, and in the life of the body to an orderly way of life. And to this they add for the lips a fitting praise, in imitation of the purple dye,
by their adornment, which he himself interpreted and called beautiful speech.
We examined this above: how the beauty of the lips is adorned by the service of the teeth,
for through the teeth, which are the interpretations of the teachers, the mouth of the Church also speaks together with them.
Therefore the teeth are shorn before the lips, and they are washed and become twin-bearing, and there is no barrenness among them. And only then do the lips bloom with purple colour,
when the whole Church becomes, through that good unity, of one voice and one word.

The figure depicts a twofold beauty, for it does not ordain for the lips merely a plain cord, but has also added the bloom of colour, so that the mouth of the Church may be adorned in two ways by the purple cord, distinctly by each aspect.
For by the cord it signifies unity of will and mind, so that the Church may become wholly of one cord and one weaving, joined and woven together from various strands [?].
And by the purple it teaches us to look toward that blood by which we were redeemed, and always to carry in the mouth the confession of him who purchased us with his own blood.
For by both of these the beauty of the lips of the Church is made perfect, when faith shines through confession and love is woven together by faith.
And if we must encompass this figure as if by some definition, we define what has been said thus: the purple cord is faith
made perfect by love, so that the purple may be referred to faith and the cord may be interpreted as love; hence the truth bears witness to the adornment of the bride's lips by these things.
But the beauty of speech does not need any more minute examination or other interpretation, for the apostle anticipated this and interpreted it beforehand, saying:
"His word is the word of faith that we preach,
for if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth you confess unto salvation." And this is that beautiful word through which the lips of the Church, like that scarlet thread, bloom with divine beauty.
And after the beauty of the mouth, the Bridegroom also dwells with satisfaction on the coloring of the cheeks,

and customary speech calls this part of the face the "fair cheek," and it likens the form of the cheeks to a slice of pomegranate rind, and with such praise it depicts these words, for it says: "Like a slice of pomegranate are your fair cheeks, apart from that silence of yours."
And that the meaning of this saying is modesty is not difficult to understand from what was said before,

for the word has given the Church a body in the likeness of a bride and has distributed the individual virtues in a manner resembling the beauty of the face, and now, by the coloring and ruddiness of the cheeks, it fittingly praises her purity, and by the figure of the pomegranate it adorns her modesty.
For this fruit is nurtured by the harshness and astringency of its rind, and hence it is well and fittingly portrayed as a figure of purity by the comparison,

For just as the harshness and astringency of the pomegranate's rind nourishes and protects the sweetness of the fruit inside, so too the austere, astringent quality of ascetic struggle and a hard life becomes the guardian of the beauty of purity.
But the double praise of this virtue is also shown here, guided by the colour of an orderly life and by the soul's freedom from passion,
whose praise, according to the word of the apostle, "is not from men but from God,"

for it has praise and acclaim appropriated and assigned to the radiant modesty shown in deeds through those conspicuous colors, yet that is apart from the silent and hidden wonders, which are seen only by that eye which sees hidden things.
And from the following words we learn that all the deeds of the God-clad saints become a model and an instruction for advancement in the virtues,
namely marriages, migrations from land to land, wars, and the raising of buildings. All these things, then, were figured as a legislation for the later way of life, as it says:
"All this was written for our instruction, upon whom the end of the ages has come,"
for war against the foreigners counsels us to courage and manliness against evil.
And eagerness for marriages figuratively teaches us the union of the virtues.
Likewise sojourning as a pilgrim sets before us dwelling in a virtuous life, and as much as one is eager to raise buildings, for those spiritual houses of ours,
he commands us to the struggle and way of life of those who are built up by the virtues.

So I think that the famous tower in which David stored the very choicest spoils shows the Church's progress toward the virtues and the struggle of a virtuous life, and prefigures it through that deed,
which he built on the mountain, and it rose to a great height, and in its time it was rightly regarded as a guard and storehouse for the spoils,

and as many of the foreigners as King David subdued, together with what remained of their weapons, and took as his own possession, he makes clear and known by his own wisdom the kind of good things that human life looks toward, and, as someone who plans something of the life to come,

by that building of the tower he left us, for our instruction, the understanding depicted in it. For he intended to praise each of the members of the body of the whole Church by comparing it to some figure,

and therefore, proceeding in order, he depicts in his words what sort of people those who are reckoned among the people as the likeness of the neck ought to be, and for this reason he mentions that tower
which is called David's and also has distinction from its battlements, for "Talpioth" is translated as "battlement."

The text reads: "Your neck is like the tower of David, which is built in Thalpioth. A thousand shields hang upon it, and all the arrows of the mighty." The visible building of this tower has no small distinction. First,

it was built by David. Second, it is distinguished by the renown of the place itself and by the choice quality of the weapons placed in it, that is, shields and arrows, whose great number the text shows by counting them in thousands.
But what we must seek is to understand the force of these divine words, and how this tower corresponds to that part of the Church which is called the neck.
First we must understand which place in the structure of the body is called the neck, and then join it to the members of the Church by comparison and interpretation. Now then,
that which is set between the shoulders and arms, which bears the head by itself and is prepared for it in place of a seat, is named the neck,
whose back part is strengthened with bones, while the front part is free from any enclosure of bones.
The structure of these bones is not like that of the arms or of the shins, but they are set in the manner of beads. And so those bones,

jointed and fastened and molded together by sinews and ligaments, are fashioned into a neck, and they go up to the head and reach up to the brain, like pipes and channels, and they enter and unite with the inner recesses of the crown of the head and the storehouses of mind and knowledge.
The structure of the front part, of the throat and gullet, is likewise borne by the neck, and within it are set the storehouses of smelling and of breathing out,
by which that fire of the heart is kindled and roused to eagerness in its proper work.

It also contains the members that convey food downward, which are called the gullet and the palate, by which it delivers everything that goes down through the mouth to the receiving storehouses of the belly.
The neck also has another superiority over the other members,

for above the courts of the heart it holds the storehouse of the voice, in which the whole structure of melodies and tones is prepared and, in the manner of an organ, rises up within the courts of the heart,
adorned and softened by the breath.
Now since the bodily form of the neck has thus been described by us, it is easier, by means of what has been examined, to perceive the neck of the body of the Church. Understand as the neck
whoever it may be who through deeds resembling it has truly acquired this name, and is called a neck and likened to the tower of David.
First, then, let us speak of the first and highest quality, that is, of the one who by himself bears that true head of all.
And I mean that head which is Christ, "from whom the whole body is joined together and made firm."
To such a one this name truly belongs. And further, if he is a receiver of the Holy Spirit, who warms our hearts and kindles them like fire, he serves the word with that sweetly speaking voice.
For in human nature God created the human voice for no other purpose than to be an instrument of the word and by itself to make known the movements of the heart.
And let such a neck also have the power and the nourishing work, which is teaching, by which the whole body of the Church is strengthened.
For as long as nourishment is continually given to it, the body remains in being, but if nourishment is lacking, it dissolves and perishes.

Let him therefore also resemble the jointed structure of the neck, so that by that bond of peace he may bring all who are among the people into one body, by bending and raising himself, by looking this way and that, and by turning about in due order.
Such a neck was Paul, and anyone else who has directed his own life as an imitator of him,

He who bore the name of the Lord and became a chosen vessel of the King, and to whom the Head of all things was so firmly joined as to a member that whatever he said, it was no longer he who spoke, but that Head spoke through his mouth,
as he writes to the Corinthians: "It is Christ who speaks in me." The courts of his heart were sweet-voiced and loud-voiced,
which the Holy Spirit strengthened with the word of truth; and he sweetened his palate with divine teachings, and by his life-giving instructions he nourished the whole body of the Church.
And if you should inquire, this truly was that God-beautiful neck of the Church. For who so joined together and made into one body all people by that bond of peace and love?

Or who has taught so brilliantly how to bend one's neck in humility and to lower oneself with the lowly, and again with heavenly thought to lift up and exalt oneself, and to look this way and that, to keep watch, and to look around skillfully at the manifold devices of the enemy, and to slip past them and guard against them?

and such a tower is built by David. Understand by him also the King and Father of the King, who in the beginning built man as a tower that would not fall, and who built him again a second time by divine grace and guarded him with those many kinds of shields,
so that he could no longer be easily captured by those who fight against him. The shields are hung up rather than lying on the ground: they are in the air, forming a wall around him,
and together with the shields, the arrows of the mighty terrify and frighten the attackers, so that they cannot even come near the foot of the tower.
And by this, as I think, it signifies the protection by angels of such a tower, whom the word depicts for us through that multitude of shields.
And the mention of the arrows confirms this understanding, for it did not say simply "arrows,"

but by the addition "of the mighty" it showed their assistance and power. Hence this word agrees with the word of the Psalms: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them."
And the counting by thousands signifies multitude,

as this is the custom of the Scriptures, which use such words in place of multitude, as David says, in place of multitude, "thousands of those who prosper" and "more than thousands of gold and silver."
So then understand the neck as founded between the shoulder blades and the shoulders,
and by the shoulders we understand the zeal of struggle and labor, through which our arms carry out our life,
and whoever listens with understanding to these sayings will surely perceive the growth toward what is higher of the soul lifted up to God; for at first it was the bride's desire
to be likened to a horse

that crushes the tyrant of the Egyptians, and after that to the beads of [?], which encircle and adorn the throat. But now, what great perfection and multitude of good things the divine Scripture testifies concerning her! For it no longer speaks of the beauty of any beads, but appoints her a tower on account of her greatness, which is made conspicuous and discernible even to those far away not only by the beauty of the building alone, but also by the height of the place
on which it is built and has reached its height,
for it is by nature higher than all the surrounding places. And when the structure of the tower has been built by the King and its foundation established upon a lofty way of life,
Then the Lord's saying is fulfilled: "A city that is built on a mountain cannot be hidden." In place of the city, understand the tower.
And, as I think, it is now time to understand also the two fawns of the gazelle, which were called breasts and which rest on the bosom of the bride, as it says:
"Your two breasts are like two kids, twins of a gazelle, that feed among the lilies," for between them lies the structure of the heart, and their pasture is neither hay nor thorn,
but the lily, which through all the times of their grazing prolongs its flower along with it, and does not blossom at one time and wither at another,
but lastingly gives these kids nourishment from itself, until the pursuits of the deceptions of this life no longer cast their shadow,
But when every place shines with light, and the light blows from every side through the day, as it says:
"Until the day breaks and the shadows are moved."
But you already know, having learned from the Gospel, that it is the Holy Spirit who blows wherever he wishes, and wherever he blows he spreads light on those who know [?] [him],

"whence it comes or whither it goes", and the present passage now sets this forth: "Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows move."
And I think that there is no one who would doubt this saying: that the Holy Spirit is called by the name of "day", and wherever it blows, it spreads light on all those over whom it spreads.

for if those who are born of the Spirit become sons of light and sons of day, what else could anyone call the Holy Spirit except day and light, whose breathings become what drives away the shadows of vanity?
For beyond all dispute, when the sun rises, the shadows flee and become invisible.
Now the mystery of the two fawns of the gazelle, whose birth is twin and whose food is the flower of lilies,
and whose place of pasture is the good and rich earth, which is the heart,
according to the word of the Lord's parable, where they feed and grow fat on the flower of pure thoughts.
And the flower of lilies has by nature a double grace, in the blending of fragrance and color,

so that each of these is desirable to those who partake of it. And whether one smells it or whether one gazes at it, it gladdens in both respects: the sense of smell is filled with the fragrance of Christ,
while through sight purity and spotlessness are beheld.
And perhaps in this way too the hidden meaning of the saying may become known, for in every human being two persons are seen:
the one fleshly and visible, the other intelligible and invisible. And the birth of both is twin, and both come into the world together,
for neither is the soul prior to the body, nor is the body prepared before the soul, but they enter this life together.
And their natural food is purity and fragrance and all such things as the virtues bring forth.
But some, instead of food, take even deadly foods: those who do not feed on the flower of the virtues, but rejoice over thorns and thistles,
for so the parable of the Gospel names sin, of which the wickedness of the serpent became the producer.
And since a discerning eye is needed, so that one may be able to distinguish and recognize precisely the thorn and the lily,
so that the saving one may be partaken of and the deadly one abhorred, for this reason, because, in the manner of the great Paul,
it would serve as a breast for infants and nourish with milk those newborn of the Church, he gave the name of two breasts, likened to those twin fawns of the gazelle.

About such members of the Church, the testimony bears witness that they are tested in every respect. Both alike advance in feeding on those holy lilies, in seeing quickly, and in telling thorns apart from food. And it is in the mind
that governs that it dwells. The image of that mind is the heart, which nourishes those breasts from itself.
And again, because it does not shut up the grace within itself, but makes it spring forth, like a breast, for those who stand in need of the word, and "as a nurse cherishes her own children,"

as the apostle both said and did. Up to this point the discourse has set forth the praise of the Church's members, but from here on it presents the eulogy of her whole body, when "through death he destroys
the one who held the power of death" and again raises himself up to his own glory of divinity, which he had before the creation of the world.

For when he said, "I myself will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense," he meant the passion by the myrrh and the glory of the divinity by the frankincense. And at once he added: "You are all beautiful, my close one, and there is no blemish in you." By these words he teaches us, first,

that no one takes his soul from him, but he has power to lay it down and power to take it up again, since he went of himself to the mountain of myrrh, and not because of our works, so that no flesh might boast.

Instead, by his own grace and his own good pleasure, he accepted death for the sake of sinners. And then: there was no other way to cleanse human nature of its blemish unless the Lamb of God, who took away the sins of the world, made all evil disappear by himself.

Therefore he said, "You are all beautiful, my close one, and there is no blemish in you." He portrayed the mystery of the passion through the figure of the dead, and then he mentioned frankincense, which signifies the divinity. By both of these he teaches us this: whoever shares in the myrrh will without doubt also become a sharer in the frankincense.
for whoever suffers with him will surely also be glorified with him. And whoever has once come to belong to the divine glory becomes wholly beautiful and a stranger to the blemish of the adversary,
which may be granted to us as well by him who died for us and rose again, to whom belong glory and power, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

The heading of this discourse: 4:8 Come, bride, from Lebanon, come from Lebanon. You will come and pass on from the beginning of faith, upon the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the dwellings of lions and from the mountains of leopards.
4:9 You have made us long, our sister, bride; you have inflamed our heart [?] with one of your eyes and with one bead of your neck.

When the great apostle told the Corinthians about those great visions, he showed that his own mind was uncertain whether he was in the body or in the mind at the time he saw the mysteries in paradise. Yet he testifies thus about himself: "I do not yet count myself as having attained, but I am still pressing on to reach what lies ahead, and I forget what is behind."
And he said this after reaching as far as the three heavens, which he alone knows and about which Moses did not speak in the account of creation,
and after hearing the unutterable mysteries of paradise, he still ascends toward what is higher and never ceases from ascending,

but makes the good things he has attained a foundation for desire of higher ones. And, as I think, by this he teaches us that of the nature of that blessed good there is much that is always being found,
But what lies higher and beyond comprehension is many times greater than what has been fully comprehended. And this happens forever among those who receive,
for the growth of those endless ages, however far one may advance, makes the advance of the one advancing endless, through the boundlessness of the divine good things,
for the one pure in heart, according to the unerring divine voice, forever sees God,
according to his own power and capacity, and as much as he is able to contain, so much of the contemplation of him does he receive.
But the incomprehensible and boundless glory of the Godhead stands above all comprehension and contemplation,
for he of whose magnificence and glory there is no limit, as the prophet testifies, is always seen at one and the same height and in one and the same incomprehensibility.
Thus the great David, who set those good ascents in his heart and went forever from strength to strength, cried out to God in this way: "But you are most high forever,
O Lord." And, as I think, by this utterance he indicates that throughout all those endless ages,
whoever flees to you forever becomes higher than himself, and continually surpasses and grows in a manner corresponding to that good ascent of his.

But you yourself remain at the same height, for it is not even possible that you should appear lower to those who ascend, since you always stand equally above the height of those who have been exalted.

In this way, then, we have learned about the nature of those ineffable good things, of which the Apostle says that they are the good things that "eye has not seen": for although it sees forever, it does not see as much as they are, but as much as the eyes are able to contain;
"and ear has not heard," that is, how great is what has been announced, for although it forever receives the hearing of them,
what is unheard is many times greater; "and it has not entered the heart of man," although the one pure in heart forever, as far as he is able, also sees,
yet what he has comprehended is undoubtedly higher than what was comprehended before, but it cannot enclose what is sought within itself;
rather, the end of what has been found becomes for those ascending the beginning of the ascent toward what is higher,
and the one ascending never stops receiving beginning from beginning, nor is the beginning of ever higher things ever brought to completion,

for the desire of the one ascending never rests at the heights already known, but from higher things toward yet other, higher desires, one after another, that God-loving soul ascends, and by continually ascending toward higher things it becomes boundless and endless.
Now since we have set this forth, from here on it is time to take up the interpretation of the divine words, for it says:

"Come, bride, from Lebanon, come from Lebanon; you shall come and pass on from the beginning of faith to the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the dwellings of lions and from the mountains of leopards." What then is it that we are to understand by these words?
The fountain of good things always draws the thirsty to itself, as is written in the Gospel: "Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink."

And by this command he made the manner of these three acts unlimited, that is, of thirsting and drinking and going to him; rather, that imperative command makes everlasting the eagerness for thirsting and drinking and going to him.
But those who taste and learn by experience that "the Lord is sweet,"

for them that tasting, as something attractive and compelling, becomes an inviter and arouser toward a higher communion; hence the one who ascends to the height never lacks the call and invitation to rise toward what is higher.
Let us also recall a few of the calls to the bride that the text has made many times above. For it says: "Come, my close one"; and again: "Come, my dove"; and again:
"Come, you, into the shelter of the rock." And there are many other such words, which call, draw her, and stir her toward higher desires and longings.

the Word set forth to the soul, and when by all of them she had been raised up to him, he bore witness to her beauty and goodness and said: "You are all beautiful, my close one, and there is no blemish in you." And so that she should not grow self-assured because of this testimony and be held back from ascending to higher advances,
again by this call he commands her to ascend to loftier advances and desires, and says to her: "Come, bride, from Lebanon."
And the meaning of this saying is as follows: You have obeyed me well and followed me well, and you have come with me to that mountain of myrrh,
for you were buried with my death through baptism, and with me you also came up to that hill of incense,
for with me you arose and with me you were exalted by participation in the divinity, which the name of Lebanon signifies.
Now therefore come up with me from here to another mountain, advanced and exalted in understanding; hence come from Lebanon no longer as one betrothed, but as a bride.
For life with me is impossible unless you are changed by the myrrh of death into the incense of divinity.
Now then, since you have come this far and have been made worthy of this height, do not stop rising, so that you may ascend to that lofty perfection.

For this beginning of faith becomes frankincense, which you came to share in through the resurrection. And this beginning, which is faith, has become for you the beginning of the advance toward higher goods.
"You shall come and pass on" -- that is to say, even now you shall come, and you shall never cease from coming by such ascents.
"You shall come and pass on from the beginning of faith to the summit of Sanir and Hermon" -- and by these mountains he sets forth the mystery of the second birth,
for they say that the springs of the Jordan come out from here, which are divided into two mountains, and these are called Sanir and Hermon.
And since the river of these springs became the beginning of our deification, she therefore hears the voice of the one who calls her, who says to her:
"Come from Lebanon, and from the beginning of faith, and from the summit of these mountains," from where the springs of the mystery spring up for you;
hence he has fittingly brought in the mention of lions and leopards, so that by means of these distressing images he might make sweeter the delight of those who bring good tidings,
For since man once stripped himself of the divine image, he became beastly through likeness to the nature of brute animals, and through evil deeds he became a lion and a leopard.

For whoever is dragged off by the lion, who lies in wait in his lair, as the Psalmist says: "and by his snare he shall be brought low"; and since that beast has overpowered his mind, he is changed into the likeness of its nature, as it says:
"Those who make them shall become like them, and all who trust in them."
And likewise, in the same way, he becomes a leopard who stains and spots his soul with the defilements of this world; and since it once was,
when humankind lived among these things, led astray by idolatry and the error of the Jews and the wickedness of sins of every kind,
but after that, through the Jordan and myrrh and incense, it was so greatly exalted

that it even became a fellow traveler with the divine height and was exalted together with it. For this reason the Word multiplies the joy of its good things by recalling the lawless deeds it once committed,
what state the soul was in before Lebanon, that is, incense, and before the beginning of faith, and before the mysteries revealed to us at the Jordan.
For just as a life of peace becomes sweeter after war,

relieved of those grievous reports, and the blessing of health delights our bodily senses all the more if nature returns to its own state from the bitterness of pains, in the same way the good Bridegroom arranged a kind of growth and multiplication of the joy in good things for the soul ascending to him.

For this reason he not only shows his own beauty to the bride but also recalls that terrible image of the beasts, so that she may delight all the more in the abundance of his good things, when she learns through figurative speech what she has gained and in exchange for what.
And perhaps some other good thing is also being prepared for the bride through these things by providence? For since we are changeable by nature,

The Word wishes our change never to be toward evil. Instead, by always growing toward what is better, we should use this calling as a helper toward higher ascents. In this way, through our changeable nature, we may achieve unchangeableness with respect to evil.
For this reason the Word set forth the mention of our estrangement from those beasts that once held power over us, as a kind of teacher and a guard against evils,
so that by turning away from evils we may achieve steadfastness and unchangeableness in good things. Then we will neither cease from changing for the better nor change for the worse.
For this reason he commands the bride to come from Lebanon, and he reminds her of the dwelling of the lions,
in which she used to dwell, and of the mountains of the leopards, in which she used to live, when she shared in the food of the beasts.
But since the voice of the Word is always a voice of power, and just as at that first command of creation light appeared and the firmament was spread out along with the other created things,
in the same way, was not the soul strengthened by the Word and made such as the Word willed,
and was it not divinely changed, and did it not ascend from glory to glory through that good change,
Then [?] this became a marvel to the assembly of the angels, and they all uttered this cry of praise and wonder about her, saying:

"You have made us long, our sister, bride." Since the image of freedom from passion shone on her in imitation of the angels, her achievement of freedom from passion while in the flesh won her kinship and sisterhood with the bodiless beings.
That is why they said to her, "You have made us long, our sister, bride," and by these two names they showed the true praise due to her.

They called her "our sister" because of their kinship in freedom from passion, and "bride" because of her union with the Word. This saying, "You have made us long," means: you have increased our desire and made us eager for divine love. It is as if they were saying to her: you have given us heart.
And so that what has been said may become still clearer, let us bring in the holy Apostle as its interpreter,
for he says in the Epistle to the Ephesians, when he recounts to us the great mystery of the Incarnation and of the manifestation of God,
that not only did human nature learn the divine mysteries through this grace and dispensation, but to the principalities and powers of heaven also was made known the manifold wisdom of God,
revealed to human beings through the dispensation of Christ. And the passage is as follows:
"So that the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers of heaven, according to the purpose of the ages,
which was accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom we have boldness and access in hope through faith in him."
And indeed the Church truly taught those higher powers the manifold wisdom of God,

which through contrary wonders worked wonders gloriously and marvelously: that is, how life came about through death, and righteousness through sin, and blessing through a curse, and glory through dishonor, and power through weakness.
For before this, in former times, the heavenly hosts knew only the simple and uniform wisdom of God, which worked wonders in keeping with its own nature.
And there was nothing manifold among the things they saw, except this alone:

that the divine nature is able to create all creatures by its power, and by a mere nod of its will to bring the nature of beings into existence, and so to make everything to be good and very good, and to have its root and its growth from that fountain of good things.
But this varied form of wisdom, brought to perfection by the combining of opposite things,
they have now learned from the Church, in a manner befitting God: how the Word becomes flesh, how life is joined to death,

how by his own wound he heals our wound, how by the weakness of the cross he crushes the power of the adversary, how the invisible one appears in the flesh, how he redeems captives and is himself both the ransom and the purchaser,
for he gave himself up to death as a ransom for us,
and how he both accepts death and is not separated from life, and how he is both joined to slaves and remains king.

For all these and such things, the works of wisdom, not simple but manifold, the friends of the bridegroom learned from the Church; and they became stout-hearted and added desire upon desire, and through this mystery they understood another form of divine wisdom.

And if it is not presumptuous to say so, did they perhaps also behold the beauty of the Bridegroom through the bride? Were they astonished and amazed at how the one who is invisible and incomprehensible to all beings,
"whom no one has ever seen, nor is able to see," made the Church his own body and, by adding those who are saved, builds himself up in love?
"until we all become a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ."
Now therefore, since the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is the head of the body, and by his own likeness he forms the face of the Church,
perhaps the friends of the bridegroom perceived this too, and their hearts burned with desire, for they see the invisible one more plainly in her,
just as those who cannot look upon the disc of the sun see its likeness in the purity of water,

so too they contemplate the Sun of righteousness in the Church as in a polished mirror, that is, the invisible through the visible. And for this reason it has been said more than once to the bride by the friends of the bridegroom:
"You have filled us with longing," which is to say: you have implanted in us, through yourself, a certain power and understanding for contemplating the light, greatly desirable and longed for;
and they return a second time to the same word, so that by this they may make what was said more credible, and they say:
"You have set our heart on fire with one of your eyes," and this is the source of what made the friends' love for the bridegroom all the more astonishing,
for since the power of sight in the soul is twofold, and with the one it contemplates the truth, while with the other it strays toward vanities,

and since the spotless eye of the bride is opened only toward the one who is by nature good, while the other is shut, for this reason the friends set forth the praise of one eye, by which alone she sees the Only One. And by the Only One I mean him who is known in the unchanging and eternal and incomprehensible nature,
that is, the true Father and the only-begotten Son and the all-holy Spirit, for he is truly the Only One,
who is beheld in one nature and admits no division or severance on account of the properties of the persons. For there are some
who see insubstantial things in many forms, and with their roving eyes wickedly contemplate a division into many natures, and with their sharp and keen gazing at fantasies are torn this way and that.
These are the ones who are called many-seeing,

who by their seeing many things do not see even one thing, and who at one moment look toward God and then again are torn this way and that toward material marvels; by being nailed to those insubstantial marvels they are unworthy of the praise of the angels.
But whoever looks keenly and sharply toward God alone, toward all other sights,

is blind to the things toward which the eyes of the many look. For this reason the bride amazes the friends of the bridegroom with one eye, since the many-eyed person who looks toward vanities with many eyes is blind,
but keen-sighted and seeing with the soul is the one who, with that one eye of the soul, looks only toward the one and only good.

What that one eye is, and what that one bead of the bride's neck is, is not hard to understand from what has been said above, even if their meaning is not perhaps made plain. For the passage says this:
"You have given us heart with one of your eyes and with one bead of your neck."
for that "one" and the phrase "with one of your eyes" are one by being joined with that one soul.
For in each untrained person many souls appear. Among these, the passions take the place of the soul by tyranny and seize the soul's places.
These passions are grief and pleasure, anger and fear, cowardice and rashness. In this same way they [?] exchange themselves for the form of the soul, and they become many souls within it.
But whoever looks toward the Word by that simple, God-pleasing life, such a one is attested to live with one soul; hence, by "one" it gives us to understand the force of the first phrase,
whether as one soul, or as one life and one way of conduct.
The next phrase has another force. That is: "with one bead of your neck," which is understood in this way:
that your eye is one by looking toward the one, and your soul too is one for this reason, that it is not divided by love toward many things,
and the structure of your neck too has acquired a lofty perfection, which is the bearing of the divine yoke upon it.
For since, through the one bead of your neck, we discern the divine yoke upon you, and through love of those true goods we acknowledge one eye and one soul, for this reason we confess
that: "By your wonders you have made us stout-hearted, for you show one eye and one soul with that one bead of your neck." And the one bead of the bride's neck is the yoke of Christ, as we have said.
This, then, is the praise of the angels, which they set forth concerning the bride, for we understand these to be the friends of the bridegroom.

And so that no one might suppose that their praise is set forth without having been seen and examined, the Word confirms their acclamation and of himself adds greater wonders by testifying to her beauty, and portrays the beauties of her members in his own words,

which we shall add next, in order, by the will of God, if the divine power helps us to discern the mysteries, for the understanding of the Church and for praising the glory of his grace through Christ Jesus our Lord,
to whom belong glory and honor, now and always and unto the ages of ages, amen.
The heading of this discourse: 4:10. How beautiful your breasts have become, more than wine, my sister, bride!

How much more beautiful your breasts have become than wine, and the scent of your ointments above all spices! 4:11. Your lips drip honey, bride, honey, and milk is under your tongue. And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon. 4:12.
A secluded garden is my sister, bride, a garden shut up and a spring sealed. 4:13. Your sendings-forth are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruit of the orchard, henna with nard; 4:14.
nard and saffron, incense-reed and cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloes with all the first ointments. 4:15.
A spring of the garden and a well of living water, rushing down from Lebanon.
"If you have been raised with Christ, think on heavenly things and not on earthly things": this is what he says to you, the one who spoke in Paul, for he testifies that:
"You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God, and when Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear in glory." Now therefore,
if we have died to earthly nature, let us raise the hope of our life from earth to heaven; and if the life of the flesh is hidden from us, according to the word of the Proverb that says:
"The wise conceal perception," and if we await the manifestation in us of the true life, which is Christ, so that we too may appear in glory, divinely transformed,
then let us hear these passages now read as if we had died in the flesh, and let us not be drawn by these words toward even one thought of the flesh,
for whoever has died to passions and desires receives the disclosure of the divine words as a power of purity and incorruption, since he thinks on what is heavenly,
where Christ himself is, seated at the right hand of the Father, where the stain of base and passionate thoughts is not seen, but forgetfulness of everything of this kind comes about.
Now therefore let us hear those divine words by which divine Scripture depicts the beauty of that spotless bride,
but let us hear them as those who are estranged from flesh and blood and spiritually changed in nature, for it says:

"How beautiful your breasts have become, more than wine, my sister, bride; how much more beautiful your breasts have become than wine, and the scent of your ointments above all perfumes." Now this, namely that:
everyone who does the will of God is his brother, and sister, and mother;
and that whoever is joined to the Lord is called a holy virgin and a partaker of that incorruptible bridal chamber, is plain and evident to everyone who is not ignorant of the divine Scriptures.
But I have examined the force of this divine saying, and in such a form of address I see not simple praise offered to the bride by the word,

but I say that the causes of her growth in beauty are being set forth by the Bridegroom, for she would not have been made beautiful, as with a spring of those good teachings which he figuratively names breasts, if she had not first shown herself by good deeds to be a sister of the Lord,
and if she had not been renewed by a second birth through holy virginity, and betrothed, and shown to be the bride of the one who betrothed her.
Now therefore, he who has named her his sister and bride states this as the reason for the surpassing and more perfect transformation of her breasts,
which no longer bring forth milk, the food of infants, but well up with incorruptible wine, which gladdens the perfect, whose grace the merchants' mixing with water could not spoil;
Now perhaps some joy of marriage and ardor of love are shown by these sayings: on both sides it is bestowed upon each other, in the manner of bridal passion and ardor.
For with words imitating her own, the bridegroom praises the church, in the same way that she first glorified his beauty.
For at once, in the very first words, when she became desirous of hearing the divine word and voice from his mouth,

He depicted this in the form of a kiss. As the cause of such desire he set forth the goodness of her breasts, calling them better than the nature of wine and surpassing the fragrance of all ointments and spices. He said:
"Your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments is better than all spices."
And since we have learned this teaching in all the other divine theological writings as well: God always changes toward us according to the disposition that we show toward God.

For David testifies prophetically and says, "How good is God to the upright in heart," whereas for those who have become bestial in their way of life, another prophet designates him a bear and a leopard; and he presents this figuratively through the teachings of the Gospel, according to which he appears in one form to those on the left and in another form to those on the right,

to the one group sweet and kind, but to the other terrible and dreadful, for he changes in both directions in conformity with their will and mind. For this same grace, then, now too the bridegroom's recompense is shown in conformity with the bride's will, and with praises like those with which she glorified the king's beauty, the king responds to her.
For he also takes into account that her breasts were changed for the better through good deeds. They stopped producing milk, and they now bring forth not milk but wine,

Through it, joy comes to the hearts of the perfect, who are no longer tossed about by childishness. Instead, they are able to be filled from the cups of wisdom and to eat solid food by mouth. So he praised her breasts by comparing them to wine, and he added fragrance to the praise as well, saying:
"And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices";

but we must understand such praise, named from the holy Scriptures, not as though it spoke of those ointments which through their smell become a delight to the nostrils; rather, it speaks of those ointments
which we have learned of from the holy Scriptures, as when Noah offered a sacrifice to God and the Lord smelled it as a scent of fragrance, whence such a sacrifice becomes an ointment to God.
And many other such sacrifices were offered to God after this under the Law: propitiatory offerings, thank offerings, offerings of salvation, purification offerings, and offerings for sins.
Understand all these as ointment, and also the whole burnt offerings, the incense offerings, and those divided offerings of cut portions [?],
the priestly breast, the lobe of the liver, and the fat of the kidneys, and with these, incense and fine wheat flour,
kneaded with oil, and the incense of aromatics, and everything else that was purified by fire: place these in the ranks of these same perfumes.
Now therefore, when we hear that the fragrance of the bride is greater than all perfumes, we understand this as something honorable and acceptable:

that the mystery of truth, brought to fulfillment by the teaching of the Gospel, is a divine fragrance and surpasses all those perfumes of the law, since it is no longer hidden by any figure and shadow,
but is made fragrant by the revelation of the truth.

For although the Lord did smell some of those former perfumes as an odor of fragrance, each of them was made worthy of his acceptance according to the power and mind of those who offered it, and not according to the form and rite of the deeds visibly performed. And this is clear from that lofty prophetic voice which says:
"I will not accept bullocks from your house, nor goats from your flock, for I will not eat the flesh of bullocks, nor will I drink the blood of goats."

Although offerings were many times made by the slaughter of animals, yet even if some such thing is done, the law taught to you through that figure is another one, namely the slaughter and killing of the passions, as it says:
"The sacrifice of God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise."
And in the same way the sacrifice of praise is prepared by us, which is made for the glorification of him

who smells such fragrances as a fragrant odor. And since that soul has passed through all those figures of the perfumes of the law and has risen above them, the soul which, according to the apostolic saying, has become the fragrance of Christ by a virtuous life, and priestly myrrh and compounded incense,
made fragrant by the flower of the various virtues and well perfumed, whose scent the Bridegroom's sense of smell received as an odor of fragrance, therefore the divine sense,
as Solomon names it, prefers to those bodily perfumes of the law that immaterial and pure fragrance compounded of the virtues, and says:

"And the scent of your myrrhs is above all perfumes." And the following word raises the praise to a higher praise, and testifies and confirms that the wealth of those spiritual graces was acquired by her through discipline and diligence,
since the word of the Proverbs commands the disciple of wisdom to go to the bee. And you, understand from the teachings who that teacher is, for he says to those lovers of wisdom:
"Go to the bee and learn how it is a worker, and its work,

as something precious, it displays, whose labor kings and the poor receive for life." And he declares it desirable to all and praiseworthy, weak in strength but strong in wisdom, and says that it honored wisdom. And for this reason it was presented as an example to those who struggle and those of virtuous life, for it says
that it honored wisdom and displayed it.
And by these sayings he counsels that one neglect none of the good teachings,

but so that it may fly to and fro, and from the flowery [meadow] of good words, and by the power of wisdom, gather the flower of each book and prepare divine honey for itself; and, as in a kind of hive, store up this love of labor in its heart; and as in some cells of honey,
keep those many-formed teachings by unconfused memory in those four-walled treasuries.
And thus, like that wise bee, whose honey is sweet and whose sting does not wound, may it trade perpetually in this precious labor of the virtues. For truly that person trades
who has bought those eternal good things with this labor of the present world, and has distributed the fruits of his labors to kings and to the poor for spiritual life.
And through this such a soul becomes desirable to the Bridegroom and longed for by the angels, and in weakness it accomplishes strength by the honor of wisdom.

The parable of the wise bee is an image of learning and striving, and the many different distributions of spiritual graces are won by those who strive, in proportion to their zeal. For this reason he says to the bride:

Your heart has been filled with the honeycomb of many kinds of teaching. From there, out of the good treasures of your heart, you bring forth the dew of honey-dripping words, so that your words are mixed with honey and milk. That is why he says:
"Honey drips from your tongue, O bride; honey and milk are under your tongue."
For such are your words that they do not offer a simple benefit to their hearers, but are changed according to the capacity of those hearers,

so that they are suited particularly both to the perfect and to infants: for to the perfect they become honey, and to infants milk. Such was Paul, for to some, as to newborns, he became a nourisher by means of soft words,
And among the perfect she spoke wisdom, hidden in mystery from the ages,

which this world cannot contain, nor the rulers of this world. He says that she keeps this mixture of milk and honey under her tongue, stored up and ready for whenever she wishes to bring the word forth. For whoever knows how to answer each person as is fitting, and has the many-sided power of the word, offers each hearer the manner of speech that suits that hearer's need.

And having bestowed such praise on the mouth and tongue of the bride, he rises again to higher praises and says: The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon, that is, of frankincense. And this saying is philosophy, which shows toward what it is proper

that the virtuous life of human nature should look. For the beginning and end of the virtuous life is likeness to God; and whether it be the holy and spotless purity of the soul, unmixed with any passionate love, that is pursued through labor among the virtues
for the sake of this grace, or some other of those great labors, it is so that some likeness of that surpassing nature, of that height and of immaterial life, may come to be among them too.

And since the rule of virtuous conduct is not of one kind or of one form, but just as the structure of a woven fabric is prepared by means of many warp threads and weft threads, and in this way, by weaving, the cloth for a garment is completed,
so likewise for the virtuous life it is necessary to prepare many materials,
by which the divine life is woven, just as the holy Apostle enumerates such materials, by which the holy order of such weaving is completed.

For he speaks of love and joy and peace and long-suffering and kindness and all such things, by which that person is adorned who, in place of an earthly and corruptible life, has put on the incorruptibility of the heavens. And for this reason he reckons the adornment of the bride's garment as the fragrance of frankincense.

Although before this he showed the bride's myrrh to surpass all ointments in fragrance, so that it may be supposed that this undoes that praise of her fragrance, since that which there exceeded all ointments
is now likened to a single incense, for he says: "As is the fragrance of frankincense, so is the fragrance of your garments."
However, since by some dispensation frankincense has been set apart for divine honor,
for this reason that which is greater than all ointments has been likened to the one incense set apart for the Godhead. And the meaning of this figure is as follows:

O bride, the excellence of your virtues becomes like the divine blessedness through purity and impassibility, having become an imitator of that incorruptible nature; and such is the fragrance of your garments
that it is like the frankincense which has been appointed for divine honor and offering.

Again, from the praises that follow we learn how someone may become a royal bride and a sister of the Lord, for he says: "My sister, my bride, is an enclosed garden." This means that whoever wishes to become a bride through divine communion, and to become his sister by doing the will of God, as the Gospel says, must first become a flowering garden, and the beauty of every kind of plant must bloom in it.
that is, the sweetness of the fig, the fruitfulness of the olive, the height of the palm, and the clusters of the vine.
No thorny bush should stand in it, nor thistle, nor brier [?], but cypress and myrtle. For this is how the great David and the loud-voiced Isaiah adorn such a garden. The first says:
"The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree,"
and "Your wife is like a fruitful vine," and "But I am like a fruitful olive tree."
And another prophet calls blessed the one who rests under his own fig trees, while Isaiah commands cypress and myrtle to spring up in place of the juniper and the bramble.
But it is superfluous now to set out in detail the symbolic meaning of each of these plants, since it is clear to everyone
what the sweetness of the fig is, ripened from that bitter unripeness, which at first is bitter and useless, but at the last becomes the fruit of peace and sweetens the senses of the soul.
And again, if the fruitfulness of the olive: what does it grant us from that astringent and bitter taste which is seen at the beginning in that fruit,

and then, step by step, through ripening and the labor of the workers, it is changed into the nature of oil. Oil becomes the material for light, rest from labors, comfort in afflictions, something that makes the head shine, and a help in the contest for those who strive lawfully.
And as for how the palm keeps its fruit out of the reach of thieves:

it stores its fruit up high, not low down and not on the ground. Then there is the generosity of the vine, the fragrant cypress, and the delightful myrtle.
