Through figurative interpretation all of these are turned into meanings of virtue. No one who thoughtfully examines what each of them means, and what the text is pointing to, is unaware of this, even though we have passed over it.

Now therefore, whoever appears as a garden of such plants and becomes a delightful paradise, guarded on every side by the wall of the commandments, so that he gives no entrance to himself either to beasts or to thieves,

for whoever is surrounded by the wall of the commandments is inaccessible to the raging wild beast, and the boar of the forest cannot ravage him. Such a one becomes a guarded garden, and becomes sister and bride of him who said to such a soul: "A guarded garden is my sister, the bride."

But since this garden also has need of a spring, so that its grove may become flourishing and unwithered through constant watering and enrichment by the waters, for this reason he joined a spring also to the praises of the garden, and said:
"A garden locked, a spring sealed." And concerning the spring, the Proverbs teach us the word in a parable and say:
Let the spring of water be set apart for you, and let it be for you alone, and let no stranger share it with you,
For just as there he keeps strangers from drinking the water of the spring, so here too he testifies that this spring is never to be reached by strangers, through the word that he spoke,
namely: "sealed." This is the same as saying "guarded."

What is said here means this: in our way of speaking, the understanding power of our soul is called a fountain, because it brings up all the thoughts within us and makes them spring forth. But this movement of the mind comes about for us at that time
when it is moved toward what is better for us and gives us every help toward gaining the good.

But when it turns the help of its thoughts to the planning and contemplating of wickedness, then its stream is drained off to strangers, when with the help of its thoughts it readily waters and nourishes that nursling, the thorn-like life, while it dries up and withers those plants and spiritual paradises, and spreads not one stream of good thoughts to nourish and enrich the roots of that divine vine.
And since sealing makes what is sealed by it safe from theft, by means of the seal it frightens off the thief, and everything unstolen is kept without loss for its own master.

In this place he sets forth the full and surpassing praise of the bride through these words, and by this testimony he confirms the extolling of her virtues: that her mind remains untouched by enemies, kept in purity and freedom from passion for her own King.

For purity seals this fountain, when no muddying material thing muddies the purity and spotlessness of the heart. And so that we may tell you the force of this saying more clearly, understand it thus:
since, among the things in us, some are truly ours, namely all that is proper and particular to the soul,
and some we claim as ours, by which I mean the bodily and external, and by some mistaken supposition we call that foreign thing our own,
for what communion does the immaterial nature of the soul have with the coarse constitution of material things?

And therefore the word of the Proverbs counsels us not to spend the fountain of our mind on foreign and external things, which are the body and bodily affairs, but to let it flow within its own garden and enrich that divine paradise.

Now the virtues are called the paradise of God. The understanding power of our soul, nailed to their discipline and flowing out toward nothing external, is sealed with the seal of truth and imprinted with the love of the good.
But let us also look at the force of the praise that follows, for it says:
"Your sendings are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruit of the orchard, henna with spikenard;
spikenard and saffron, incense of reed and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon;
myrrh and aloes with all the first ointments; and a fountain, a garden, and a well of living water, rushing down from Lebanon."
For indeed a great and astonishing meaning is hidden in these sayings, by which the beauty of the soul lifted up toward God is proclaimed through these various adornments with surpassing praise.
This is clear even from these words themselves, spoken simply.

But a precise understanding of it is possible only for Paul, or for one like him, who knows through the Spirit the counsel of the divine mysteries. For how is the sending of the bride a paradise of pomegranates,
or how does the fruit of pomegranates suit the fruit of the orchard, or how do the fruits of trees become myrrh and ointments of every kind,
for along with the fruit of the trees are mentioned henna and spikenard and saffron and incense of reeds and cinnamon and all the trees of Lebanon,
While no separation is yet made between the trees of Lebanon and the many-colored and various spices,
to which are added myrrh and aloes and all the chief spices. For what was called a garden earlier by the one who praises her
is now named a fountain, a garden and a well of living water, flowing strongly from Lebanon. But the true understanding of these things, as I said above, is surely known to those
who were able to search out through the Holy Spirit the depth and wisdom and riches of the knowledge of God.
But as for us, in this place, so that we may not be left wholly without enjoyment and without a taste of the good things set before us, let us touch only a little on the force of the saying.
And let us make the Word of God himself the guide of our endeavor.
All these ranks of praises, as many as were spoken before this and as many as the discourse has now set before us concerning her, do not aim at some mere encomium,
but through these sayings they give strength to the heart and fortify it to rise to greater and higher ascents.

And understand it thus: she is called sister and bride of the Word, and each of these names joins the soul to the Bridegroom in a twofold way. For by signifying bridehood it makes her "one flesh and one body" with the incorruptible Bridegroom, according to the apostolic saying,
and by zealously fulfilling his will it raises her to the kinship of sisterhood, according to the voice of the Gospel.
And next the nature of her breasts is praised, which bring forth wine instead of milk.

And thus it becomes clear that it is deeds that are praised, and that what is presented is not some insubstantial and idle encomium. And next, along with these, her ointment is declared to be above all perfumes, and it would not have been praised in this way
if she had not, through her progress, ascended to such a true height.
And next the honey-dripping of her words, which came forth from her mouth, is made a marvel, and also the blending of her wisdom, treasured under her tongue, which imitates milk and honey.
And these too are powers, not words, for, guided by the Word through surpassing ascents, she grew so greatly
that she showed her mouth to be a spring of honey and made her tongue a treasury of that blended wisdom, like the land of promise, which brings forth honey and milk.
And through ascents the Word raised her this high, and yet he leads her higher still, for he called her garment fragrant,
like the fragrance of libanos, by which the Word testifies concerning her that she has put on Christ.
But the perfection of every virtuous life comes about through divine communion, for by libanos, that is, incense,

divinity is signified. Nor did the Word stop even here in raising her to what is higher, but after the soul's likeness to the fragrance of incense, he showed her to be a garden, in the likeness of paradise,
a garden, however, not such as that of the first human beings was, left loose and unguarded, but one locked and walled on every side by the remembrance of the commandment.
Do you see what power she has received for ascending to the height? Wait for me a little, then, and I will show you once more her surpassing excellence,
for not only did she appear as a garden, locked and yielding its own food, but she also becomes drink for the thirsty by changing into the nature of a spring, and a sealed spring.
And she did not stop here either, but so far surpassed herself in growth that from her mouth she brought forth paradise.
who carefully understand the meaning of this passage as written in Hebrew. In place of this it is written "sendings" [apostleships], as follows:
"From your mouth, a paradise of pomegranates." This means: "Your word, which is the sending forth of your mouth, is a paradise of pomegranates."
These pomegranates produce many kinds of fruit, and the fruits are henna with nard, and saffron, the reed of incense [calamus], and cinnamon.
and all these trees of Lebanon, and myrrh and aloes and the first perfumes.

For since, according to the beatitude of the Psalm, the help of God has come to be with her, and she has set these good ascents in her heart, ascending forever from strength to strength, the sendings-forth of her mouth are rightly called a paradise
of pomegranates. For the completeness of its order, and in conformity with the sense that follows, this joining of these words was made,
For a sending passes from the one who sends toward the one to whom it is sent. This is clear from the usage of ordinary speech, and the Gospel also says it,
for the Word called "apostles" those disciples whom he sent out to preach the truth.
What, then, is it that the bride's mouth sends forth? Is it not clear that it is the word of faith,

which, when it reaches those who receive it, becomes a paradise in those in whom it is planted through the ears? By custom, a place where plants and many-colored trees are gathered together is called a paradise. So that we may also learn what kind of plants the word plants in the soul of believers, the text calls the fruit-bearing plants that are planted by the word sent forth from the bride's mouth "pomegranates." The pomegranate is hard for thieves to lay hands on,
for it puts out thorny branches, and it encloses its fruit in an astringent and bitter covering and nourishes it inside.
which in its own time, when it ripens and that covering splits, shows forth [?] from within, beautifully arranged and desirable to look at,
and delightful and honey-like in flavor, and with its wine-colored juice sweetening the senses of taste.
And as I think, it is for this reason that the word sent forth from the mouth of the bride prepares paradises of pomegranates in the soul of the hearers:
so that we may learn from these sayings not to go slack in this present life, nor to grow soft through any delight and luxury, but to acquire a harsh life by struggle and fasting;

so that in this way the fruit of virtue may become unapproachable to thieves, and, enclosed in that harsh covering of simplicity and by that venerable and unsmiling composure, may ward off, as by the sharpness of thorns, those who wish to approach and harm us;
so that when the time of rest and of the gathering of the fruits of all the orchards comes,

that paradise of pomegranates may become fruitfulness and delight for us, and not an acorn and [?], or anything else of that kind, but may change into the many-colored and many-formed nature of perfumes, that is, into henna and nard and the fragrance of the remaining perfumes that it names.
And how good is that fine pairing of henna and nard: the heat of the one and the fragrance of the other.

For heat alone, taken by itself, is not praiseworthy when that heat turns rank from burning; rather, that heat must be tempered by the fragrance of purity, so that one may become fervent in the Holy Spirit, purified from that unsavory heat.
And together with the fruit of these orchards other fragrances are also found, for it says: nard and saffron.

We have spoken above about the fragrance of nard, and now it is fitting to speak of the symbolism of saffron. Those who have studied this flower's power say that it is neither hot nor cold. It is free from leaning to either side and is balanced, and it has the power to soothe pains. As I think, this figure teaches, in a philosophical way, the form of the virtues,
for every virtue is a mean between two vices: an excess of the good and a deficiency of it. Examples are courage and cowardice,
fearfulness and boldness, and stinginess and prodigality. Fearfulness and stinginess fall short of the proper measure, while prodigality and boldness belong to excess.
But flight from immoderation on either side is called virtue, and it is virtue. And for this reason I said of saffron that it is a figure of the due virtues,
which are neither excessive nor deficient.
But I say that the symbolism of saffron fits the word of faith even better, for this flower is seen to be threefold;

And the flower that it puts forth is like the air and pure; and when it blooms, this threefold flower is found to be fragrant and well suited for healing. In size, goodness, fragrance and the particular nature of its power these flowers are alike, and nothing can compare with them.
of which, as I said, the color and beauty and fragrance and character are equal and of one form. Along with it are seen three other flowers, yellow in appearance and useless for any needful purpose,
by whose worthless color the ignorant and unlearned are deceived, and in place of the good ones they gather those [?],
which is what those people also do now who pervert the faith, and who in place of the right and sound teachings choose that invented and concocted error.

Now then, let the hearer's ears on both sides choose whichever he wishes, either one side of what has been said or both, for both are one, whether it be the acquiring of perfect virtue or of God, since virtue is not outside God.

But let us proceed to the examination of the other ointments, for the fragrant reed and cinnamon are fruits brought forth from the gardens of the bride. Concerning the reed they say that it surpasses the other incenses in fragrance, so that it was even what gave fragrance to the priestly incenses of the law. But concerning cinnamon they relate many and varied things about its natural constitution and power, most of which deserve ridicule rather than belief. For they say that if someone brings this ointment near a boiling [?], it immediately cools, and if someone brings it into heated baths, it at once changes the heat in the air to coolness,
and that it makes the worms born of decay disappear. And they say another unbelievable thing as well, that
if it is placed in the mouth of a sleeper, it causes no hindrance at all either to his sleep or to his speech,
but whatever anyone asks him, he answers just as one who is awake. To testify that this is so, and to affirm an untested matter, betokens no small folly and rashness.

However, since by some mystical word this too has been counted among those fruits of paradise and ointments, which did not in truth sprout from a pomegranate, and indeed it is not possible for visible gardens to sprout from the mouth of a bride, but rather so that some understanding and figurative speech of profit might be conveyed to us concerning the praise of the bride,

it is not good that we should entirely dismiss that talk of the storytellers about cinnamon, which we have now related concerning it and which others relate, lest perhaps some profitable word be found in it, one that depicts the perfection of a virtuous life.
For this cinnamon is found in those trained, learned and understanding souls, when someone either burns with desire,
or boils with anger and quenches that passion with good thought; or if, in the sleep of this life, he carries in his mouth that vigilant cinnamon of thoughts, and like

those sleepless, wakeful angels, unerringly and without disturbance shows forth the power and meaning of these sayings, and by the truth of his word imitates that unsleeping nature of the angels, whom no compulsion of any marvel separates from the truth. And perhaps this is that cinnamon which came forth from the mouth of the bride,
by which the boiling of desire and anger is quenched, and speech becomes pure and undisturbed by the dreamlike marvel and confusion of all this life.

And let no one find fault with this account of the cinnamon because it seems hard to believe, as though the praise we offer the bride were not based on truth. Holy Scripture often makes use even of certain outside fables to help convey its own spirit and meaning. Without embarrassment it borrows certain names from fabulous tales so as to make plain
the meaning it intends. So it is with the daughters of Job: the text made their beauty astonishing and showed how far their wonder exceeded others through their names, and it said,
that he called the first Day, and the second Cassia, and the third Horn of Amalthea.
And this is clear to all: the notion of Amalthea was put forth by pagan myth. She was a goat and became the nurse of certain persons, as they tell in their tales,

and one of her horns was torn off, and from the hollow [?] of that torn-off horn countless good things came forth. And for this reason it was called the horn of gladness, as the tale named it. Now then, did the divine book believe it? Far be that tale from it!

Rather, it testified to the adornment of Job's daughter with all the goods of virtue, and through this name it showed her truth. Hence the reader or hearer of the divine books, with understanding, perceives through the name only the aspect of praise, and pays no attention at all to the lies of the tale.
And just as, when we hear Cassia and Day, neither the substance of fragrances,
Nor do we understand the course of the sun by those names; rather, we speak of the loftiness of their names in order to make their virtues known,
of which Kasia displays the purity and fragrance of her deeds,
and Day displays beauty, according to the word of the Apostle, for he gives those who live blamelessly the name of children of light and sons of the day.
So too here, it is not unfitting as praise of the bride that cinnamon should be mentioned, spoken figuratively by way of interpretation;
and she who became so great and attained the height of such praises through her way of life, and who through all things displayed in herself the likenesses of the divine image,
and this is made clear by the word that says: "from all the trees of Lebanon."

For those who know them by experience do not speak of the trees of Lebanon, from which frankincense comes, as being of one kind; rather, there is a certain difference among these trees, which alter the kind of incense through their own variation. Now therefore,
Whoever carries out all the works of this life by his own effort in a way beautiful before God displays in himself the beauty of all the trees of Lebanon, through which the divine image is depicted.

But no one becomes a sharer of the divine glory who has not first been conformed to the likeness of his death. For this reason, in the harmony of the fragrances, the composition of the praise mentions this as well.
that there are also those other perfumes, the orchards of pomegranates, which the word mentioned above, and together with them myrrh and aloes and the first perfumes,
for by myrrh and aloes it signifies participation in the burial, as the loud-voiced Gospel says,
for these perfumes were prepared for the burial of the Lord, who tasted death for us.

And by the first perfumes the word indicates purity and freedom from any admixture of all hidden malice, as Amos says to those who take their delight in such things: that those who drink strained wine and anoint themselves with the first perfumes, and again, before this,
that those who eat kids from the flock and tender suckling calves from the pomegranates [?] and clamor to the sound of instruments,
neither did dregs make the wine turbid, nor did any admixture corrupt the preciousness and fragrance of the perfumed oil.

Yet there the prophecy speaks in reproach of the Israelites, for they were sated with the undiluted words of the Scriptures, strained of all dregs, and they had the guileless fragrance of the perfumes and delighted in all spiritual delicacies.

And they gained no profit from such delight, for the wickedness of their wills made even the purity of the wine appear foamy and turbid, and corrupted the fragrance of the first perfumes by mixing in evil intentions.
But here the word testifies on behalf of the bride to undefiled and pure teachings through the fruitfulness of the first perfumes.
Nor did it stop at these, for neither did the bride grow weary of advancing toward higher measures, nor did the word cease from assisting her and raising her up.
For the one whose shoots (literally 'sendings-forth') are a paradise of pomegranates and ointments now becomes a fountain herself, watering the paradises that have sprung up from her.
It is not as we have learned about Paul and Apollos, where one planted and the other watered.
Instead, the bride does both, for she plants the paradises and waters them at the same time. And might this praise perhaps point to some higher power?
For it calls her a spring, not as one giving rise to any waters but to gardens, not as one flowing with streams,

but as one who herself waters and raises up those very gardens. In this way the holy apostle rose up for those spiritual gardens, and whomever he approached, he prepared by his teaching into a paradise of the church.
And then the word, through these praises, raises the bride to the summit of praises and gives her the name of a well of living water, rushing [?] from Lebanon,
for this is what we have learned from the Scriptures about the life-giving nature, since at one point it says, "They have forsaken me, the spring of living water."
And again, the Lord said to the Samaritan woman: If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who is saying to you,
"Give me water to drink," you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water. And again:
"Let whoever is thirsty come to me and drink, for whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly."
"And he said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were going to receive."

And in every place living water is presented as an image of the divine nature. And here the unerring testimony of the word calls the bride a well of living water, whose springing forth is from Lebanon.

And this is exceedingly wonderful and astonishing, for all other wells have their supply of water from gathered drops and trickles, but the bride alone has her wealth of waters from a river: the depth is that of a well, but the water is from a swiftly rushing river. And who could worthily express the wonders of this power
which have come about in her through likeness to God?

And there is almost no higher measure left to be found to which she might raise herself, since she has been made like that firstborn beauty in every respect. And consider how exactly she has been made like it,
for she has been made like the spring by being a spring, like life by life, and like water by water. And since the word of God is living, the soul that receives the word is living too.
That water comes forth from God, as he says: "I came forth from God and have come."
And she receives it in the well of her soul and becomes a treasury of that living water coming from Lebanon, or rather rushing down with force, as the word has named it.
May we also be made worthy of it and obtain that well, so that according to the commandment of wisdom we may drink our own water and not a stranger's,
through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom glory and honor are fitting, now and always and forever and ever. Amen!

Chapter. This passage: 4:16. Arise, north wind, and come, south wind. Blow upon my garden, and let my spices flow. Let my brother's son come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his orchards. 5:1.
I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride. I have gathered my myrrh with my spices. I have eaten my bread with my honey. I have drunk my wine with my milk.
Eat, my companions, and drink and become drunk, my kinsmen! 5:2. I sleep, but my heart is awake.

The present examination of the divine words set before us, taken from what follows in the Song of Songs, has a meaning that is hard to reach, hidden, invisible, unrevealed, and lying in inexpressible depths;

and we need greater reverence, and still more abundant help through prayers, and the leading by the hand and the guidance of the Holy Spirit, so that the same thing may not befall us, in our astonishment at those lofty wonders, as befalls us in our wonder at the stars.
For we marvel at their beauty from afar, but we cannot devise a single means of laying hands on them; only one delight is afforded us by them, which is the wonder of seeing them.
For truly the lights and radiances of these divine words are stars, shining from above and raised above the eyes of the soul as far as the heavens are distant from the earth, as the prophet says.
But if what we hear concerning Elijah should happen to our soul as well, and our mind should be lifted up to the height by a chariot of fire and should ascend to the beauties of heaven
(and it is clear that by fire we mean the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord came to spread upon the earth and whom he distributed to the disciples in the appearance of tongues),

then it would not be beyond hope for us too to draw near to such stars as these, which are the divine meanings that, through these heavenly and spiritual words, sparkle upon our souls and enlighten them. So lift up the eyes of your soul.
To you, the hearer, I speak the word that came from God to the patriarch:
"Look up toward this heaven and see these stars, if you are able to count the height of their power and meaning."
Look at the queen's authority, and judge her power from her commands. Through these words she shows the sovereignty of rulers.

She does not carry out her will through prayer but by her word, in keeping with the unfailing divine promise spoken to the faithful and wise servant and steward, that he would become lord of all the royal possessions.
Such authority has she received, and royally she accomplishes the desire of her will over those two strong winds, for she dismisses the north wind with command and authority,
but the south wind she summons [?] and hastens it to come to her, and she says: "Arise, north wind, and come, south wind!" And, as I think,
the force of these words spoken here is not foreign to the words of the centurion, at which the Lord marveled, as the evangelist says,
and he showed the centurion's faith to be greater than Israel's, not the faith of this people of Israel,

but of that patriarch Israel himself, who in that wrestling with the adversary, even after divine help, barely escaped a fall, and even so did not remain wholly free of the injury that befell him, for he received that injury of numbness in the broad part of his thigh.

Now this centurion of whom we are now speaking had been sent by some royal power to take hold of some foreign authority, for which he became a marvel and attained what he desired. For he speaks of the authority over the soldiers who were under him: to send with authority whomever he wishes, and likewise to summon whomever he pleases,
and to assign to his slave the fitting service. And there, too, the centurion's word is not something [?],
but philosophy, for he does not call back to himself the one he has once sent away; rather, when he sends that one away, he takes another for himself in his place.
For he says of that one, "Go, and he goes; and to another, Come": not the one he sent, but another.

And as I suppose, he teaches us something like this: that it is not in the nature of things opposed to one another to be together with one another at the same time, or to live together, for, according to the word of the apostle,
there is no fellowship of darkness with light,

but it is beyond dispute that when darkness vanishes, light spreads in its place, and when evil is driven away, virtue enters. And when this is thus accomplished, the mind of the flesh can no longer overcome the mind of the spirit, for neither is it able, once it has been put to death, to display any opposing power,
but it becomes ready for all due service through the strength of the spirit, obedient and uncontending.
For when the soldier who is the helper of evil is driven away, and in his place enters the armed man of virtue, armed with the coat of mail of righteousness,
and holds in his hands the sword of the Spirit, and carries what completes the armor, that is, the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation, and bears upon himself all the spiritual armor,

then the slaves of the flesh fear that ruling mind and eagerly heed this command of their lord, by which virtue is brought to perfection through the service of the body. And this is what the word of the centurion shows, who said, "And to my slave: Do this, and he does it."
But let us hear from the queen how she rouses from herself the north wind, her adversary, so that it may turn back its blowing,
for she does not command it to be still, as God once commanded the sea and the winds to be silent and changed its stormy billows into calm,
but she commands it to depart and flee, so that the south wind may blow unhindered and no breeze may hold back its blowing. For she says, "Arise, O north wind."
And what is the reason for rousing this wind? The north wind is harsh, as the word of Proverbs says, but by name it is called "right,"
yet in reality it is in no way right, unless someone has the east at his shoulders [?] and makes his course toward the west.
And surely you recognize the parable in these sayings: for whoever has parted from the East, since Christ is so called by the prophet,

And if anyone drives himself toward the west, away from the light, where the dominion of darkness lies, he has the north on his right hand, which feeds him with evil provisions and sends him on his way. By these means, the one whose course has been toward darkness
finds the north on his right hand. That is the unclean one, who rushes and runs along with the passions of defilement.
In this way this wind of wickedness becomes a right hand. It does the same for greed: when it [?] the things that greed desires, it treats them like so much earth and dust.
In this way it gives its help to every kind of lawlessness, and it becomes a right hand to everyone it joins.

It is truly harsh by nature, but it conceals its harshness by means of pleasures. And for this reason the bride, that conqueror of the passions and trampler of them, pursues the north wind and drives it from her domain, and says to it: "Arise, O north wind."
And by this name she signifies the opposing power, and no one who knows the correspondence of natures and names is ignorant of this.
For who would not know the course of the sun, and that it passes from the east through the regions of the south and reaches the west,
while the shape of the earth is round, as those who are knowledgeable in such matters say.

And where the sun does not shine forth, without any doubt, that place is darkened by the opposing body, cut off by the thickness of the gloom and made shadowy [or: northern]. And since that place is without light and remains always dried up, and is neither warmed nor made bright by the rays of the sun, therefore also the ruler and power of darkness,
who, in the manner of water by freezing, turns the tender nature of souls to stone and hardens it, is called "north" [or: "shadow"] and "harsh" by the word which announces to us the sorrowful winter,
and I mean that winter in which, according to the word of the Gospel, flight from tribulations is made impossible, and in which the beauty of those who have blossomed in virtue withers.

So the queen's word rightly drives it away with authority and calls the south wind, which is hot and bright. She calls it a [?] (perhaps 'stream'), and from it the river of delight flows out, as she says:

"And come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let my spices flow." And this happened through the powerful blowing of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples in the upper room of Zion, when he blew upon those spiritual paradises and stirred up those divine plants to send forth rivers of fragrance;
and the fragrances of prophecy poured forth from their pure and living mouths, the fragrances of salvation
and of the teachings of the faith, in those many and varied tongues, without hindrance, and the fragrances of instruction,

came forth like rivers. In this way those hundred and twenty disciples, planted in the house of God, blossomed through the blowing of such a south wind, by the teaching of the tongues of fire. This is why the bride speaks of such a south wind: "Blow upon my garden,"
since she became the mother of gardens through the voice of the bridegroom, who made her, as it is written, a garden and a fountain.
And therefore she wants the Holy Spirit to blow upon her garden, which is the Church, filled with spiritual trees, so that spices may flow out from it.
The prophet says, then: "His wind shall blow, and the waters shall flow,"
but the bride, adorned with royal wealth, raises the rivers to a higher order, so that the trees of the garden may send forth rivers of spice through the powerful blowing of the south wind.
From this we may clearly learn the difference between the old law and the new, for the prophetic river was filled with water, but the river of the Gospel with fragrant ointment.
A river of such ointments, sprung up by the Spirit from the garden of the Church, was the holy apostle Paul, whose river was the fragrance of Christ;
such also were John and Luke and Mark and Matthew, and all the other plants, the distinguished ones of that bridal garden,
who were fanned by that bright blast of the south wind and became a spring of ointments, and poured forth the graces and fragrances of the Gospel.
And then she says: "Let my kinsman come down to his garden and eat the fruit of his orchards."
O precious and richly gifted soul, and O this voice full of boldness, which surpasses every power and height of the mind!
For whom does she receive to supper from her own fruits, and for whom does she prepare rest from her own good things, and whom does she call to dinner from those prepared delicacies?
Him by whom all things are, and through whom all things are, and from whom all things are, who "gives food to all in due season,

who opens his hand and fills every living thing," according to the will and virtue of each, with "the bread which came down from heaven and gave life to the world," who makes it spring up for all beings from the spring of his own life. For him the bride spreads a table and prepares a supper.
And the garden is the table, planted with spiritual trees,
and we are those trees, if only we too set before him the salvation of our souls as food. For he said in this way that our salvation is his food and delicacy, saying:
"My food is this, that I do the will of my Father." And the purpose of the divine will is evident, for he wills the salvation of all and their coming to the knowledge of the truth.
This, then, is the food prepared for him, namely our salvation,

and our fruit is will and zeal, which, of themselves, as if from some orchards, hand over our soul to God who gathers the harvest from us. And this too must be understood: first the bride is delighted by the fruit of the apple tree, as she said, "and his fruit is sweet to my palate."
And then she herself also becomes fruit, ripe and sweet, set before the husbandman to gladden him. And this word, namely:
"Let him come down," has the force and meaning of prayer, as if one were saying "Hallowed be your name" and "Your will be done,"
For just as there the wording of the phrase has the force of a prayer, so also here "Let him come down" is the bride's prayer, which shows God the fruitfulness of the orchards of virtue,

and the coming down signifies the work of love for humankind. For our being raised to the heights is impossible in any other way, unless the Lord, who exalts the meek of heart, bends down in humility.
For this reason too the soul ascending to the height asks for his lofty helping hand and entreats him to come down from his own height, so that he may become accessible to the lowly,
and he who said through the prophet, "While you are still speaking, I will say to you:

'Behold, here I am,'" before the bride's prayer had even been completed, both heard what she was entreating for and looked upon the readiness of her heart. And he came down to the garden blown upon by the south wind, and he gathered the fruits of the spices and was filled from the fruit trees of virtue, and he proclaimed that refreshment and made it something to be recounted.
And thus he said to the bride: "I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride.
I have gathered my myrrh with my spices. I have eaten my bread with my honey. I have drunk my wine with my milk.
Eat, my companions, and drink, and become drunk, my nephews!"

Do you see how, by the abundance of his gifts, he exceeds what was asked? The bride prayed that her plants might become a spring of spices in her garden, blown upon from the south by the blowing of the south wind, and that with the fruit of the fruit trees she might host the chief of the laborers.
And it is clear that every fragrance becomes a delight to the sense of smell,
while fruits are weaker than the strength of bread for filling and making fair those who are nourished. But he who came down to his garden
changed the nature of those fruits into something higher and more honorable,
for he gathers from the garden myrrh together with his spices, because every good thing that is seen or conceived, all of it is his and is from him, as the prophet sings.
And instead of fruits, he grants those plants to yield the food of bread, seasoned with honey,
which he eats with his honey, for the honey too is his, like those other good things. And from them he also draws up wine mixed with his milk,
"for from him and through him and to him are all things."

O blessed garden, whose plants were attested as bearing such fruits, so that the delights of all delights, according to the desire of those who receive them, have gathered together among them at once! For to one who takes delight in fragrance it becomes myrrh with spices,
so that a pure and fragrant life, seasoned with the varied and many-colored spices of virtue, may make fragrant the putting to death of the earthly members.
But for one who seeks perfect food, it is changed into bread, not to be eaten with bitter wild herbs, as the Law commands,
for bitterness is short-lived and belongs to this passing world. Rather, it makes honey its own delicacy, when in its own time the fruit of virtue sweetens the senses of the soul,
the type of which the disciples plainly saw after the Lord's resurrection, that is, bread sweetened with honeycomb.

And again, for the thirsty it becomes a cup full of wine and honey, not a sponge full of gall and vinegar, which the Jews held out on a reed to their benefactor and doer of good in return for his good deeds.
And as I think, there is no one who does not know the figures of these sayings, how Paul was a tree full of myrrh,
"who was dying day by day, and who himself passed the sentence of death on himself, and who, made fragrant by holiness and impassibility, became a breath of life to those who live."
But as for how the spiritual plants of the garden nourish the Lord, the King of the garden, the Lord himself testifies, seated on the thrones, saying: "I was hungry and you gave me food."
And indeed almsgiving is the bread of joy, sweetened with the honey of the commandment. And again, how the delightful plants of that bridal garden produce wine,
of which he says this: "I was thirsty and you gave me wine to drink, mixed with milk and not with water,"

as is the custom of tavern-keepers." For milk is the first food of human nature, pure and simple and childlike and guileless and cleansed of every evil way of life. Having said this to the bride, the Word transfers and passes on the mysteries of the Gospel to the companions and says:
"Eat, my companions, and drink and become drunk, my brother's sons."
Whoever knows the mysteries of the Gospel will introduce no difference between these words and those that were spoken to the disciples at that mystical supper,
for just as then, so also now the Word says: "Take and eat."
But as for the invitation to drunkenness that the Word makes here to the brothers, let no one think that it alters anything in the word of the Gospel,
for what he commanded his friends here, this he fulfilled there in deed, since all drunkenness throws the mind of the drunken into astonishment and ecstasy,

and what he commands here comes about through that same divine eating and drinking; it came about then [?] too, and it always comes about among those who eat and drink, by a change and an ecstasy from lower things to higher ones. Thus they become drunk,
as the prophecy says, those "who drink of the fatness of the house of God and are watered with the torrent of delight."
Just as once the great David too became drunk,

he went out even from himself and was astonished and in ecstasy, and he saw that invisible beauty and uttered that all-desirable cry: "Every man is a liar," when he was entrusting to speech the interpretation of those ineffable good things.

Thus young Benjamin too became drunk: Paul, when he was astonished and said: "For if we were in ecstasy, it was for God" (for his ecstasy was directed toward him), "and if we have become wise, it is for you,"
which he showed when he was conversing with Festus and said: "I am not raving, but I speak words of purity and truth."
I know the blessed Peter too in the form of such drunkenness, for he was at once both hungry and drunk, for before receiving bodily food,
when he had become hungry and wanted to eat, and while they were still preparing it for him,
there came upon him the divine and sober drunkenness, by which he was astonished within himself and went into ecstasy, and he saw that sheet of the Gospel let down from heaven by its four corners,
and the whole race of humankind was held within it, in myriad forms of birds and four-footed creatures and reptiles and beasts, changed according to the differences of their forms of worship,
whose bestial and brutish form the word commanded Peter to slaughter, so that, once they had been purified, what remained might become food,
when the mystery of godliness and the word of faith were portrayed nakedly and simply. For not just once did the divine voice say to him, "That is not defiled

which God has purified," but such a proclamation was made three times, so that through the first voice we might learn the purification of God the Father, through the second the purification of God the Son, and through the third the purification of God the Holy Spirit.

And since such drunkenness comes from the wine which the Lord has set before those drinkers, and through which the divine ecstasy of the soul comes about, the Lord rightly commands those who through virtues have become his companions, and not those who are far removed:
"Eat, my companions, and drink, my neighbors, and be drunk." For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks to his own condemnation.
And those who are worthy of the eating he rightly called his brothers,
for whoever does his will is called, by the word, both brother and sister and mother.

And sleep fittingly follows that drunkenness, so that through digestion it may be changed into righteousness and strength for those banqueters. Hence, after that feast and rest, the bride falls asleep.
But that sleep is something strange and outside natural custom, for the custom of sleep is this:
neither is the one who is asleep awake, nor does the one who is awake sleep,
but the two, sleep and wakefulness, give way to each other, driven off by succeeding one another, and each in turn likewise arrives in its own manner at its own time.
But here a new and wondrous mixture and union of opposites is seen in her, for she says:
"I sleep and my heart is awake." What then ought we to think about this? For sleep is a likeness of death, and every activity of the bodily senses is suspended in it.

and neither sight, nor hearing, nor smell, nor taste, nor touch can perform its own work during sleep. The strength of the body is also loosened, human cares are forgotten, fear is released, anger is calmed, the harshness of the embittered is softened, and all evils go unfelt,
for as long as sleep holds the nature of the body.
From this we learn that he who boasts of this and says the following became higher than himself:
"I sleep, but my heart is awake."

And indeed, truly, when someone's mind is vigilant and lives in a God-illumined way and is not tyrannized by any of the senses, the nature of the body is suspended as if by a kind of sleep and torpor, and it is fitting to say
that it sleeps with idle sight and despises those sights which dazzle childish eyes.
And why do I speak only of those things which come from the materials of the earth, such as gold and silver and those stones and carbuncles,

which by some colouring and brilliance stir the eyes to greed, but also those wonders that are seen in the heavens, that is, the roundness of the sun, the beauty of the stars, the many-coloured changes of the moon, and everything else that delights the eyes,

since none of them is unchanging and everlasting, but each changes with the changing of the seasons and passes away. So by despising all these and such things, and by contemplating those true goods, the eye of the body is slackened and fallen asleep, and the perfect and lofty soul is drawn toward nothing of what the eye shows,
for with the mind it contemplates only that which is higher than visible things.

In the same way hearing also becomes dead and idle when the soul has turned to loftier words and refuses to listen to the affairs of this world. As for those animal-like senses, it is not even proper to speak of them,

for the soul casts them far away like the stench of corpses: that is, the sense of smell that dulls the nostrils [?], the sense of taste that is devoted to serving the belly, and with these the inward betrayer [?], the blind sense of touch, which nature perhaps made only for the blind.
And by the idleness of all these, as if seized by a kind of sleep,
the soul is pure in heart and unstained by earthly deeds, and looks toward heaven with the mind, as one free from pleasure, unmoved and untroubled by the tumult of the senses.
For since in human nature desire is twofold,
arising in the soul through freedom from passion, but in the body through the passions, and since between these two, whichever the will chooses prevails over the other,

therefore, if someone turns to the senses and is drawn to the bodily desire that springs up from them, he will not be able to perceive the taste of divine joy, for the inferior darkens the superior for him.
But those in whom divine desire abounds, their good becomes undarkened before them and an object of longing.
For this reason the soul, when it rejoices only in those true visions, stays awake to nothing at all of the motion, activity and desire of the senses,

but puts all bodily tumults to sleep, and, naked and pure in mind, through divine wakefulness receives the revelation of God. May we too be made worthy of this, and by the power spoken of above may that longed-for wakefulness of the soul be granted to prosper in us through Christ Jesus,
our Lord, to whom glory is fitting, now and always and forever and ever, Amen!
The heading of this discourse: 5:2. The voice of my kinsman knocks at the door:
"Open, my sister, my near one, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is filled with dew and my hair with the drops of the night." 5:3.
I have taken off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? 5:4. My kinsman put his hand in through the window, and my belly was stirred for him.
This too is one of the great commandments of the Lord, by which the mind of the disciples of the Word shakes off from itself all the material of nature,
like some dust, and is lifted up to desire those higher and immaterial goods,

That is, those who look toward the heavenly life must rise above sleep and be perpetually awake in mind, and must drive away the drowsiness of the eyes as if it were some deceiver of souls and enemy of truth.
And by drowsiness and sleep I mean those things through which these dream-like fantasies are formed in those who have given themselves over to the deceptions of the soul,
which are dominions and powers and riches and arrogance and the sensations of desires and pleasures and love of glory and luxuries and love of honor and everything

that in this life is eagerly pursued, with a kind of wonder, by the heedless; which flows away with the passing of times and years and vanishes; which is merely supposition and doubtful as to whether it perhaps has any being at all.
But what is merely supposed does not exist, nor does even the supposition remain with it forever; rather, it at once both came to be supposed and perished, like waves
raised up from the waters, which swell for a moment from the stirring of the wind and have no firmness in that swelling,
but are lifted high by the wind in an instant, and when the wind subsides again, the surface of the sea likewise becomes level, just as it was before.
Therefore, so that our mind may be separated from such fantasies, he commands us to drive this heavy sleep from the eyes of the soul,

so that through eagerness for things without being we may not fall away from those things that exist and are firm and truly unchanging. For this reason he also teaches us the means of wakefulness and says:
"Let your loins be girded and your lamps lit,"
For when the eyes look upon the light, they cast off the heaviness of sleep, and the loins,

Those who are made firm by a belt make sleep unwelcome to the flesh, because the labor and pain they have from being girded keeps them from being overcome by the rest of sleep. And I think the power and meaning of these parables are hidden from no one,

namely this: whoever is made firm and girded with purity lives in the light of a pure conscience and lights up his life with the lamp of boldness. Through these, while it gazes on the truth, the soul stays sleepless and free from error, and none of the deceptions of dreams leads it astray.
And if this proceeds according to the teaching of the word, the angelic life will adorn our life, for the divine command orders us to the likeness of the angels and says:
"And you, be like those men
who wait for their lord, when he comes from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once."
For these are the ones who await the Lord's ascent from the wedding, sitting with wakeful eyes at the gates of heaven,
so that through them again the King of glory may enter, when he returns from the wedding to that blessedness above the heavens, from which, according to the word of the psalm,

"the bridegroom came forth from his court," as it were, and joined us to himself as a holy virgin through the mystery of the second birth, we who had departed from idols, and he adorned our nature with the incorruption of virginity.
When such a wedding was completed and the Church became the bride of the Word, as John says, "He who has the bride is the bridegroom,"
and he brought her into the bridal chamber of the mysteries, the angels were waiting for the Church to rise up to the King's natural blessedness.
And of these he said that our life must be like theirs, so that, just as they are far from all evil and delusion and by that spotless way of life are ready to receive the coming of the King,
so we too may keep watch before the gates of our house and make ourselves ready to obey and to listen when he comes and knocks, as he says:
"Blessed are those servants whose lord comes and finds them awake."

And since blessed is the one who obeys the voice of him who knocks, therefore the soul that guards its treasures well, keeps watch over them, and looks always toward blessedness perceives the King standing at the door and says:
"The voice of my kinsman knocks at the door."
For how could anyone worthily comprehend, through these words, the bride's exaltation to divine height,
she who with such authority and confidence drove the harsh north wind away from herself, drew the bright breeze upon herself, and brought forth from her mouth a paradise of pomegranates,
Her fruit and produce were the spices, and she spread her garden as a table for the King of created things.

Of the things she set before him, nothing was rejected or despised. Instead, all were called good: myrrh and spices and honey and bread and milk and wine. The Word bore witness to their perfection and said:
"You are all beautiful, and there is no blemish in you."

Now such a soul regards herself as though she were only now becoming worthy of the experience of God, and as though she had never yet received the Word standing before the doors. She marvels at the power of his voice. She speaks not about herself but about the divine voice of the bridegroom touching her doors, and she sings:
"The voice of my kinsman knocks at the door."
Do you see how boundless is the course of those who ascend toward God, how what is attained at each moment becomes the beginning of something higher?
For when, because of the words that were said to her, we expect some completion of her course toward the higher ascents (for what greater testimony of perfection could anyone seek?),
Then we see that she was inside. She had not yet passed through his doors, nor had she yet rejoiced in the sight of his face,
but only through a brief hearing is she brought forward to share in good things.
And what we learn from these sayings is this: however much the saints advance, that apostolic saying befits them, which says:
"If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know."

For however far upward toward the height the soul reached, it understood everything there. But what it had not yet reached was many times greater than what it had reached. Therefore, although the bridegroom often appeared to her, the invisible bridegroom of souls has promised through his voice to reveal himself to the bride as one not yet seen.
But so that we may understand this more clearly, let us set an illustration before our discourse, and it is this:
Suppose someone came near that spring whose rising the book of Genesis spoke of, which is so great in abundance and richness that it suffices to water the face of all the earth,
and suppose the one who approached that spring were amazed at the countless abundance of waters that continually spring up and come forth from it,

yet he could not say that he has seen all the water, for how could he have seen what is still hidden in the bosom of the earth? So even if he were to watch that perpetual springing up for a long time, he sees only the beginning of the water,
For that water does not stop flowing,

or springing up. Both of these are everlasting and without end. In the same way, whoever gazes on that divine and boundless beauty keeps marveling at what is always being seen, because what is always being found is higher and more wonderful than what has already been found and reached.
but never at all ceases from the desire to see, for what is awaited is more beautiful and more radiant than what is seen.
And so it is here also: the bride is continually astonished and amazed at the things she has come to know, yet she never quiets her longing for the things still to be seen because of those she knows.
And now likewise, as though only now perceiving the Word knocking at the door, she rises to hear his voice and says: "The voice of my kinsman knocks at the door,"
and then in silence she lends her ears. Through the voice she hears the voice of the Word speaking such words as these: "Open, my sister, my close one, my dove,
my perfect one, for my head is filled with dew and my hair with the drops of the night."

Now the force of these sayings is this: perhaps it may be found to be thus also in the vision of the great Moses. The divine manifestation began from light, and after that God spoke to him through a cloud.
And then, when he had become more perfect and more exalted, he saw God in the mist.
What we learn from this is the following: the first separation from the false and erroneous suppositions devised about God is the passage from darkness to light,
and the next after it is the approach to hidden things, which by means of visible things leads the soul to the contemplation of the invisible nature;

it is like a cloud, which covers everything apparent but accustoms the soul to seeing hidden things and guides it. And the soul that ascends to the height by these means, as far as it is possible for human nature to attain,
enters within the inaccessible places of the knowledge of God, surrounded on every side by that divine mist,
where it is left outside everything visible and comprehended, and by the sight of the soul alone it contemplates the invisible and incomprehensible one,
who is God, as the word says concerning the lawgiver: "But Moses entered the mist" where God was.
Now that we have contemplated this, from here on we must also look at how the words set before us agree with what has been said.
There was a time when the bride was black, darkened by unenlightened words.
when the sun harmed her and, through temptations, withered the rootless seed on the rock, when she was defeated by those who fought against her and did not keep her own vineyard,
when she could not know herself and was pasturing a herd of kids instead of sheep.
But since she separated herself from communion with evil things and became desirous, through those mystical kisses, of drawing near to the mouth of the fountain of lights,
from then on she became beautiful and shone with that light of truth, and the blackness of ignorance was washed away by water.
And then she became like a horse in swift running and like a dove in the eagerness of faith,
by which she ran past everything attained and visible, like a horse, and flew upward, like a dove.

And at first she rested in the shade of the apple tree, as her heart told her, which she called a cooling shade in place of a cloud; but now she is enveloped by the divine darkness. The one who comes within it is the Bridegroom, yet he does not appear, for how could he appear in the night,
he who is invisible? He gives the soul a certain sense of his coming, but flees from manifest appearance, hidden by the invisibility of his nature.
And what, then, is the mystery told to the soul by this night?
The Word, then, touches the door, and by the door we understand the mind, the examiner of things inexpressible, through which what is sought is understood and enters into us.
Truth, then, stood outside our nature, and little by little through knowledge, as the Apostle says,

That is, by certain parables and figures he was knocking at the door of the mind and saying: "Open." Along with the word he was showing the way the door ought to be opened. And he was holding out to us these good names like a kind of key, by which what is shut is opened.
And it is clear that in the expression of these names, which open hidden things, there is a power equal to keys: "sister," and "near one," and "perfect dove." And he says to her:
"If you wish the door to be opened to you and the gates of your soul to be opened, so that the King of glory may enter, you must
become a sister to me as well, by receiving my will into your soul, as it is said in the Gospel: 'Whoever lives according to his will, that one becomes his brother and sister and mother.'
And again you must draw near to the truth and become truly near, so that nothing may be a dividing wall and separator for you, and so that you may have perfection in the nature of a dove,
that is, so that you may be without defect and filled with all innocence and purity.

So take such names as these, O soul, as keys, and by them open the entrances of truth, and become his sister and dove and perfect and near one. And by receiving me and my dwelling in you, the dew of my head will become profit and gain for you,
with which I am filled, and the dew and drops of the night which flow from my hair and locks."
And from these, according to the word of the prophet, we learn this, that the dew from him is healing, as he says: "The dew from you is healing for them."

And likewise, the dews and drops of the night have the same force as the saying quoted above, for it is not possible to enter inside invisible and inaccessible things, nor to come upon any rains and torrents of understanding,

But it is enough, and something to be cherished, if truth should kindle [?: perhaps "moisten"] one's understanding, as with dew and drops, from the flow of those dews of the holy and God-clad words; for human weakness cannot contain anything greater.
And by the hair and locks hanging from the head of the Lord of all, so called figuratively, it teaches us to understand the prophets, evangelists and apostles,

each of whom, as much as he could contain, filled himself from those dark, hidden and invisible treasuries and became for us a river full of waters. Yet in comparison with the true Truth they are dews and drops of dew,
even though in the abundance and height of their teachings they may be great and overflowing, as Paul was,

the stream of whose waves of understanding had been raised higher than the heavens, as far as the three heavens, as far as paradise, and as far as those unspoken and inexpressible words, and who, with the teaching of all such lofty speech, surged like a torrent [?] and whirled like an abyss.
Yet even so he himself made it clear that it is only a drop of dew when compared with the true Truth, as he says: "We know some small part and prophesy some very small part," and:
"If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as one ought to know," and: "I now [?: perhaps "not yet"] reckon myself as having attained."

Now then, if a drop of dew and the moisture of the hair are a river and an abyss and a wave when compared with our capacity, what ought one to conceive about that Spring who said: "Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink himself"?
Let each of the hearers, by comparing these things that have been said, understand it for himself and be amazed: for if a drop and dew were able to grow into a river,
what could anyone conceive about that divine River itself, or to what could he compare it?

Let us see, then, this also: how the bride listens to the Word and how she opens the door to the bridegroom, for she says: "I have taken off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?"
She listened well to him who commanded her to become near, and a dove, and perfect, so that through these things truth might dwell in the soul.

For as she heard, so she did: she took off that garment of skin which she had put on after sin, and she washed from her feet the dust that had settled on them when she returned from the life of paradise to the earth, when she heard:
"Earth you are, and to earth you shall return,"
and by these he opened the entrance of the soul to the Word and drew back the curtain of the heart, which is the veil of the flesh, that is, the old man,
whom the holy Apostle commands to be stripped off and cast away by those who wish to wash away the stain of soul and mind with the washing of the Word.
Therefore, whoever has stripped off the old man and cast away the veil of his heart has opened the entrance to the Word.

But when he had entered within, the soul made him its own garment, according to the apostolic word, which commands the one who strips off the old and ragged garment of the human condition to put on the new garment, created by God in holiness and righteousness, which is our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore the bride confesses and says that it is impossible to put on again the garment she has once cast off, but that she is content with one garment, the one given to the disciples according to the law,
which the soul put on when it was renewed by the second birth. And she confirms the word of the Lord, who commands that those who have once been adorned with the divine garment
should no longer put on the garment of sin, nor have two garments, but only one, so that there may not be two garments together, made to resemble one another.
For what fellowship has a darkened garment with the one that is the color of light and immaterial?
And the law says not only this, that "one must not have two garments," but also "one must not sew a new patch onto an old garment,"
so that the shame of the one who wears such a thing may not become worse, for then the new does not hold, and the old tears worse and becomes hard to mend.
for he says that the new takes away the fullness of the old garment and tears it all the more, until through it its ugliness is exposed before everyone. Therefore he says:
"I have put off my garment; how shall I put it on?" For who would there be who saw himself clothed in that sun-coloured garment of the Lord,

which is woven of holiness and incorruption, such as the Lord put on upon the mountain at his transfiguration, and who would then still take it upon himself to put on that beggarly and patched garment?
which the drunkard and the fornicator wear, as the Proverbs say?
And again, she will not consent to defile her washed feet by treading on the earth, as she says, "I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?"

For neither is it written of Moses, when by divine command he freed his feet from the sandal of dead skin as he was about to go up onto the holy and illuminated ground, that he ever covered them again with shoes.
Therefore, when he adorned the priestly garment according to the pattern shown on the mountain, and beautified it with many colors and many forms,
he took no pains over any ornament for the feet; rather, nakedness and freedom from every covering were what adorned those priestly feet.
For since it is fitting for the priest to walk on that holy ground, it is not proper that he should go upon it in dead skin.
For this reason the Lord also commanded the disciples not to use shoes, since he commanded them not to walk on the way of the Gentiles, but to run on that holy and spotless way.

And you are surely not ignorant of that holy way on which the disciples were commanded to walk, for you will have learned it from him who said, "I am the way," the touching of which is [?] by one who has not taken off the garment of this dead man. And the bride has been made worthy of that way, for the Lord washes the feet of those who walk on it with water and wipes them with the towel with which he was girded. And that girding of the Lord is the power that cleanses from sins, as it is written: "The Lord clothed himself with power and girded himself."

Therefore, once her feet have been cleansed for the royal way, she guards them so that they may not turn aside either to the right or to the left, so that by turning aside in either direction her footsteps may not leave the way and defile her feet with mud. And do you now understand the force of these sayings?

It is this: that one who through baptism has once taken off his sandals (for loosing the strap of the sandals belongs properly to the Baptist, as John testified, saying that for the Lord alone he was not able to do this; for how indeed could he have loosed the straps of him who did not even admit the beginning of the cords of sin?), this one has washed his feet, has wiped away all the filth of the earth, and has cast it away together with the sandals. So he takes care of his feet and keeps his footsteps undefiled for the sake of that paved way, as David also did,
when he washed his feet of the mud and mire and set them firmly on the rock, and said:
"He brought me up from the pit, from misery and from the mud of the mire, and set my feet firmly on the rock and directed my steps."
And by the rock we mean the Lord, who is light and truth and life and incorruption and righteousness, by which that spiritual way is paved,
from which, if a person turns aside neither to the right nor to the left, he keeps his footsteps spotless and is never in any way defiled by the mud of desires and pleasures.
And this, according to my account, is that by which the door is opened by the bride to the Word,

for confession and promise no longer soiled the feet with that mud which had been cast away, nor is there any entry for the other things of life to stain, with the soil and dust of earthly deeds, the holiness of the soul thus prepared.
And holiness is the Lord.

And this is what we have examined concerning the things said above. But then, after this, the soul advances to higher ascents and no longer speaks of a knocking at the heart by a voice, but proclaims the touch of that divine hand itself through the window, and says:

"My kinsman put his hand through the window, and my belly was stirred for him." Now it is surely clear and evident to the intelligent how much higher this present saying is than what was said before. For the Word says to the bride, "Open," and strengthens her by those divine names; the bride obeys the Word by opening and becomes what she heard, that is, "both near one and dove and perfect." And she strips off that garment of skin, casts away the filth of her feet and washes, and she does not put on that loathsome and tattered garment again, nor does she any longer consent to set her foot on the earth.
For she heard his voice and obeyed his command,

she opens the door to him, and casts away the veil of the heart, and strips the veil of the flesh from the door. And thus she opened to him every gate of the soul, so that the King of glory might enter,
but the breadth of that gate was reckoned as some small window and a hole, narrow and little, so that not only the Bridegroom himself, but even his hand could hardly fit through it,
so that through it he might enter within and touch her who longed for the sight of the Bridegroom, she who had gained so much, until she knew that this hand was that of her Beloved.
But as for what teachings he shows us through the philosophy of these sayings, perhaps we shall learn them if we linger a little over these sayings. That is:

The human mind stands between two natures. One of them is incorporeal, intelligent and incorruptible, and the other is corporeal, material and irrational. And when the soul is purified by the virtues from sharing in that coarse and earthly life, and the eyes of the mind are opened,

it does not cease, in keeping with its kinship with the divine, from searching out and investigating the beginning of beings: what the source of the beauty of beings is, whence power springs up, and whence this wisdom comes forth which is seen among visible things.
But when it has stirred up all its thoughts and every searching power of the mind, and scrutinizes back and forth how to attain what it seeks,
it sets as the limit of that attainment only the works and powers of God, which reach as far as us and which we perceive through our life.
And just as the air rising up out of the earth at a spring does not remain in the depths of the pools,

but becomes a bubble and rises toward what is akin to it, the air, and when that bladder or bubble has passed the surface of the water, reached its edge and mingled with the air, only then does it stop its upward movement,

The same sort of thing is seen in the soul that searches out divine matters. When it raises its mind from earth to that higher understanding and comprehends the wonders of God's works, it is not able, nor does it have the power, to advance any further through that searching,
but it marvels and glorifies him only for this: that he exists in being, and that it knows its Creator from created things,

It contemplates the beauty of the sky, the brilliance of the luminaries, the swift revolution of the sphere of the heaven, the orderly and harmonious movement of its stars, and the ordering of the year,
which turns back upon itself through the four seasons, and the earth and its plants and everything that is in it, and the distinctness and variety of those that walk upon it,
and the life and form and order and that manifold nature of living creatures, as many as move about in the waters and as many as are in the air, those which live upon the earth,

and the form of those many-coloured plants and the various kinds of vegetation, distinguished from one another in richness, potency and colour, and the particular qualities of fruits and tastes, and all the rest.
through which the works of God are made manifest, the soul contemplates their wonder, reflects within its mind, and affirms that "God exists."
And as I think, in the age to come, when all these visible things pass away according to the word of the Lord, who said:
"Heaven and earth shall pass away," when we are transferred to that life

As for that which is higher than eyes and ears and mind: then we shall no longer know that nature of the Good through works, nor in part, as we do now, nor will that beginningless essence be known any longer through visible works,

but that ineffable blessedness will be seen in another manner, and the form of that delight will be of another aspect and another kind. It is something that human nature now has no capacity to let enter the heart.

Yet [?] the boundary of the soul's understanding of those ineffable things is the creation, operation and structure of these visible created things, which you have [?] understood figuratively; and we have been taught this teaching through these divine words,
by which the pure soul no longer dwells in earthly and material life, so that she may not defile her feet with the [?] of the earth,

for she hopes and waits to receive the Bridegroom himself, coming wholly as a guest and arriving at his house, even though she was found worthy to see only the hand of the one she loved. Her nature could hold only that much. The hand is interpreted as the one who gives being to all that exists and as the power of creation, as it says:
"My kinsman put his hand through the opening." For human poverty cannot take that infinite and uncircumscribed nature into itself.
"And my belly was stirred for him": this phrase, "was stirred," signifies a kind of astonishment and trembling at the wonder that has been revealed.
For all the power of her understanding was stirred at the wonder that the divine hand created, the contemplation of which,
being exalted above human power, itself interprets the incomprehensible and uncontainable power of that creating nature,
for the whole creation of beings is the work of that hand which was revealed to us through the window, as John cries out and says: "All things came to be through him."
And likewise the prophet sings the same words and cries out: "All these things my hand has made."
And since all other things and the beauty of the heavens are the work of that hand, and the inquiring human mind has not attained to what the essence of the heavens is,
or of the sun, or of any other of the wonders among these visible creatures, for this reason her heart is stirred and trembles at the divine powers and works.

For if she cannot contain the comprehension of these things, how could she reach or how could she contain the understanding of that nature which surpasses all of them? And if anyone understands these figures of these words in some other way also, their contemplation will not be outside what is fitting.
The house of the bride is understood to be the whole of human life,
To this the hand came, the Creator of all beings, to the smallness and worthlessness of human life, in order to conceal himself by putting on our nature in every likeness, except only for sin.
But when he made his dwelling among us, the souls and minds of men were stirred and astonished and trembled: how God was manifested in the flesh, how the Word became flesh,
how birth within virginity and virginity within a mother came together, how that light was mingled with darkness and death was dissolved by life, how that lowly window of life contained that hand,

the Creator of all beings, who measures the heavens and weighs the earth and holds the waters. As a house [?], then, the grace of the Gospel is prophetically signified by the bride through the parable of the hand,

For when the Lord appeared on earth and lived among people, we came to understand the holy and immaterial beauty of the Bridegroom, the divinity of the Word, and the radiance of the true light through the power of the hand.
We call "hand" the power that works wonders, by which the dead were brought back to life and the eyes of the blind were opened,
the disease of leprosy was driven away, and every kind of incurable and evil suffering left the body at a command. So here, before us, is this twofold understanding of the hand.

One of these tells us that the divine nature is entirely beyond reach and without limit, and is known and understood only from its works. The other says that through these words the bride announced the grace of the Gospel beforehand by prophecy.
Now let the hearer choose between them,

deciding which one better matches the meaning of the words before us, or fits them better. But whichever one is chosen, only benefit to souls will be seen in it. The understanding of each will show us a form of good on both sides, and by the grace of God this good shines clearly in both interpretations.
For the first one makes us understand, in the words of Paul, that:

"The invisible power of God is clearly seen from the creation of the world." When we understand this, we keep away from searching into what cannot be searched out, so that heresy will not use speculation about natures concerning that incomprehensible and inexpressible nature as material to attack the truth. But if we understand this figure of the hand as a parable of the Gospel,

then in this way too the faith of the mystical teachings would become firmer for us, when the truth of those words foretold by prophecy is made indisputable by Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and power, now and always and forever and ever, amen!
The heading of this discourse: 5:5. I rose to open for my kinsman. My hands dripped myrrh; my fingers, full of myrrh, on the doors of the bolt. 5:6.
I opened to my kinsman. My kinsman had gone away, and my soul went out at his word; I sought him and did not find him. I called him and he did not answer me. 5:7.
The watchmen who go around the city found me. They struck me and wounded me, and the guards of the wall stripped me of my garment.
those who set out on a voyage across the sea in hope of wealth,

when they see the ship leaving the harbour, and the pilot sitting at the helm turns the ship and steers it toward the deep, the sailors pray at the start of the voyage that God will grant them good success and guide their voyage. The prayer begins like this: "May a sweet, gentle breeze that carries the ship well fill the sails, and may favourable and good winds blow from the stern as the pilot wishes."

And when the wind blows as they want, the sea becomes pleasant before them. Stirred [?] by calm waves and deep blue, it carries the ship swiftly along with a bright sound, takes them untroubled through the depths of the abyss and across the broad seas, and sets the wealth of trade before their eyes,
