…even before the trading, the gain that is expected through success and prosperity.

And what does this discourse of mine mean? For here I am making a beginning. Or rather, the nature of the beginning set before us is clear to those who are intelligent and listen diligently: a great abyss lies before this discourse of ours, the examination of the divine words, and by this voyage much wealth of understanding will be stored up for us as treasure.
And this spiritual ship of the Church, together with its whole full company, lifted up in mind, awaits the wealth of the interpretation.
And the shipmaster, which is the word, does not undertake to take the helm until prayer has been made to God by the whole full company of these sailors,

so that the power of the Holy Spirit may blow upon us and stir up the waves of understanding, and through them make our discourse run well, so that in this way we may cross the abysses of contemplation and gain by trade the wealth of understanding,

if only the Holy Spirit, through your prayer, comes upon our discourse and fills the sails of our thoughts. And let the beginning of our discourse be the recollection of those divinely inspired words, which say thus:
"I arose to open to my beloved. My hands dripped myrrh; my fingers were full of myrrh,"
for otherwise the living Word of God, who is that holy and bodiless Bridegroom, who unites the soul to himself through incorruption and purity, does not dwell within us,
unless someone, by putting to death the earthly members, strips off the veil of the flesh and thus opens the door to the Bridegroom, through which he comes to dwell in the soul.
And this is clear not only from the divine teachings of the Apostle alone, but also from what has now been said by the bride, for she says:
I arose to open the door to my beloved, because I made my hands a spring of myrrh, hands that of themselves dripped ointments, and I showed the fullness of my fingers full of myrrh.

And the means by which the door is opened to the Bridegroom she recounts to us through these sayings, and says: "For this reason I arose, because I was buried with him through baptism into his death."

And [this shows] that if that voluntary death had not gone before, the resurrection would not have taken place. And that it was voluntary is made known by the drops of myrrh flowing down from her hands and by the filling of her fingers with this same ointment,
for it does not say that myrrh was poured onto her hands from somewhere else.
For if this were so, what is reported about the myrrh would be taken from this to have happened by chance and involuntarily, as an accident;
but it speaks of those hands as her own, and by the hands it signifies the powers and deeds of the soul;

and by the myrrh dripping of itself it signifies the putting to death of the fleshly passions, done of her own accord and by her own will, in connection with which it speaks of the filling of all the fingers,
[meaning] the zeal to accomplish the virtues, which are divided into various kinds, and which it teaches us about under the name of fingers. And the whole force of these sayings is this:

"I received the power of the resurrection by putting to death my members that are on earth, and I carried out the putting to death of such members by my own will, for it was not by another that myrrh was poured onto my hands,

But from my eagerness [?] it came down to me [?]. Hence, in all the works of virtue, each of which you named one by one, such diligence was seen to be without deficiency. For among those who practise virtue incompletely, there is seen death in one respect and coming to life in another.
So we see some people who, even if they put fornication to death in themselves, yet diligently nurture pride or some other soul-killing passion, such as love of possessions,
or anger, or love of glory, or anything else of the kind. When such a thing is wickedly alive in the soul, a person cannot show his fingers full of myrrh,
for his putting to death of evils and estrangement from them does not appear in all his deeds.
But when such fingers are all filled with that intelligible myrrh, the soul both rises and opens the door to the bridegroom.
Therefore the great Paul rightly understood that royal saying, which says: "The ear of grain cannot spring up unless the grain is first dissolved through death."
And this teaching proclaims that death must go before life, and that it is not possible in any other way for life to come about in a person unless its entry takes place through death.
For since the nature in us is twofold, one part of which is fine and intellectual and light, and the other coarse and material and heavy,
it is indisputable and necessary that each of these be unmixed with the other and have its own distinct will, inclination and life,
for the intellectual and light part has as its own the ascent toward heaven, while the heavy and material part has a downward pull and perpetual lowering.
And since by nature there is an opposition of motion between them, the first cannot prosper unless the second is weakened in its natural motion.
And standing between the two is our self-governing power and choice, which of itself gives strength to what has been weakened and weakens what has been strengthened,
for to whichever side it turns, to that side it gives victory over the other.
Thus the wise, prudent and faithful steward is praised in the Gospel, who is, as I would say, the will, our good overseer and manager.
For he is praised because he feeds the king's servants by putting the adversaries to death, since their corruption becomes food and health for those higher ones.
But that wicked servant is condemned, who, by falling in with drunkards, tormented and beat the servants of God. And indeed the prosperity of wickedness is truly a wound to the virtues.
Therefore it is good,
if we take up the zeal of those prophetic words and make the dawn shine forth for ourselves by slaughtering all the sinners of the earth and destroying them from the soul,
which is the city of the Lord, all the thoughts that work lawlessness, whose destruction becomes life-giving for good things.
Thus then we are made alive through death, according to the word of the prophet, when within us something is put to death and something is made alive by the word that said:

"I will put to death and I will make alive," just as Paul, though dead, was alive, and though weak was strong, and though bound he ran, and though poor he grew rich, and by possessing nothing he had everything, and he always carried the death of Jesus in his own body and continually manifested his life in himself.
Now then let us go up to the matter before us. For by death the soul rises from death, for if it does not die,
it remains forever in death and becomes unable to receive life; but by death it becomes alive and casts away all death.
And this teaching is confirmed for us by the present passage, for thus the bride said: "I rose to open the door to my kinsman.
My hands dripped myrrh; my fingers were full of myrrh." Now that myrrh is a figure of death no one disputes
who has read the divine books; but as to how death raises from death, perhaps some may seek a clear explanation on this point, which let us not neglect,
but according to our ability let us briefly set it out step by step. Everything that God made "was very good," as Genesis testifies.
And one of those very good things was man, adorned with beauty even more than all the others; for what could be as good
as the image and likeness of that incorruptible goodness? And since everything was very good, and with all things and before all things man too was good,
death was not with man. And this is beyond doubt and indisputable, for what would man's goodness be if he had in himself that gloomy likeness of the ugliness of death?
Rather, he was the image and likeness of that eternal life, and he was truly good, and very good, adorned with the likeness of that radiant life, and he had
also the divine paradise, which by the fruitfulness of its plants made life spring up, and the divine commandment was also a law of life, which commanded that he should not die.
Now among the plants of paradise there was the tree that brings forth life, concerning which we must understand what is meant, whose fruit was life,
and [he] gave [?] concerning the tree clothed with death, whose fruit the text presents as good and evil at once.

And that tree also stood in the middle of paradise. But two trees cannot stand in the middle place at the same time. For of the two, whichever one we grant possession of the middle place without any dispute, the other is removed from the middle. By "middle" we understand the point in a circle drawn with compasses, on which the other leg of the compasses rests, and from which the circumference drawn around it is equally distant on every side.
And since there is one circle and one point,
there is no way that, within one circle, two points could both be the centre at the same time.
for if the point is moved, then another circle must be drawn around it, so that the point may undoubtedly take the middle.

And when this happens, the first circle and point and middle depart from being the middle, and the second takes the middle. But although this is so, Scripture nevertheless indicates that both are in the middle, even though they are opposed to each other in constitution.

And by their meaning I refer to the tree of life and the tree of death, which Paul called sin when he said: "Death is the fruit of sin." But, as I think, from the philosophy of these sayings it is necessary to understand
that the middle of God's paradise is life,
whereas death in itself is unplanted and rootless and has no place of its own at all, but it is planted through the lack of life, when participation in life ceases among the living.
And since life is in the middle of God's plants, and the nature of death receives its being through separation from it, for this reason that death-clad tree as well,
about which that teaching philosophized figuratively, it says is in the middle of paradise, and its fruit is said to be mixed of good and evil.
And, as I think, it indicated the nature of sin by this,
for since some desire and pleasure precede all evil deeds, and sin is not separated from desire and from the pleasure of the passions,

as much as arises from desire or love of pleasure, for this reason it is called good-fruited, through the judgment of an erring supposition and the reckoning of what is not good as good, as though one named that erring and vain desire good and thought it so,
But after that, through that bitter tasting and eating, it became the parent of the bitterness of death, as it says in the Proverbs: "Honey drips from the lips of wickedness,
for for a moment it sweetens your palate, but afterwards it is found more bitter than gall" to the one who was sweetened in an evil way.
And since man departed from that abundance of good fruit and was filled with that corrupting fruit of disobedience,

and the name of that fruit was sin, the bringer of death, he immediately died to that good life and acquired this brute and animal life in place of that divine life; and once death had mingled with nature,
In the succession of those who are born, that deadness came in, and the dead life received us, as though in some manner our life itself had died.
And because our life is truly dead, like a dead thing and deprived of immortality, for this reason he became the mediator between these two lives,

he who was made known between the two living creatures, so that by destroying the worse he might make the higher victorious. And just as man fell from the true life into this dead life through the death of man,
so too, when he dies, he may pass from this dead and brutish life into everlasting life.
Hence it is certain and indisputable that attaining that blessed life is impossible in any other way for one who does not die to sin.

And for this reason the Word has said, speaking philosophically, that the two trees stood together in the midst of paradise, one of which exists by nature, while the other comes about through deprivation of the good,
for by participation and deprivation there comes about, from the one to the other, a mutual exchange, that is, of death and life,
since whoever dies to the good lives in evil, and whoever dies to evil is made alive by virtue.

For this reason the bride rightly shows her hands full of myrrh, and through death to all evil she rises to open the door before the Word and to prepare an entrance into herself. And the Word whom she receives
is called Life, and is Life. And to such a height did that soul that gazes toward God ascend,

as we have now observed; and yet, after the manner of Paul, she does not yet know as one ought to know, nor does she consider herself to have attained, but still runs toward what is higher and strains forward,
for the sequence of the words that follow indicates this about her, since she says: "I took up the key of the door-bolt and opened to my beloved."
And then she added: "My beloved went away; my soul went out at his word."
By these words, then, she teaches us that there is one way of attaining the power that surpasses all things: not to stop at what has been attained,
but never to cease from seeking what is greater than what has been attained. For she who was filled with myrrh in all the labors of virtue and in the deeds of this life,
which she displayed figuratively through the fingers, and who signified her death to evil things and made manifest her voluntary virtues by the flowing of myrrh of its own accord from her hands,

then speaks of touching the keys of the door, which means bringing herself by her deeds close to that narrow and strait gate whose keys the Word placed in the hands of Peter and those like him. So she opens the door of the kingdom for herself in both ways: by the hands,
by which labors are signified, and by the key, by which faith is proclaimed,
for by these two, I mean deed and faith, the key of the kingdom is prepared in us by the Word.
But when she hoped, like Moses, for a manifest revelation and to see the face of the Beloved, then the one she sought passed beyond her grasp, for she says:
"My kinsman has gone away." Not that he abandoned her longing soul, but he drew it toward himself, for she says:

"My soul went out at his word." O that blessed going out, by which the soul goes out longing for the Word, of which the Psalmist sings and says: "The Lord will guard your coming in and your going out."
And this is truly the coming in and going out of the worthy, guarded by God,
for the going out from wherever we may be becomes an entrance to those higher good things.
By this going out, then, the soul went out and gained as its guide the Word, who said: "I am the way and the truth and the life and the door," and also:
"If anyone enters through me, and goes out," and never ceases,
and brings neither the entering nor the going out to an end, but always by progress keeps entering toward higher things, and is forever coming to be outside what has already been attained.

In this way the desired face of the Lord once passed by Moses too, and in the same way the soul of the lawgiver also, wherever it was, always went outside itself. It followed the Word as he passed by, and it never stopped growing toward what is higher,

For at the beginning he grew strong, when he counted the reproach of Christ higher than the kingship of the Egyptians, and chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to possess the pleasure of sin in this transient world.

And he grew again when the Egyptian was fighting with the despised Hebrew, and in vengeance on behalf of the Israelite he killed the Egyptian. You will recognize in these events the pattern of growth, if you transpose the narrative into the mode of figurative interpretation.
Again he became higher than himself when for a long time, by ascetic struggle in the deserts, he kept his life undisturbed.

And then he was enlightened by the fire of the bush, and after that his hearing too, together with the beam of light, was made radiant by the word. With these things he bared his feet of the coverings made from what is dead, crushed the serpents of the Egyptians with his rod, freed his people from the tyranny of Pharaoh, and led them by the shade of the cloud.
He split the deep, drowned the tyrant, sweetened Marah, drank from the rock, and was filled with the food of angels.

He heard the trumpets; he drew near to the blazing mountain; he climbed to the summit of the mountain; he passed through the cloud; he went inside the darkness where God was. He received the Law. He was changed into a sun, untouchable and unapproachable [?], and lights shone out from his face. Who could put into words all his ascents and his many different visions of God? And yet even so, this man, so great and of such a kind,
who entered into such great deeds and was raised up toward God through such great heights,
still has an insatiable desire for higher longings, and he prays to see God face to face.
And this was when the word had testified of him that he had been found worthy to converse with God face to face.
But neither speaking with God as a friend speaks with a friend, nor talking with God face to face, could hold him back from higher desires. Instead he said:
"If I have found grace before you, show yourself to me openly."
And he who promised to grant the grace that was asked, and who said to him, "I know you above all," passed him by,
when he covered him with the divine hand in the divine place, in the cleft of the rock, so that only after he had passed did he barely see his back.
And as I think, the word teaches us this by it: that whoever longs for the sight of God beholds that kingdom by always following him.
And the sight of his face is to go toward him without ceasing, guided on the way by following the Word.
So likewise now the soul too: when she rose from death, when she was filled with myrrh, when through the labors of her deeds she put her hands to the lock and hoped to bring the Desired One inside,

then he went away, but she went out and no longer stayed where she was; rather, as the Word went on ahead, she followed behind him. And the words that follow confirm all the more this sense of our interpretation,
that the height of the divine nature is known not by attaining it, but by passing beyond every wonder and power of attainment.

For behold, the soul that has risen above nature, so that none of the things that exist may hinder her from seeing the invisible, neither ceases seeking the one who cannot be found nor stops calling the one who cannot be called, for she says:
"I sought him and did not find him." And how could he be found, of whom nothing among known things gives any indication, neither form,

nor color, nor shape, nor state, nor quality, nor place, nor kind, nor conception, nor understanding, nor comparison? Rather, he is always found outside every means of attainment and flees from the hands of all grasping and from the nets of searching. Therefore she says,
that: I sought him by those finding brides [? perhaps "powers"] of the soul, and by thoughts and conceptions, and he was outside them all and fled from the approach of the mind.
But how could he who is outside every image bearing a mark be seized by some named form?
And for this reason she devises every power of names to give a name to that ineffable Good, yet every power of verbal expression is defeated and is shown to fall short of the truth.
Therefore she says: I called on him as far as I had power, for I devised in pursuit of him certain illustrious utterances, likened to that ineffable blessedness,
but he was higher than those forms and significations. Thus the great David did, and many times he called God by myriad names. And they confess that they are defeated by the truth, for he says:
You are "God merciful and compassionate and long-suffering and greatly merciful" and true, and "power and strength and refuge and helper and upholder and horn of salvation," and things like these.
And again he confesses that his name is not known over all the earth, but is marveled at, for he says:
"How wonderful is your name in all the earth!" And to Manoah too, he who announced the birth of the child spoke thus when he asked about the name,

"... that it is wonderful and beyond the grasp of human hearing." For this reason the soul also puts it into words as far as it is able. But it is not able to do as much as it wishes, for it wishes more than it is able,
and it is not even able to desire as much as he is,

but only as much as the will is able to will and as much as it has the power to do. And since the one who is called is beyond the reach of the eager desire of the one who calls, she says: "I called him, and he did not answer me."
But as for what the bride adds to these words: although she shows an appearance of grief, yet as I think,
she sees the same form and walks the road of those high ascents, for she says:
"The watchmen who went about the city found me. They struck me and wounded me, and the guards of the wall stripped my garment from me."
And perhaps someone may think that these words belong to one who mourns rather than to one who rejoices: "They struck me and wounded me and stripped my garment from me,"
but to one who understands them closely, these words will appear as a cause for good boasting. And so that these sayings may become clear to us,
Let us recall what was written a little earlier, before this, when the word testified to her cleansing from every covering and veil, where it says in the person of the bride:
"I have taken off my garment; how shall I put it on?" And here again it speaks of her taking back her own garment. She who said "I have taken off," where does she now get this garment?
unless it is clear that by this too an ascent to the height is shown?
For she who took off that old garment and became pure of every veil became so much purer than herself that, in comparison with this present purity, it would seem
that she had not taken off the garment at all, but as if, after that stripping, there were still something on her to be cast off, which she has now cast off.
Thus her ascent toward God always shows the height she has attained to be coarser.
Hence, in comparison with this present purity of hers, the stripping off of that first garment, as if it were a covering,

is taken from her by the watchmen who found her, who went about the city. Understand the city as the soul, and the watchmen as the mind and divine thoughts, which prick and beat the soul with holy and spotless reflections until they strip from it all coarseness and unite it to God.
And for this reason I said that this present taking of the garment is understood as a form of good, so that without covering or veil she may contemplate the beauty of her Beloved,
which the apostolic word also confirms, which ascribes the removal of the veil to the power of the Holy Spirit and says:
"When one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed; and the Lord is Spirit."
And since that which prepares one for the good is good, no one will dispute with us about this.
And since the taking away of the veil is good, surely the wounding and the beating are also good, through which that removal of the veil comes about;
But since a simple and quick glance at these words appears somewhat sorrowful, that is, "They struck me and wounded me," it is good
So let us understand from the Scriptures the force of such words, whether their mention was made in a good sense, and so examine their meaning: how wisdom saves the soul of a youth from death,
or what it advises doing so that he may not die. Let us hear it from wisdom itself, for it says: "If you beat him with the rod, he will not die," for you will indeed beat him with the rod,
but you shall deliver his soul from death." See, she has interpreted the word "beating" as something that brings immortality, as she says:
"If you beat him with the rod, he will not die," and that otherwise the soul is not delivered from death unless it is beaten with the rod.

See how good beating is, and how desirable is the deliverance of the soul from death, which is brought to us through beating. And the prophet testifies to this same order concerning God, that he gives life through killing and heals through wounding, for he says:
"I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike and I will heal."
And David called such a rod and staff of his not a wounding but a comfort, and said: "Your rod and your staff, these have comforted me,"
through which comes about the preparation of that divine table itself, and all that the psalm goes on to set forth in succession,
that is, the anointing of the head, and the unmixed drink of the cup, which produces that sober drunkenness, and that good accompaniment of mercy, and the length of days in the house of God.

And since that sweet wounding brings all of this, according to the word of Proverbs and the teaching of the prophet, good indeed is the beating with the rod, through which comes the multiplication of so many good things,

and let us rather search out what remains of what was said before: how the Word passed by the bride and could not be held by the hands of her who longed for him. He passed by, then, not in order to abandon her whom he passed by, but rather to draw her to himself.
For she says: "My soul went out at his word."
First, then, the soul goes out from where it was, and only then is it found by the watchmen of the city, as she says: "The watchmen who go about the city found me."
If the torments of hell had found her, or robbers, such a finding would have been evil,
for "the thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy."

But the guards who find her, those who go about the city, are such that she is rather blessed for such a finding, for whoever is found by guards is not stolen away by thieves and robbers, nor carried off captive.

And who then are those guards, and who else could they be, but the servants of him "who keeps Israel," who by that guarding shelters his right hand, to whom has been entrusted the guarding of the soul from all evil, who becomes the guard of going in and coming out? He is the guard of the city, of which it has been said
that:
"Unless the Lord guards the city, its watchmen keep awake in vain,"
Hence, by the "watchmen" who "go about the city" the word refers to those ministering spirits sent forth to serve those "who are to inherit life."
And understand the soul as the city, as we said, the dwelling place of God.
Through these things the soul was found, as the lost sheep was once found by the good shepherd, over which all the hosts of angels were moved to joy, according to the word of the Lord.
In the same way the drachma was also once found by the light of the lamp, and at its finding all the friends and neighbors rejoiced.
In the same way David too, the servant of the Lord, was found, as the psalm says in the person of God:

"I have found David my servant, and with my holy oil I have anointed him." Since he became the possession of the one who found him, let us hear how he was made worthy of gifts, for he says: "My hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him,"

the enemy shall gain nothing from him and the son of lawlessness shall be unable to harm him," and: "I will cut down his enemies before his face and destroy those who hate him," and all else that is written in that array of blessings.
Hence it is good for the soul to be found by those watchmen, the angels,
for so David gives us to understand when he says: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them."
Now then, as for the word that says, "The watchmen struck me and wounded me," she gathered through them some increase of progress and boasted of it;
and understand her wound in this way: it signifies the mark made by the divine rod in the depths of the soul,

for the spiritual city does not receive the discipline of the divine rod in such a way as to remain without mark or sign and to have no form of remembrance of it. Rather, it is made illustrious by that wound, and the bride makes the divine wound public in the manner of a boast. And understand this as follows.
The divine instrument and rod of consolation, which grants healing through striking,
is the Holy Spirit, whose fruits are all those fruits that Paul enumerates, and among all the others the teacher of the virtues,
which is fasting and ascetic struggle, of which Paul himself also boasts, saying: "I bear the wounds of Christ in my body." And so he makes it public
that all the weaknesses and afflictions undergone for the sake of the virtues perfect the power of Christ through that weakness. And the meaning of the wound has also become well known to us,

for through it came about the removal of the theristron from the bride. This is a kind of bridal veil that covers the head, the face and the whole body, as is written concerning Rebecca: "She put on her veil, that is, the theristron." It was removed so that the beauty of the soul might be revealed and the shadow of the covering might no longer darken it.
But now let us return to the earlier word and complete this examination of these words.
That is, the soul that looks toward God and is seized by that good desire for the incorruptible beauty always advances toward a higher desire and never dulls that desire with satiety,
since it always advances onward and onward and does not cease from advancing; where it is, it goes out from, and where it is not, it enters; and in every case,
whatever appears great and wondrous to it, it reckons as lesser than what comes after, because what has not yet been found is always found to be higher and more wondrous than what has been found,
just as Paul died daily, since he was always passing over to some new life and was forever dying to what had been completed, and forgot the labors that were past.
Therefore the bride too, running toward the Bridegroom, finds no rest in her progress toward what is higher,

for behold, she has made orchards of pomegranates spring up from her mouth, and things flowing with sweet ointments; she prepared food for the King of creation and entertained him with her own fruits;
she has watered the gardens, has become a well of living water, and has become altogether beautiful and unblemished, as the Word testified of her. And again, when she had become higher than this,

in a manner beautiful and worthy of God she perceived the coming of the Word, when his head was filled with dew and with the drops of the night, which is the array of his locks. She washed her feet, took off her garment, and made myrrh flow from her hands;

she put her fingers to the lock, opened the door to him, sought the one who cannot be grasped, and desired to attain the unattainable one. She called to the boundless one to answer her; she was found by the watchmen and received the blow of the rod;
she became like the rock which "the rod struck, and waters came forth," as the prophet said.

Do you see to what height the bride has risen? For this reason she was struck, like that unhewn rock struck by Moses, so that, like it, she too might make the word of life spring up for the thirsty from that longed-for wound.

And then, after this, she revealed and laid bare the beauty of her face, when the watchmen took from her the veil that covered her loveliness, which is the theristron. This, then, is what we are able to attain in the likeness of her desire, and there is no envy at all [?],
if something higher should be revealed to someone by him who reveals hidden mysteries, and he writes it down for the benefit of souls.
And might not the vision of Isaiah also have some share in common with this present discourse?
I mean that vision which he saw after the death of the leprous king, how the Lord was sitting on thrones,
whose form and likeness and immeasurability and greatness his sight could not contain; for if it had contained them, he would have spoken of them too,
just as he spoke of those others whom he saw, enumerating their wings and telling us of their standing and flying; but he speaks only of hearing the voice,

when the curtain over the doors was lifted by the voice of the seraphim and the temple was filled with smoke, and through one of the seraphim the glowing coal touched his mouth. And when this happened, not only the lips,
but the ears too were purified for receiving and hearing the word,
For just as here it speaks of the beating and wounding of the bride by the watchmen and of her being stripped of her garment, so also there, in place of the veil, the curtain was lifted up,

so that through it the vision of those inaccessible and invisible things might become unhindered, and in place of the watchmen seraphim appear, in place of the rod a live coal, and in place of the wound a burning.
And the perfection of both, of the bride and of the prophet, became one and the same.
which is purity. And just as the prophet was not pained by that coal when he was burned,

but was glorified and shone with radiance, so also here the bride does not indicate distress because of the wound, but boasts of an increase of boldness through the taking away of the covering, which the text called a veil.
There is, then, also another understanding of this present passage, equal in force to those already examined,

for when the soul went out at his word and sought the one who cannot be found, and called, by the sign of voice and name, the one who cannot be comprehended, she was then informed and taught by the watchmen
that she desires the unattainable and longs for the inexpressible.

And by these words of theirs, as if figuratively by wounding and beating, she was thus wounded by despair at not finding the one she desired, for she thought that the desire for the good was imperfect and without enjoyment. But that covering of sorrow was stripped from her,

for she learned and came to know that constant progress in seeking and never ceasing from ascent is the true finding and enjoyment of the one desired, whenever the desire that has been found becomes the beginning and parent of another desire.

And so, when the covering of despair had been stripped from her and she saw the boundless and uncircumscribed goodness of that beloved and desired beauty, increased and multiplied ever more and more along with the endless ages,
she was inflamed with greater longing and made known through the daughters of Jerusalem the eagerness of her heart for her beloved,

and that she has received into herself that chosen divine arrow, with the arrowhead of faith, and has been wounded in the heart and pierced [?] in the depths of the soul by receiving the arrows of love,
and, as John says, "Love is God," to whom belong glory and might, now and always and to the ages of ages, amen!
The heading of this homily: 5:8. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field, if you find my kinsman anywhere, tell him that I am wounded by love. 5:9.
What is your kinsman more than another kinsman, O fairest among women? What is your kinsman more than another kinsman, that you have adjured us so? (5:10)
My kinsman is white and ruddy, chosen from birth out of ten thousands. (5:11) His head is gold of Ophaz;
the plaits of his hair are like hammered work [?], black as a raven. (5:12) His eyes are like doves upon the fullness of the waters, washed in milk, sitting upon the fullness of the waters.
He who through Moses laid down as law the mysteries of the law, and through himself fulfilled the whole law and the prophets, as he declared in the Gospel:

"I did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it"; he who made murder disappear by dispelling anger, and who stripped away the defilement of adultery by destroying lust, likewise drove out of this life the curse and the evil of the false oath as well, and by the complete prohibition of the oath he bound and made idle that slaying sickle of it which the prophet saw,

for transgression of an oath is impossible where there is no oath." Therefore he says: "You have heard that it was said to those of old: 'You shall not swear falsely, but you shall render your oath to the Lord,'
but I say to you not to swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God,
nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
Nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black; but let your word be 'yes, yes' and 'no, no,' for whatever is more than this is from the evil one.

But the soul that has been testified to by the perfection of the praise of the Song of Songs, and has been stripped bare of the veils of the heart by putting off that old garment, the soul that has cast away the veil of the face, which is the theristron, that is, every doubting and disturbing thought,
so that it may look upon the truth purely and spotlessly, makes the daughters of Jerusalem swear neither by the divine throne, which the word calls heaven,
nor by the kingdom of God, which is Jerusalem, nor by that honored head, whose hair cannot be changed either to white or to black,
but it changes the oath to the field, and makes the maiden swear by its powers, and says to her:
"I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and the strengths of the field."

She who was testified to as wholly beautiful and spotless clearly says nothing superfluous, which would belong to the devil's portion, but she counsels from God, from whom, according to the word of Zechariah, nothing else comes to pass except whatever is good and beautiful in God's sight; she who was testified to by God for the advances she had gained, as a royal bride.
And no one has any doubt concerning her, who cast away every form of improper oath and made the maidens swear neither by the royal city nor by the throne of God.
And by this he teaches us how far one ought to venture upon an oath, for he permits us to swear neither by the throne, nor by the city, nor by the honored head,
which a little later he designates as gold, whose hairs are neither black nor white, for how could gold be changed to black or to white?
And this is clear, that she makes the maidens swear some such oath,
one that does not violate the law of the Gospel and that becomes a cause of praise for those who swear it, as the prophet says:
"and let everyone be [?] who swears by it." Therefore the force of these sayings is not foreign to the law of the Gospel, by which he confirms the truth and says:
"Let your yes be yes and your no no." Now then, since the rules about oaths forbid swearing by the throne, by the city, and by one's very own head,
and only "yes" and "no" are permitted, and the same truth is seen through both, this present oath of the bride also signifies the same pattern, for she says:
"I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: if you find my kinsman, tell him that I am wounded by love."
These words were also examined above, as the order of the discourse required there, and now let us speak of them again, if anything is needful.
The Apostle ordains the oath as an unshakable thing, as a confirmation of truth and an end of every dispute,
which is why the bride puts the maidens under oath, so that they may keep her word unalterably.
But since every oath is made by one who is greater, as the Apostle says, for no one adjures by something contemptible rather than by what is greater than himself,
it is necessary to understand what that greater thing is by which the bride adjures the maidens, for she says:
"I adjure you, daughters, by the powers and strengths of the field."
And what could be greater than us in this? For this world is called a field, according to the word of the Lord, and of this we are not ignorant.
But these powers and firmnesses which are seen in him and which surpass our understanding,

By whom are those oaths confirmed, and what might they be? For this reason it is fitting for us, for the sake of greater clarity, to recall what is written in another translation concerning these words, for it says that:
I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the deer of the field.
And these names inform us in what the power and strength of this world consist, which is presented through the oath as a confirmation of truth.
There are two things that make a person God's own.

The first is that he should not stray from the true Truth, through true understanding and knowledge, and that he should not accept concerning God the error of the straying minds of pagans and heretics; and truly such right theology is "yes."

The second is a pure mind, which drives every passionate love out of the heart; and this too is not foreign to that same word, "yes." So these two good ways, of which the one fastens us to the true Truth, which is God, and the other drives away those passions that corrupt the soul, are depicted and understood through the mention of the gazelles and the deer,
of which the one sees unerringly and keenly, while the other is a killer and destroyer of unclean reptiles and beasts.
And this "yes" the bride sets before the maidens, which is to look toward God with orthodoxy and to pass through this temporal life in purity and without passion.
If we accomplish these things, that unshakable thing will be established among us,
which is "yes," and this is the truth that confirms the oath, and whoever swears in this way will truly be praiseworthy, as the Psalmist sings.

For truly, whoever by his own effort perfectly sets upright the height of these two mysteries, when the word of his faith looks unerringly toward the truth and by his way of life he is made pure of all diabolical defilement, he swears to the Lord not to go up onto "the couch of his bed," nor to give sleep to his eyes, nor slumber to his eyelids,
until he finds in himself a place for the Lord and becomes a dwelling of God, who has settled within him.

Now therefore, if we too are children of the heavenly Jerusalem, let us listen to this teaching of the bride: how the vision of the Desired One comes about, and what it is that she teaches us. It is this:
if we swear by the powers, which is the gazelle that sees hidden things, and by the strengths, which is the deer that makes evils vanish.
Through these comes about the vision of the holy Bridegroom and of the archer of love, and from then on each soul is able to say to him with hope:
"I am wounded by your love." And how good the wound of love is, we have been taught by the Proverbs. For it says: "Better are the wounds of a friend than the kisses of an enemy."
And who that friend is whose wounds are more honorable than the kisses of the enemy is clear and known to all who are not ignorant of the words of life.
So the friend is true and steadfast, who, even when we had become enemies, did not cease from loving us; but the enemy is faithless, implacable and savage,

who, although we had done him no wrong, brought death upon us and put us wretchedly to death. To the first-created the separation from evil things required by the commandment seemed a wound, for estrangement from sweetness was reckoned a wound, while the enemy's enticement toward sweetness and beauty was reckoned a kiss.
but experience made it clear that the friend's command, thought to be a wound, was far better and more desirable than the enemy's deceitful kisses;
And since the good lover of the salvation of our souls revealed his own love, and while we were still sinners,

Christ died for us. Therefore the bride loved him passionately; in return for his love she loved him, and she showed the arrow of his love lying in the depths of her soul, which is participation in the divinity,
for God is love, as has been said, who by the arrow of faith is driven into the heart.
And if we must also speak the name of the arrow, let us say what we have learned from Paul: it is faith perfected by love.
Let me look then also at the question put to the teacher by the maidens:
"What is your kinsman more than a kinsman, that you so adjure us?"

This saying has the following meaning, as the sequence of what was said before suggests. For the maidens saw that good going-out of the bride's soul, when she longed for the Word, she who said: "My soul went out at his word,"
and they understood that, having gone out, she was seeking through signs the one who cannot be found, and was crying out and calling to him who answers no one by names.
For this reason they say to her: How shall we know him, who is not found through signs and wonders, who does not answer when they call him, and who is not caught when they seek him?
Now therefore, you too strip from our eyes that veil which the watchmen of the city stripped from you, so that this may become for us a guide to what we are seeking.
Tell us, who is your kinsman, and what is his nature?
Give us some form and sign by which to recognize him, you who have been filled with good things and for this reason have become beautiful among women.

Make known to us what is sought. Teach us by what gifts the invisible one is found, just as he informs you about that arrow of love by which your heart has been pierced, and kindles your desire through that sweet tenderness.
For it is better that we recall the same saying again, so that the force of these words may be joined together and blended.
What is your kinsman, O beautiful among women? What is your kinsman more than another kinsman, that you have so adjured us?
Let us then listen to her, from whom the veil had been entirely stripped and who beholds the truth with the unveiled eye of the soul,
to hear how through them she portrays what is sought, how in words she depicts that wholly desirable form, and how through the maidens she makes visible that unknowable and unbeholdable one.

For since the Lord is understood, that is to say, as both created and uncreated, we call him uncreated with respect to his being without beginning, his eternity, and his endlessness, and we know him before the ages as the creator of all created things. But we call him created on account of our nature, which he received from us through the incarnation, when he was conformed to this body of our lowliness. And we speak so in order that through the divine words we may set forth the force of this mystery, for in this way it is more resplendent.
We call uncreated and unmade the Word who was from the beginning with God, and the Word was God,
through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made of all that was made. But we call him created because he became flesh and dwelt among us,
he who, even though he became incarnate, is made manifest by the glory dwelling with him, for God appeared in the flesh.
This is he who was in the bosom of the Father, the only-begotten Son and Word of God, concerning whom John said:

"We beheld his glory, and although the one who was seen was a man, yet the one known through him was God"; therefore he added: "glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." And since his uncreatedness, his birth before the ages, and his endlessness are beyond the reach of all natures and inexpressible, for this reason he is glorified and worshipped in silence, whereas his appearance in the flesh can in some part be made visible and understood.
And the teaching of the bride looks toward this mystery and speaks concerning it, as much as can be contained by her hearers, and she sets forth that great proclamation of godliness,
by which God appeared in the flesh, he who was in the form of the Godhead and in the form of a servant lived in the flesh among human beings.
And since he once took human nature to himself, through himself, from the incorrupt and all-holy Mother of God,

so from that beginning he continually sanctifies the common lump of human nature through union with it by communion in the mysteries, and through himself he nourishes the body of the Church. And, fitting together each member raised up with him through faith, he unites it to the common body, and in this way he adorns and beautifies all.
And he arranges and joins together the company of believers as eye and mouth and hand and the remaining members, beautifully and fittingly, as Paul says: "The body is one, but the members are many."
And all those members do not have the same function, but one is an eye in the body and cannot despise the hands, and the one who is the head cannot be separated from the feet,

but through himself he blends those many kinds of functions, as the body does through its members, so that there may be no collapse of the body and no division of the members. And having first set forth such meanings in a figure, he then made his word plain and said:
"God has appointed in the churches apostles and prophets and teachers and shepherds, for the establishing of the saints for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ,
until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ."
And again he says: "Let us grow up toward him in all things, of whom Christ is the head, through whom the whole body, joined together and strengthened by every joint of supply,
according to the help of the measure of each member, make the growth of the body for the building up of yourselves in love."
Therefore whoever looks upon the Church looks upon Christ, who builds up and magnifies himself by the addition of those being saved.

And for this reason the bride, who has cast the veil from her eyes, beholds with a purified eye the ineffable beauty of the bridegroom, by whom she was also wounded with the incorporeal and fiery arrow of passionate love.
Now seething and inflamed love is called passionate love,

with which there is no longer any shame, especially when the arrow of love does not become a wounder of the flesh, but one even boasts of the wound, when one receives that immaterial arrow in the depths of the soul. This is what the bride has now done as well, and so she says to the maidens:
"I am wounded by love."

And since she has reached such perfection, and it was right that she should show the beauty of the bridegroom to the maidens as well, she does not speak of that which was from the beginning, for it was not possible by the power of words to utter and reveal what is ineffable. Instead she recounts to the maidens the manifestation of God in the flesh, which the great John also did. For that which was from the beginning he passed over in silence,
but what he saw and heard, and how with his hands he ministered to the Word of truth, he set forth in exact detail.
So the bride says to the maidens: "My brother's son is radiant and ruddy, and chosen from birth out of myriads.

His head is of the gold of Ophaz. The plaits of his hair are like wrought work, black as a raven. His eyes are like those of a dove upon the fullness of the waters, washed in milk, sitting upon the fullness of the waters. His cheeks are like bowls of ointments, giving off the fragrance of the perfumers. His lips are lilies, dripping myrrh in abundance.
His hands are of gold, finely turned, filled with tarshish. His belly is like a tablet of ivory set with sapphire stones.
His legs are of marble, set upon bases of gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the fir. His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desirable.
This is my beloved kinsman, and this is my close one, O daughters of Jerusalem."
And all these things, through which the portrayal of his beauty was made, did not make known the invisible and incomprehensible Godhead,
but rather him who was revealed by the divine dispensation, who appeared on earth and lived among men and put on human nature, through which,

according to the apostolic saying, his invisible nature is clearly seen in these created things, made manifest by the creation of the world of the church. For the building of the church is the creation of a world, in which, according to the prophetic voice,
a new heaven too is created, which is the firmament of faith in Christ, as Paul says, and a new earth is prepared,
which drinks the rain that comes upon it. And another man is also created, renewed through the second birth in the image and likeness of the Creator.
and another nature becomes a luminary, concerning which it says:

"You are the luminaries of the world," and "that you may shine as luminaries in the world." And a not small multitude of stars shines in that firmament of faith, and this is not surprising, for a multitude of stars shines in this new world;
those whom God numbers and assigns by name, but because the Creator of such stars inscribes their names in the heavens; for thus the Creator of this new creation said to his own luminaries:
"Your names are written in heaven."
And this alone is not what is marvelous, that a multitude of stars is created in it by the Word; but many suns also rise in it,
which light up the world with the brightness of good works. For thus that Creator said to such suns:
"Thus let your light shine before men," and also:

"Then the righteous will shine forth like luminaries." And just as one who looks upon this visible world and contemplates the true wisdom through its manifest beauties, so through these sayings one perceives that invisible beauty and that abyss of wisdom
whose depth created the beauty and the nature of the things that exist.
likewise, whoever has looked upon this new heaven and earth of the Church's creation
beholds in it him who is all in all, and through the things that can be grasped and attained comes to an understanding of the things that are invisible and incomprehensible to our nature.
And since at this point the virgin souls come before the soul that has reached perfection, so that she may tell them about the Beloved,
Therefore, through the things revealed to us in him as Savior, she has portrayed the wonders of the one sought by the virgins, and all

the church she shows to be the one body of the Bridegroom, and she depicts and makes [?] her own understanding through the beauty of each of the members; and by naming these one by one she completes the beauty of the whole body.
And she takes the starting point of her teaching from the structure of our bodies, just as Matthew also did, who began from Abraham and David to recount the mystery of the Incarnation
by genealogy; and to the great John was reserved, through the portrayal of such members, the account of the birth without beginning and the gospel of the Word who was from the beginning.
So too the bride, through such understandings, makes the virgins wise and teaches them that our mind cannot ascend to what is inaccessible and invisible
unless we first hold fast by faith to what was revealed; and the revelation is a matter of the nature of the flesh. For when she says:
"My kinsman is white and ruddy," she portrays the honor and the property of the flesh by mingling these two colors. And she used this same image above as well,
when she called him an apple, whose coloring, by its twofold mingling, signifies this same thing.
For the apple is white and red: the whiteness portrays the flesh, and the coloring portrays the blood.
But since all flesh enters this world through marriage, a man and birth,

and so that no one, accepting some fleshly birth in the mystery of godliness, should go astray in mind through the workings and passions of nature, and imagine for the Lord's flesh the same sort of birth as that of all who are born on earth, for this reason,

she confessed that he who shared in flesh and blood is ruddy and white, and by these two colors she signified the nature of flesh; but she separated the manner of his birth from that of those born of sexual union and made it foreign to the likeness of those born on earth, saying:
"From among all the myriads." Since men were created, and as many as nature has brought in until the end of time,

This alone is the new form of birth that has entered into this life, in whose birth nature was not a helper but a servant; hence it says: "This one is ruddy and fair." He who entered the world in flesh and blood
is the only one of all the myriads born of virginal purity,

whose conception took place without seed and whose birth was without corruption and without pain; whose bridal chamber was the power of the Most High, which, like a cloud, overshadowed her all-holy virginity, and the God-radiant nuptial splendor was the light of the Holy Spirit,
while the marriage bed was impassibility and the wedding was incorruption.

Now therefore he who was born from such things was fittingly named "chosen out of all the myriads," which signifies his seedless and incorruptible birth, he who alone was born apart from the laws of birth.
For this reason, for that unwedded and incorrupt mother neither a manner of giving birth nor a name for it is to be found,
for a name for birth and virginity together is not to be found and cannot be devised;
but as a Son was given to us without a father, so too a child was born for us without corruption,
for just as the Virgin did not feel any formation of the Lord's flesh by way of corruption within her own spotless flesh, so neither did she perceive the pain of childbirth,
as the prophet testifies to his painless birth, saying: "Before the coming of the pains she escaped from the pains and bore a child."

For this reason both those mysteries were set apart and strange, surpassing natures: he neither began from desire, nor was brought forth from pains, nor was born through agonies; and this came about worthily and not outside what was fitting.
For since nature brought in death through sin, along with sorrow and sighing, and was sentenced,
hence it was indisputable and fitting that the mother of life, just as she began her conception from joy, should likewise accomplish the birth through joy,

…surpassing all knowledge. For thus the archangel said to her: "Rejoice, favored one, the Lord is with you." And at once, through those words, he drove away the sorrow that had been imposed from the beginning through nature and childbirth.
Thus, then, he who through that new, distinct and singular birth alone was chosen out of myriads, and fair and ruddy,
on account of the nature of the flesh,
was rightly so called, and called incorrupt and impassible on account of the conception and birth and all those wonders of the mysteries of birth. Such words did the bride utter concerning him.
But I think you are not ignorant of his being firstborn, how many times he became so and how many times he was so called:

the firstborn of this new creation, and the firstborn among many brothers, and the firstborn from the dead, who first loosed the pains of death and made a way for all to be born again from death through the resurrection.
In all these, then, he became firstborn, yet not in such a way that he came to birth by the law of birth,

since the font of second birth is also foreign to the passions of birth, as are the second birth of resurrection from the dead and the divine firstbornness of this new creation; for in all these births he was a stranger to the laws of birth. Therefore it says: "chosen out of myriads."
Now as to how she recounts his beauty through each of his members, it is time to make these known, for she says: "His head is of the gold of ophaz."
This word is Hebrew, and it signifies gold that is pure and shining and free from all admixture.
The translators left it untranslated, for no word corresponding to it was found in Greek.
But we have understood that ophaz signifies gold that is pure and shining and free from all admixture, and its application is this: the head of the body of the Church is Christ.
We call the Lord Christ, yet we do not assign this name to the divinity, but to the deified man,

who appeared on earth and lived among men, in whom the whole fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily, the firstborn of the common [?lump], through whom the Word took on our nature, made it incorruptible, and freed and cleansed it from all its passions. For the prophecy says this about him: "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth,"
he who was tested in every likeness of our nature, only without sin."
Now therefore the head of the body of the Church, that firstborn, the beginning of all our nature, pure, unmixed with all evil and not admitting it, is of gold;

and the locks of hair, which were once dark and black, like ravens in appearance — and I mean those ravens whose work is the plucking out of eyes, according to the word of the Proverbs, and which are to be eaten by the young of the eagle, those that blind the seeing ones in their senses and their sight —

these became tall trees, emulating the heavens by rising to the height from the depths of the earth; they adorned the beauty of the bridegroom and became the locks of that lordly head, its clusters and its forelocks [?].
And surely you are not ignorant of what the work of these hairs is, since you learned it above from the voice of the bridegroom, for he said:
"My hair has been filled with dew and with the drops of the night." These hairs, then, are those that pour forth rains,

which the prophets designate as clouds, from which come forth the rains of teachings, which make the spiritual vineyards drunk and fill the labors of God with fruit. And in figurative speech the word gives the apostles the names of hair and locks and clusters and forelocks [?] and curls, they who were at first dark and black in the deeds of the world,
that is, tax collector and robber and persecutor and others,
whoever was of this kind, made like that black, carrion-eating, eye-plucking raven, which is the prince of darkness, as it says,

he who from among ravens became a tall tree and was called a curl of that divine head, and who was "formerly a blasphemer and persecutor and insulter," both raven and beast, was so changed by grace that he became a lock of that lordly head,
drenched with the dew of heaven and watering the whole body of the Church with the stream and teaching of hidden and invisible mysteries.

So we have understood these, according to the bride's words, as the hair and locks of that golden head. They add no small beauty to their own head as they are wafted to and fro by the breeze of the Holy Spirit. They become the crown of the incorruptible goodness of that head and adorn it by their own arrangement and by the thick, encircling mass of curls,
as the prophet says: "He set on his head a crown of precious stone."

And by both these names the same people are understood, that is, the beauty of hair and the preciousness of stones, and by means of themselves they adorn that royal head. But from here on it is fitting that we also mention the comparison of the eyes, for it says: "His eyes are like those of doves upon the fullness of the waters,
washed with milk, sitting upon the fullness of the waters."
The force of these sayings, then, is beyond our comprehension,

For whatever we understand, we suppose it to fall short of the truth. But when we searched carefully, an understanding of this kind was found. The holy apostle says in his words: "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you.'" And this teaching has such power

that in both respects the body of the Church ought to do good, through right vision of the truth and through the practice of blameless ascetic struggle. For vision alone, by itself, cannot perfect the soul

if the work of ascetic struggle and a life of understanding is not joined to it. Nor can the work of ascetic struggles alone, by itself, raise one up to perfection unless true godliness goes before it, joined with contemplation and pure vision.
Now therefore, since the fellowship of the eyes with the hands is so necessary, let us come near to consider the commendation of the eyes and to examine their praise with understanding.
As for the hands, let us examine that discussion in its own place.
The work of the eyes by nature is this: to see. For this reason they are set higher than all the senses in the body, and they have been established by nature as the guide of the whole body.
Now then, when we hear the leaders of the truth so called in the divine Scriptures,
as one was called seer, another beholder, and another watchman, whom God so named through prophecy, we understand this:
that in this place he gives the name of eyes to those seers and beholders and to those appointed as watchmen,
and the wonder of them, as they are likened and compared, gives us an understanding of some surpassing beauty, for it says: "His eyes are like those of doves."
For truly good is the praise for innocence given to such eyes, a praise achieved by those who are no longer defiled by fleshly life, but live and abide in the Spirit,
for the spiritual and immaterial life is represented in the form of a dove, since the Holy Spirit himself appeared thus to John when he came down from heaven upon the Jordan. Therefore,
he who has been established by God in place of eyes in the body of the Church, if he wishes to keep watch and to behold and to see with purity,

Every stain of wickedness must be washed away with water. This water that washes the eyes is not one; rather, the nature and fullness of such waters is manifold, for as many as the virtues are, so many are the springs of purifying waters we should understand there to be, by which those eyes become ever purer.
That is to say: a spring of purifying water is purity, and others of the same kind are humility and righteousness and truth and courage and the desire for good and the hatred of evil.
These and such waters are from one spring, but from many rivers and streams they gather together into one fullness, by which comes the cleansing of every mist and affliction of the eyes;

So upon this fullness of waters are the eyes, made like doves through purity and innocence, and milk becomes their bath, as the word said: "washed with milk." Truly, then, this praise befits such eyes, and to such a dove belong this washing and adorning with milk.
Now the true test of milk is this: among liquid and moist things, it alone has this distinctive property, that no image or likeness appears in it,
for in all other flowing substances, when one looks down into them, the image of the one looking is seen, as in a mirror under the sun, but in milk alone such a form has no place.

Therefore this is the perfect praise of such eyes of the Church: that through deception they should not form within themselves anything insubstantial and without being, erroneous and vain and foreign to the true truth,
but that they should gaze upon the true truth and not accept the deceptive forms and marvels of this life.
For this reason the lofty purity of the eyes has been indicated by the Spirit through the perfect washing with milk.
And the word that follows makes us understand toward what those eyes ought to direct their eagerness, for it says: "sitting upon the fullness of waters," that is,
for through them the force of this word shows a constant abiding in the divine teachings and an attentive watchfulness with understanding; and by those holy eyes that it praises,
by those same it teaches us how we may acquire that purity and beauty of the eyes, namely, that we should always sit upon the fullness of waters.

Yet now many who have been appointed as eyes abandon sitting upon such waters and sit by the rivers of Babylon, and bring upon their own heads the accusation uttered from the mouth of God concerning such people:
"They have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and have dug for themselves pierced cisterns, which cannot hold water."
Behold, we have learned how an eye becomes good, and fitting for that golden head, and an adornment to it, that is:

so that it may be innocent as a dove, and guileless and free from error as milk, and so that no unreal temptation may present itself to it in fantasy, and so that it may sit forever, patiently and without growing weary, by the fullness of the divine waters, like the tree
planted by the streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season, and whose branches, fanned by the breeze, forever flourish with green leaves.

But now many of the eyes, as I said above, neglect these spiritual waters and have no care at all for instruction in the divine books. Instead, they only dig for themselves the pits of the love of money, or hew out vainglory, or dig out pride,
or with great eagerness they hew out other cisterns and pits, which cannot hold this water that they are hurrying after,

those who strive and wear themselves away for the honor, glory and favor of this world, and while they are still gathering it, they are suddenly scattered and leave not one trace of that vain striving among those led astray by them. But the bishops, stewards and administrators of the Church ought to be such as this:

that they be like eyelids and eyelashes, so that in this way they may adorn the eye of the soul by divine teachings, and that, as with eyebrows, they may outline it by humility, so that the bitter mote of arrogance may not fall into their purified pupil and cloud the eye of the soul. And after the eyes, let us next set forth the praise and the fitting explanation of the remaining members of the Bridegroom, by the will and ordinance of God,
who is our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen!
Chapter. This passage: 5:13. His cheeks are like bowls of ointment, giving forth the fragrance of the makers of ointment.
His lips are lilies, dripping with abundant myrrh. 5:14. His hands are of faceted gold, filled with tarshish stone; his belly is like a tablet of ivory upon a sapphire stone. 5:15.
His legs are pillars of marble, founded on a base of gold; his appearance is like choice Lebanon and like firs. 5:16. His throat is sweetness and altogether desirable.
This is my kinsman and this is my near one, daughters of Jerusalem. Paul, the nurturer of that spiritual stature,
who nourishes with that guileless milk the still infant child of the Church, as he said:
"He stores up the bread of wisdom for those who are perfected in the inner man," and he says: "We speak wisdom among the perfect,"
those who, through the practice of good teachings, have the senses of the soul trained and become able to receive the bread of wisdom,

for such people need the grinding teeth of the mind and the nourishing cheeks. Therefore it is necessary that there also be cheeks in the body of Christ, for those who no longer tolerate the milk of the word,
but seek solid food. Concerning them the Bride now brings forward the word and says: "His cheeks are like bowls of ointment, giving forth the fragrance of the makers of ointment."
This is clear to all who listen with understanding: after mentioning the eyes, he went on in fitting order to the words praising the cheeks, since they are next to the eyes,
which had been standing by the fullness of the spiritual waters,
to be washed with that guileless and unerring milk and to become like that innocent dove, and for all who belong to that body of the Church to share in their good things.
For this reason great Isaiah was commanded to climb the high mountain by way of his manner of life and to cry out with a resplendent voice,
so that through him those who heard might know the Lord coming with power, and his arm, the ruler of all beings,
who shepherds the flock and gathers the lambs and comforts with the hopes of good things those who are well with child, who measured the heavens with a span and holds the whole earth in his palm.
Concerning all this the prophecy says: It is necessary that he preach from the top of the mountains. And since by this means the power to know the truth is given to those eyes through milk and water,
the cheeks are fittingly praised next, whose task is the fine grinding of food, by which the strength of the body's nature is preserved.
But let us see what this praise of the cheeks is, and let us hear from the bride herself how she utters praises of them, for she says:
"His cheeks are like bowls of spices, breathing out the fragrance of steaming spices." By this name "bowl" the word indicates a spread-out vessel,
which by its construction is unconcealed and open, for it is neither very deep and hidden, nor entirely flat and spread out.
And this is the reason why the bride presented its form as a figure of praise; and by this figure she praises such cheeks,

which is the simple, plain and guileless form of teaching. And for this reason she mentioned this name "bowl," in which that reproved and shunned form, from which the prophet flees, cannot be contained, for he says:
"I was rescued from those who hate me and from the depths of many waters."

Now therefore, by this name "bowl" we understand the truth simply shown, without any crafty depth or twisting, whose material is spice and whose function is the giving off of the fragrant vapor of spices,

as it says: "Your cheeks are like bowls of spices," which are not made from gold and silver, or glass, or any other such material, but from the spices themselves, and they in turn prepare spices. And, as I suppose, the understanding seen in what is said in these words is clear: it belongs to those holy eyes of the Church to prepare such food for the body by the grinding power of the cheeks, so that nothing deep, perverse or crafty may be seen in what is said, but that everything may be bright, evident and free, and removed from all guile, concealment and depth, so that it may be suited even to infants, as the prophet says:
"The testimonies of the Lord are faithful, making infants wise," and also: "The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes."

And since such are the bowls of the word, it is clear that they are not fashioned from earthly materials; rather, their very nature comes from the perfumes themselves. By these I mean the perfumes that the bride mentions at the beginning of the Song.
Such a bowl was Paul, who did not falsify the word with cunning, but by the manifestation of the truth bore witness to himself,
who cast away earthly matter, since through baptism he shed the scales from his eyes and separated himself completely from the flesh and from earthly affairs,
and so he was blended from that fragrant perfume and became a child of the Holy Spirit,
who, since by such forging he had been built into a chosen vessel and prepared as a drinking bowl of the word, no longer had need of anything human, but himself brought forth mysteries,

for he did not make it known to flesh and blood, but himself welled up [?] from within himself and brought forth those divine perfumes and drinks, and by the fragrance of Christ he spread that varied perfume of the virtues among his hearers on every side,
and so, according to the differences and particular character of his hearers, he filled each person with suitable ointment:
Jews and Gentiles, women and men, masters and slaves, parents and children, those without the law and those under the law.

And thus the grace of his teaching was many-formed and perfumed with every virtue, and through those many-colored instructions, like a perfume variously prepared, he made everyone fragrant from that bowl of graces with which he was filled.

Such cheeks as these, then, are praised by the one who depicts the beauty of the Bridegroom's body. And that this praise of the cheeks looks toward this meaning, the following verse confirms by its testimony and by the harmony of its sense,
for after the cheeks she praises the lips, from which that fragrant word comes forth, and she says: "His lips are lilies dripping, full of myrrh."
By these twofold names the verse testifies to two virtues together, of which one is truth, radiant and enlightened,
for such is the appearance of the lily, whose radiance depicts the purity and truth of these sayings,

while the second makes manifest through his teaching the invisible and immaterial life, when, by contemplating those good things that are beyond contemplation, one comes to hate this earthly life and dies to whatever is accomplished through flesh and blood. For that myrrh flowing down from the mouth and filling the soul of the one who receives it becomes a herald of the putting to death of the flesh,
for many scriptures teach us that the name of myrrh is a figure of death. Therefore that holy and spotless eye,
which prepared its cheeks as a bowl that produces and mixes perfumes, and whose word blossoms like a lily, adorned with divine radiance,
for so the verse names it on account of the pure and fragrant virtues, and from it come forth unceasing drops of ointment that fill the minds of those who receive them,
which is contempt for material life, idleness from all worldly repose, and death through longing for those unending good things. With such myrrhs as these,
mingled with the lily of purity, the mouth of Paul once dripped and poured into the ears of the holy virgin.
The name of that holy virgin was Thecla, who received those streams well into her soul, gave over her outward man to death, and extinguished every will and desire of the flesh.
After that good teaching, her youth was dead, her visible goodness and beauty were dead, and all the senses of the flesh were dead,
and the word alone was alive in her, for the sake of which the whole world was dead to her and she was dead to the whole world.
In the same way the great Peter once spoke to Cornelius also with the shining lilies of the word, and filled the souls of the hearers with myrrh;
they at once received his word, were buried with Christ through baptism, and became dead to this life.

And besides these, many thousands of other examples of the saints are found, showing how they became such for the common body of the Church, filled the ears of its members with the myrrh that puts the passions to death, and made them blossom with the lily of words.

Through these words the great champions of piety and helpers of the faith, by that good confession at the time of martyrdom, were roused with zeal for the contests of piety and struggled as if they were bodiless.

And why is it necessary to prolong the discourse further, since through what has been said the meaning of the word has been made clear to us: how the mouth of the Church becomes a lily, how myrrh drips onto the lily, and how the soul of those who receive it is filled by such drops?
But now let us go on to the next word, for it says: "His hands are golden, faceted, filled with tarshish."
And that the grace of the eyes in the body of the Church is incomplete without the service of the hands,
we have clearly learned from the great Paul, for he says: "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you.'"

For the power and work of the eyes become all the more evident when the work of the hands bears witness to the keen sight of the eyes, and when they make known their guidance in the good effort toward what is better among good things.

Since it also falls to us to examine the hands of the divine body, which the praise has set before us for consideration, and how the force of their meaning applies to the body of the Church, let us read again those same divine words, so that with God's help and support we may be able to find what they correspond to as well. For it says:
"His hands are golden, faceted." Such a meaning appears from these words:
that by the same words of praise with which the form of the Lord's head is extolled, the praise of the hands is also completed.
