We understand Christ in the flesh as the head of the Church. God was with him, and he reconciled the world to himself, as the apostle says. He revealed himself in the flesh through powerful miracles. And as this head,
which we understand as being of choice gold, the word gave it this name because he was free of all sin, as it says:
"He who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." In the same way the word also calls his hands gold, and the meaning and force of these words is clear,
for by means of the hands the word teaches us complete purity and sinlessness, and being unmixed with and unreceptive to every evil.

And by the hand we understand the general order of the Church for fulfilling the commandments and the labor of mercy to the poor, to whose praise is given likeness to the nature of the head, through purity and sinlessness.
And the hand becomes pure when everything that hinders its beauty is scraped away by chiseling. For just as those who carve the image of some living creature in marble labor and strive
so that by scraping and chiseling they may carve upon it in every detail the form whose likeness they have undertaken to represent,
so too the beauty of the hands of the body of the Church requires much labor and toil, through the chiseling and scraping of thoughts, so that those hands may truly become hands of choice gold.
And it is clear to all how much material takes away beauty if it is not removed from the hand, that is: pleasing people, love of gain, love of glory,
being nailed fast to the affairs of this world, acquiring some high rank by bribes, and spending the charity for the poor entrusted to one on one's own luxury and comfort.
As long as this and everything like it is not removed by that instrument of the thoughts, leaving only the pure and guileless gold of good will, it cannot become a hand of that incorruptible head.
And so that this may become clearer, let us recall the apostolic word,
which named God faithful and seeks nothing else among stewards except only that they be faithful."
For it says: "Moreover, it is required among those hearers that one be found faithful,"

whence the faithful and wise and prudent steward is reckoned as a hand of the Church, and through faithful administration he is changed into gold and is worthy to be an imitator of his own King through a divine and good life.
Such a hand, within the body of the apostles, was not that pitiable and wretched Judas,

but rather that rough and evil-looking one, to be turned away from and fled from, who was entrusted with the provision for the poor and did not remove the dross [?] of love of possessions, but was appointed keeper of the money-bag, to guard it from thieves.
But he became a thief of himself, and what he held in his own hands he drew out [?] by his own hands, and he looked not to charity but to the goods, which became his comfort;
strangled, and by his own will, he fell out of life and became the murderer of his own soul, and by his own doing he left a memorial of wickedness for the times to come after him.
And therefore it is necessary that the hands of the Church be scraped and chiseled,
so that all that is excess and impure may be separated from them, and they may become of gold and worthy of that lordly head.
Now the word "tarshish" is mentioned in many different ways by the Scriptures, and its meaning is not found to be of one kind,
for at times what it signifies shifts to despair, and at times to divine blessedness.

Understand it in this way: when Jonah was fleeing from the face of the Lord, he looked for a ship going to Tarshish. And the great David speaks of the shattering of the ships of Tarshish by a violent wind. And, as I suppose, by the violent wind he signifies the Spirit,
which blew upon the disciples in that upper room in Zion, and which first made itself known through their hearing, as the blowing of a violent wind.
But after that it was also manifested to their eyes, shaped in the form of tongues and resembling the brightness of the nature of fire,
and by it was shattered that manifold evil spread over human nature, which the prophet named the ship of Tarshish; and this is that by which the lower sense of "tarshish" is signified.
But the great Ezekiel,
when he was depicting for the people the showing of the divine vision, presented one of those divine sights by this name and said: "Its appearance was like the appearance of tarshish."
And those who know the forms of the Hebrew language precisely say that what is invisible, incorporeal and without shape is called by this name by the prophets.

And since this word has a twofold meaning, it is evident that in this place its higher sense is signified, for its blameworthy sense would not be mentioned as a ground for praise. Hence it is fitting that we understand this word with reference to these praised hands.

For whoever casts away from himself and pours out all fleshly, excessive and disorderly life, and comes to loathe the love of vain and worthless deeds and of heavy and material things, such a person passes over to that invisible and shapeless divine life and departs from all evil, as they say of the emerald,

which gem-cutters cut and seal-makers engrave: for by grinding they wear away what is dark and earth-like, and leave unworn only that which shines and, with its greenness and brilliance, glistens moistly with the color of oil.

This the holy Apostle interprets more clearly in his words, and he counsels us that we ought to cast off the love of these visible things and make the desire for the invisible things our own, and he says:
"We do not look at what is seen, but at what is unseen,
for what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal." This, then, is how we understand the praise of the hands.

namely how they have been rubbed clean of the desire for material things and have become incorruptible and immaterial through will and zeal for the good, concerning which it says: "His hands are faceted and of gold, and full of tarshish."
And the next saying must also be joined to this, the one it spoke about the belly, that is:
"His belly is a tablet of ivory upon a sapphire stone." When the Lawgiver of natures gave Moses the law written on tablets of stone, he gave those tablets the name "tablet of stone,"
on which those divine letters were imprinted, concerning which God said to Moses:
"Come up to me on the mountain and stay there, and I will give you the tablets of stone: the law and my commandments."
But after this, when by the radiance and manifestation of the Gospel the law cast off everything bodily and earthly,
the tablets that receive the law are no longer of stone, but of bright and newly fashioned ivory,
for that which receives the law and the commandments, which he has named the belly, he calls a tablet of ivory upon sapphire stones.
They say, then, that because of its great density and hardness this kind of bone remains incorruptible for a long time and suffers no damage at all from the length of time.

And sapphire is [?]-colored and blue, and has been found to be a relief for the labor of the eyes of those who constantly strain their sight by the study of writings, for by its natural coloring this stone gives rest to such eyes.
Such is the figure to which the belly of the Church is likened in the praises.

But I, proceeding from the divine word that commands the prophet to write down the vision on tablets, and again to understand the law and the commandments, come to the question of how that tablet of the Lord, called the belly, ought to be fitted into the royal body. For the word
that commands the writing down of the vision on tablets signifies purity of heart by the name of the belly,
on which we inscribe divine visions, just as the one who opened the mouth of the great Ezekiel and placed in it the scroll of a book,
filled with writing on both sides, that is, inside and outside, and said to him: "Your mouth shall eat, and your belly shall be filled,"
which is the mind and understanding of the soul, which he named the belly, in which those divine teachings were treasured up. And likewise again the great Jeremiah,
whose heart was aching from sorrowful thoughts, named it the belly and said: "My belly aches, and the senses of my heart are being consumed."
And if this saying must be explained more clearly, let us recall the divine teaching, for thus he commanded those who believed in him:
"Whoever believes in me, as the scripture said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly."
And from all these we understand by the name of the belly the pure heart, which becomes a tablet of the divine law, as the apostle says:
"Those who show the works of the law written in their hearts, not with ink, but by the Spirit of the living God."
And such writings are inscribed not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the heart,

pure and smooth and shining, for it must be such, so that the remembrance of the divine words may be imprinted in it clearly and without confusion, as if inscribed in some beautiful writing. And well joined to such a tablet, for the beauty and praise of the belly, is also the sapphire, whose radiance is sky-colored.
And this parable counsels us this: that our mind should ponder heavenly things and look toward heaven, so that where it has stored up its treasure, there too it may rest its eyes,
and so that the discipline of the divine commandments may not become wearisome, when the hope of heavenly things gives rest to the eyes of the soul.
And so the praise of the legs follows the praise of the belly, for it says: "His legs are pillars of marble, founded on bases of gold."
The house of wisdom, which she built for herself, has many pillars, and likewise many pillars made firm the tent of witness,
adorned with materials of various kinds, whose bases and capitals were of gold, while their middle part was beautified with a covering of silver.
But the pillars of the Church, which is the house of God, as the apostle says,

that is, how one ought to walk in the house of God, the bride calls marble, founded on bases of gold. And how the bride bears witness to the wisdom of Bezalel, and likewise adorns the beauty of the pillars with bases and capitals of gold, is evident and clear to all who have read the account of the tent,
for just as he prepared a capital of gold for each pillar and set it up on bases of gold, so here she who looks with purity speaks of the beauty of the bridegroom,
for she assigns to his head pure and choice gold,
to which the word "of Ophaz" bears witness, and she says that his legs are founded on gold. But as to how the figure of these pillars ought to be applied,
if we become disciples of Saint Paul, we shall not fall away from true understanding,
who gave those chief apostles, Peter and James and John, the name of pillars of the Church.

Since we also need to know how a person becomes a pillar, so that perhaps we too may become worthy of such a calling, let us listen again to the wisdom of Paul himself, who appoints someone as a pillar and foundation of the truth.
Understand the gold as an image of the truth. It becomes the base and support of the Lord's legs, and with itself it adorns the head and the hands.
And if you understand the nature of marble as firmness, you will not err, for this is the force of these words, that the legs of the body are pillars of marble,
that is, those who by a radiant life and right faith bear up and make firm the common body of the Church,
through whom the base of faith is made firm and unshakable, and the course of the virtues is brought to completion, and the whole body is lifted up by divine hopes.

And this is accomplished through these two, truth and firmness, for gold is fitly compared to truth, which, according to the apostolic word, becomes and is named the foundation of the divine house, as it says:
"No one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus"; and Christ is the truth,
on whom the pillars of the Church are founded,
The marble signifies a shining life and a love for what is good that is firm and unchanging. Now, the pillars of the tabernacle are many, and so are those that bear the house of wisdom,

but here two are enough to bear the whole body. So I think we must turn the image of the parable to some other correspondence. Understand it like this: the commandments of the law are many and of many kinds,

and they lead us to practise virtue. In the same way wisdom tells us many teachings that look toward the same goal. But the short word of the Gospel gathers the whole perfection of the virtues into commandments that are easily counted, and it says this:
saying: "On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets."
And undoubtedly it amounts to the same force, whether someone bears a weight by hanging it or by carrying it,
for one and the same force is seen in both,
when someone bears a weight on both sides, whether with the hand
or by the shoulder [?]. And the Lord says that the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments. Here the bride speaks of two pillars set firmly on bases of gold,
and says that the body is carried by them. So this match between the image of the legs and the figure of those two commandments is surely not out of place.

Of these, the Lord makes one the first and the second like it. He calls love of God with all the heart, all the soul and all the strength the first commandment, and he makes love of the neighbour as oneself equal in force to the first.
And again Paul too, when he was preparing the great Timothy as a divine house, set up for him these two pillars, which are faith and a pure conscience.
And by faith he signified the love of God with all the heart and with all the soul and with all the strength, and by a good mind he depicted the love of neighbor.
And I think that this understanding now found is not foreign to the first figure,
for by these two one becomes a pillar, like Peter and James and John, and anyone else who becomes worthy of this name as they were, whether now or hereafter, or who was so before,
for whoever is made perfect by these two virtues changes himself into a pillar and foundation of the truth, according to the word of the apostle.

And by these two virtues, which are unswerving faith and love toward all, a person becomes unchangeable, a bearer of the body of the Church, like those pillars established on golden bases. And after these praises she completes all the beauty of the bridegroom and says:
"His appearance is like chosen Lebanon and like the cedars. His throat is sweetness and all desirable.
This is my kinsman and this is my close one, O daughters of Jerusalem." By these words she makes known most clearly
that this praise is of the beauty of the visible bridegroom, and by the visible one I mean him
This the apostle forms into a body through each of the members that make the Church complete.

For it says that his appearance is like the countless cedars that surround Lebanon on every side. By these words it shows that nothing low or worthless is seen in the beauty of the body that is not lofty like the cedars and does not rise toward the height of the summit. So let us again consider the words set before us, for it says:

"His appearance is like the appearance of Lebanon, choice." Choosing, in every matter, comes about by setting a thing against its opposite, since two things bear the same name: the truly true good and the merely apparent good;
what is not good, one falsely claims to be good. Whoever is no stranger to sound judgment will undoubtedly choose the choice good over the false and untrue one.
And since here the appearance of the Bridegroom is likened to a choice Lebanon, the text introduces a comparison of two Lebanons:
the one evil and rejected, like the calf and the broken cedars, as the prophet said, and the other choice and honorable,
whose goodness is divinely beautiful and like God.
And understand this saying thus: there is one King, himself the true and great King of all creatures, yet the world-ruler of darkness also claims for himself the name of kingship.
Hosts of angels serve the true King, and hosts of demons serve the world-ruler of darkness.
Principalities and authorities and powers are called servants of the King of kings and Lord of lords;
he too, according to the apostle's word, has principalities and authorities and powers, which are to be abolished,
when the existence of evil is made to vanish and perishes and comes to nonexistence, as the same apostle said again: when he shall have abolished all authorities and principalities and powers.
The prophet saw the King of glory seated upon thrones, high and exalted,

and that other one too spoke of setting up thrones above the stars of heaven and of likeness to the Most High. The great King has choice vessels in his house, and that other one too has vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction.
And again, the King of angels gives life and peace through angels to those worthy of him, "but that one sends wrath and affliction through evil angels."
And why is it necessary to tell one by one the ways in which that enemy of truth becomes an assailant and opponent of the good by nature, through deceit and [?]?
And since the mountain of Lebanon is splendid to behold, thickly set on every side with [?] cedars, for this reason, with reference to the opposing minds, by means of those clear parables,
in the Scriptures, as it is likened to each side, its force and meaning are divided.
And thus its name is seen to be both praised and reviled, through this division made known by the prophets,
for at one time the Lord breaks the cedars of Lebanon, and again he grinds all Lebanon and its cedars fine, like that idol of the calf which they made in the wilderness.
By this the prophecy signifies that evil itself and all the height that comes from it, exalted against the knowledge of God, will become nothing and be abolished.
And again, at times it recalls the notion of it in the better sense and says: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, and shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon."
But truly the Righteous One is the Lord himself, who for our sake sprang up from the earth, that high-crowned palm tree,

who sprang up in the matter of our nature and became a mountain for those cedars that are planted through faith and multiplied by him, who, when they have been planted in the house of God, flourish in the divine courts.
Now by the house, according to the word of the Apostle, understand the Church of God, in which the planting of God's cedars takes place, and by the courts, the eternal dwellings,
in which, at the appointed times, the flowering and manifestation of those good hopes will take place.
And since the body of Christ is made complete by its individual members, and since all the members become one body, according to the word of the Apostle,
for this reason she gave all the beauty of the bridegroom the name "chosen Lebanon," and by that name "chosen" she marked its distinction from that rejected Lebanon,
for that Lebanon is such as Isaiah said, which with its high ones [?] and shall be shattered, when the rod of Jesse brings forth a flower and that rod of authority springs up,

through whom the nature of the lion and the leopard and the asp shall be changed to tame and gentle, so that the lion is reared together with the ox and the leopard rests together with the kids, and the little child who was born to us shepherds them, whose hand is laid upon the asp's hole and touches the asp's offspring and renders their venom powerless.
And when this has come to pass, as the prophet said, Lebanon too shall fall with its high ones. But as for how great a power the prophecy signifies through these figures,
since it is known to all, we have considered a detailed interpretation of all of it to be superfluous; for who does not know that child who was born to us,
who touched the asp with his hand, whose taking hold shows that venom of the beasts to be a fellow-dweller with us and makes it forget its natural bitterness?
And since through him that evil Lebanon falls, and together with it falls that first one and head of evils,
who exalted himself against the truth, for this reason the bride likens the beauty of the Lord to that chosen Lebanon and speaks thus: "His appearance is like chosen Lebanon and like cedars."
And then she adds also the beauty of the throat, and assigns it sweetness and desirability, and says: "His throat is sweetness and altogether desirable."

And its fitting sense is this: the part of the neck toward the chest is called the throat, from which rises the voice, produced by the skill of the mind and the movement of the breath and the concord of the joints,
since good words are a honeycomb, and the instrument of speech is the voice that comes forth from the throat.
If someone were to call the disciples and ministers of the word, through whom Christ spoke, by this name as a figure, he would not sin.
For indeed, when the great John was asked who he was, he named himself a voice, since he was the forerunner of the Word. And blessed Paul gave proof of Christ speaking in him,
Whose voice spoke, and through it sweetness came to the one speaking; and all the prophets made ready the instrument of their voice for the Holy Spirit speaking within them, and it became sweetness.
And the divine honey would rise up through their throat, the honey that kings and the poor receive as life,
whose delight does not cut off desire through satiety, but rather nourishes the longing for desirable things by partaking of them.

For this reason she names him wholly desirable, and, as if by a kind of definition, she depicts that longed-for beauty through this word and says: "and all-desirable." Hence blessed are those members through which he becomes all-desirable,
blended with the fullness of all good things and adorned with that desirable beauty,

so much so that he is longed for and desirable not only for his eyes and hands and hair, but likewise and equally for his feet and legs and throat. And not one of his members falls short of that surpassing beauty. Hence she says:
"This is the brother's son, and this is my neighbor, O daughters of Jerusalem."

For she revealed his whole form to them by depicting it in words, as far as it was possible to reveal the object of the search. And then she put forward the word that unites all those words, and said:

"This is my kinsman, and this is my neighbor." That is, Christ has dawned for us from Judah, and the bride called him brother. He also became friend and neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers. He healed that man's wounds with oil and wine and bandages, set him on his own beast, gave him rest in the inn that receives all, gave the two drachmas for his care, and promised to repay any further expense on his return.
And I think it is clear about each of these things what meaning it has and toward what aspect it looks,

for that lawyer who was testing God wanted to show himself superior to others, and in his arrogance he set himself apart from equality with those others by the words he uttered: "And who is my neighbor?"

Then, in the form of a story, the Lord set forth the whole loving-kindness of the divine dispensation: that is, the man's descent from the height, the attack of the robbers, and the stripping off of the incorruptible garment,
and the wounds of sin, and the death of half of his nature while the soul remained immortal, and the unprofitable
passing by of the Law, and the unhelpful disposition of the priest and the Levite, for the blood of goats and bulls could not wipe away sins. But to him,
the one who put on the whole of human nature from that dough of Adam, in which there was a portion of all peoples, of Jew and Samaritan and Gentile and of all people together,

who with his flesh as a beast of burden came to that half-dead man and healed him, carried him on his own beast, and made his own loving-kindness an inn for him, in which all who labor and are heavy-laden find rest,
and whoever commends himself there, he will undoubtedly receive into himself, in whom he has come to dwell, for thus he said: "Whoever abides with me, and I with him."
He then receives him into his own lodging and gives rest within himself to the one who is uncontainable, from whom he receives two drachmas,
which are the love of God and of neighbor.
But since it is not the hearers of the law who are justified before God, but the doers,
one must not only receive those drachmas of faith in God and of love of neighbor, but also add something of one's own through deeds, in order to fulfill these commandments.
And for this reason the Lord told the innkeeper that he would receive the reward for all his diligence at his second coming.

Now then, the one who became a companion and one near to us through such love for humankind, and who by rising like the dawn from Judah became a brother's son to the people of the Gentiles, this is the one about whom the bride tells the maidens.
And this is the one about whom that holy and incorrupt bride informs the daughters of Jerusalem, saying:
"This is my brother's son, and this is my near one, O daughters of Jerusalem,"

to whom may we too attain, and may we find him under these proclaimed names and through confession of him as the Savior of our souls, by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, whose is the glory forever and ever, amen.
Heading of this discourse: 5:17. Where has your brother's son gone, O beautiful one among women? Where has your brother's son turned? And shall we seek him with you?
6:1. My brother's son has gone down to his garden, to the beds of incense, to pasture among the gardens, to gather lilies. 6:2.
I am my brother's son's, and my brother's son is mine, who pastures among the lilies. 6:3.
"You are beautiful, my neighbor, as good pleasure, comely as Jerusalem, wondrous as those set in array. 6:4 Turn away your eyes from before me, for they have made me take wing.

Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead. 6:5. Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing. All of them bear twins, and there is no barren one among them. 6:6.
Like a scarlet cord are your lips, and your speech is beautiful; like a slice of pomegranate are your cheeks, apart from that silence of yours. 6:7.
There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. 6:8. One is my dove, my perfect one.
She is the one of her mother. She is the chosen of the one who bore her. As for the one who was attested to have been from the city of Andrew and Peter,

Philip the apostle, this statement was not made idly; rather, being called a fellow citizen of such brothers was set forth as a form of praise for Philip, those brothers who became wondrous in the Gospel and renowned through the account written about them.
For when the Forerunner showed Andrew the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world,

he too understood the mystery, followed the one who had been shown to him, learned where he was staying, and brought the good news to his own brother as well, that the one foretold by the law and the prophets had come.

And when he heard this, he believed with all his soul and mind, and followed the Lord so fervently that through that very voice of the Lord he instantly became higher and more exalted and was divinely transformed,

For instead of Simon he was called Peter, and not only was he called so, but he also became so. Abraham and Sarah, by contrast, only at the very last, after long periods of time and after many visions of God, were given that blessing of the name and were established as heads of nations.
And likewise Jacob was called Israel after wrestling a whole night.

But the great Peter did not attain that grace after growing little by little; rather, as soon as he heard from his brother and believed in the Lamb of God, he was made perfect by faith, and from that Rock of life he was called a rock of faith and became one, as we have said.
Likewise Philip, the fellow citizen of these distinguished men, since he became one found by the Lord, as the Gospel says:
"Jesus found Philip"; at once he was called to be a follower of the Word, as it says: "Follow me."
And as he drew near to the true Light, like a lamp, he received from there a share in the light, and he enlightened Nathanael and made him shine with the mystery of godliness, for he said to him:
"Him of whom Moses wrote in the Law, and the Prophets also, we have found: Jesus from Nazareth of Galilee."
And Nathanael listened to that good news with understanding, for Philip taught him in precise detail the mystery spoken by the prophets, and told him
that the divine manifestation in the flesh took place first from Bethlehem, and that he was called a Nazarene because of his upbringing in Nazareth.

And he understood and reflected on both points: that because of David the Lord's birth in Bethlehem could not be passed over and was unavoidable, on account of the mystery of the cave, the manger and the swaddling clothes,
while Galilee, that region of the Gentiles, was enlightened by the Word's dwelling among them and became the beginning of the enlightenment of the Gentiles.
And all this Nathanael learned thus precisely from Philip, and by him he was enlightened; hence he said in amazement: "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?"
Then Philip became his guide to that grace and said to him: "Come and see."
So Nathanael left the fig tree of the Law, whose shadow was keeping out the spreading light. He went to the one who withered the leaves of the fig tree because it bore no good fruit.

For this reason the Word also testified about him that he was not deceitful but a true Israelite. He openly displayed in himself the guilelessness and simplicity of the patriarch, and for this reason he was found worthy to hear: "Behold, a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile."
But I think that thoughtful and learned hearers will easily see, from the praise that follows in the Song of Songs, to which person this opening passage refers,
which tells us that, just as Andrew followed the Lord at the word of the Forerunner,
and Nathanael was enlightened by Philip, departed from the shadow of the Law and was joined to the true Light,
so also the maidens, in order to find the good announced to them, entreat the guidance of that soul made perfect in beauty,
and speak to her thus: "Where has your kinsman gone, O beautiful among women?
Where has your kinsman turned, that we may seek him with you?"
Rightly, then, do those virgin souls question the teacher, for before this they had said to her: "What is your brother's son, O beautiful among women?"
So, having learned from those signs mentioned above, that "he is radiant and ruddy," and from those that follow, by which the form of the one sought was depicted, here they speak to her again:
"Where has your brother's son gone, and to where has he turned?"

This is so that, if they come to know and learn where he is, they may fall down and worship at the place where his feet stood; and if they understand to where he has gone, they may so prepare themselves that he may come to them also and his glory may be revealed to them too, the revealing of which becomes life for those to whom it is revealed, as the prophet said:
"Show your face upon us, and we shall be saved." And the teacher too, like Philip, who said:
"Come and see," leads the maidens to find the one they are seeking. Instead of saying "see," she shows them the place where the one they seek is.
And she says to them: "My brother's son has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices." Up to this point the word indicates where he is; but from here on, where he has gone,
or where he is looking, the teacher shows them, and she says to them: "To pasture among the gardens and to gather lilies."
So the bodily and plain sense of what the bride told the maidens is this: from it they learned where he had gone, or where he looks [?]. But it is certainly fitting
that we also grasp the benefit of these divinely inspired words through spiritual contemplation.

Now then, when we hear, "My brother's son has gone down to his garden," we learn from these sayings the mysteries of the Gospel, which reveals to us the force of the words hidden under each of these names, through him who appeared to us in the flesh as God,
who dawned from Judah and spread his light over the Gentiles, who sat in darkness and the shadows of death.

And well and beautifully is he named "brother's son" by her who was betrothed to him in that holy, spotless and everlasting marriage, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, who became also the sister of that people of the Jews.
The going down signifies the one who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and was wounded by robbers,
for whose sake he himself also came down, in order to rescue him from those who fought against him; by this it signifies the descent from those ineffable heights to our lowliness.
And from the figure of the garden we learn this: that the true chief husbandman and tiller of the earth plants us a second time, for we are his cultivated field, according to the word of Paul.
And he is the one who in the beginning, in paradise, cultivated human nature,

…which the heavenly Father planted. But the boar from the thicket ravaged it, and the fierce wild beast grazed it bare. These are the divine paradises and labours. For this reason he came down: to rebuild the desolate place as a paradise of virtues once more, to adorn it, to pour out the divine and holy fountain of teachings through his own words, and to water that royal garden.
And the cups of ointments appeared in that figure of beauty as the adornment of the cheeks,
by which the spiritual food of those who are growing up is ground fine. But here they are indicated by the word as the place and dwelling of the bridegroom. And this teaches us
…that the Bridegroom does not dwell in a soul that is barren of virtues,

nor in one stained by foul-smelling deeds and thoughts. But if someone is a bowl of ointments, as the words quoted earlier say, that person becomes a bowl of wisdom. He receives within himself that divine and incorruptible wine, which becomes joy to the one who receives it.
And the next word teaches us on what kind of pastures the flock of that good shepherd is fattened,
for the sheep are not led about through deserted, desolate and thorny places, to graze on some useless hay and grasses,
but ointment is spread as their food in the gardens, and in place of hay, the lily, concerning which it speaks of the gathering by the shepherd as food for the sheep. And such is the philosophy
that this word teaches us: that the all-ruling nature and power, which holds all things within itself, makes the purity of those who receive it its own place and resting place,
by whom the manifold garden of virtues is cultivated, and it blooms with the flower of lilies and brings forth the fruitfulness of ointments,
for the lilies become a figure of a bright and pure mind, and the fragrance of the ointments signifies estrangement from all the stench of sins.

By these, then, the word speaks of the pasturing and grazing of the rational flocks, and of the rearing of the sheep, and of the gathering and collecting of the lilies, which the great Paul spreads out for the sheep, he who sets before us food from that great treasure, that is:
"Whatever is true, whatever is pure, whatever is just, whatever is honorable, whatever is love, whatever is praiseworthy, whatever is virtuous and praised."
These, as my reason supposes, are those lilies by which the flocks are reared by that good shepherd and teacher.

And let us also hear the next word, which that holy and undefiled bride says: "I am my kinsman's, and my kinsman is mine." For this is the rule and limit of the perfection of the virtues, and it teaches us this:
that no one ought to have anything else at all apart from God. And let no one contemplate anything else in any way, and let the purified soul see nothing apart from God,
but let it so purify itself from every material deed and thought

that in every part and altogether it may be joined to what is incorporeal and immaterial, and show itself radiantly as a figure of the archetypal image, just as if someone should see on a panel the painted figure of some archetypal image, altogether like it and unchanged,

and should determine that the image of the two is truly one; and he would call the beauty of the image that of the archetype, and of the archetype he would say that it is seen in that likeness; altogether in the same way is the one who would say:
"I am my kinsman's, and my kinsman is mine": by this she signifies being conformed to the beauty of Christ himself, and that first blessedness
…shows himself to be a receiver of our nature, and an image and likeness of that firstborn, the only true beauty.

Consider how something is seen in a polished mirror. Someone carefully attends to his face, looks into the mirror, and so adorns himself beautifully and precisely and makes the image of his face handsome. In the same way, the soul casts away everything material and vain and imprints within itself the goodness of that incorruptible beauty. Such a rational and spiritual mirror is then able to speak these words:
"Since I see the whole form of my beloved within myself, all his goodness is therefore seen in me."
Paul truly conformed himself to these words and said: "He who was dead to the world is alive to God," and that "Christ lives in him." For he who said:
"For me, life is Christ," says this: that nothing of human and material passions lives in him, neither desire,
nor sorrow, nor anger, nor fear, nor dread, nor wantonness, nor insolence, nor rancor,

"Neither envy, nor a will that repays evil, nor love of possessions [?], nor love of glory, nor love of honour, nor any other of the deeds that defile the soul. Only that which is foreign to these is mine. Everything that is not seen in his nature I have removed and cast away,
and whatever is not with him, I have nothing of that kind. Therefore 'for me to live is Christ.'" And this is one with the voice of the bride, that is:

"I am my kinsman's, and my kinsman is mine," he who is purity and spotlessness and incorruption and light and truth and everything of the kind, who pastures my soul and nourishes it not with any hay or [?],

…but by the brightness of the saints. The nature of the lily, through the brightness of its colour, makes us understand this meaning. That is why the one who pastures among the lilies feeds his flocks in fields of lilies,
so that the light of the Lord God may shine upon them.

For the kind of food shapes the make-up of the body it nourishes. As an image of this, picture a glass vessel. Whatever is poured into it can be seen as it is, whether it is ink or something bright and pure. Therefore,

whoever receives the brightness of the lily into his soul makes his soul shine through it, and its inner form becomes visible on the outside. To make this clearer, understand it this way: the soul is nourished by the virtues, and the virtues are figuratively called a lily.

If someone is filled with these through good conduct, he shows by his life the form of that conduct within himself. The pure lilies are purity, righteousness, courage, prudence and all the good things of which the apostle speaks:
"And whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is praiseworthy, whatever is virtuous, and whatever is commendable."

For when all these have come to dwell in the soul, they display through it a holy and pure life, and they beautify and adorn the one who has acquired them. And all these are themselves made beautiful by the one who has acquired them.
Now then, the one who has entrusted himself to his beloved and has received his beauty into his own soul: of what kind of gifts is he made worthy by him,
who glorifies those who glorify him? Let us hear this from what follows the present words, for thus the Word speaks to the bride:
"You are good, my close one, as good pleasure; beautiful as Jerusalem; wondrous
as the ordered ranks." For glory is offered by the heavenly hosts to God in the highest, for the sake of good pleasure among men, as we have it from what the shepherds heard.
We have learned this as the Gospel tells it, when they saw peace born on earth. And that Jerusalem is the city of the great King, the Lord himself testifies.
And to what kind of beauty of the bride these words testify, by comparing her with good pleasure and with Jerusalem, is not unknown to the intelligent.

For that God-loving soul rose to such a height, from strength to strength, as it was lifted up by the virtues, until it was joined to God and appeared as God's dwelling-place. For this reason it is also made worthy to have the Lord's own wonders assigned to it.
For God, who dwelt in the high bosom of the Father, shared in flesh and blood out of love for humankind,

so that our peace might appear on earth. Now then, whoever has made his own beauty like that good pleasure of the Lord has clearly become like Christ in good pleasure, and just as Christ became this for human nature,
so he also becomes this for others, as Paul, the imitator of Christ, did, who offered up his own life

so that by that payment of his own he might obtain life for the Israelites, as he says: "I pray that I myself might be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers and my kindred according to the flesh."
and it is fitting to say to him the words of the bride,
namely: "Such is the beauty of your soul, just as the King's goodness came to be for our sake. He humbled himself, took the form of a servant, and gave himself as a ransom for the life of the world."
and the rich one became poor for our sake, so that we might be saved by his death and be made rich by his poverty, and by that form of a slave become kings.

And the beauty of Jerusalem reveals this same height, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, the free woman and mother of the free, which is the city of the great King, as the Lord said. For whoever receives within himself that uncontainable one,
so that God may dwell and walk within him, and so that he may be made beautiful by the beauty of the one dwelling within him,

such a person becomes the heavenly Jerusalem and receives her beauty within himself. And what else could the goodness and beauty of the city of the great King be, except that boundless goodness and beauty of the King?

And since he truly is, according to the word of the prophet, comeliness and beauty, as it is written: "In your comeliness and in your beauty, draw taut, and go forward and reign, for the sake of truth and righteousness and meekness," for by these the divine beauty is portrayed,
which is truth and righteousness and meekness.
And the soul that is formed by such beauties becomes lovely, like Jerusalem, and is adorned with the comeliness of the King.
And this praise is clear, for it is fulfilled in the bride and is set forth for her adornment; that is, the virtue and comeliness of Jerusalem, together with its aptness.
But the word that follows, I know, is likewise a praise of the bride.

But the meaning, how such a praise is to be digested, or how it adorns the soul made worthy of that praise, is not easy to find, for it says: "Awe-inspiring as ordered ranks," unless someone takes the praises fitted together earlier as a path and says:
By comparing her with the heavenly host and their incorporeal nature, the word praises the bride, and by her imitation of them it exalts and magnifies her,
for they are the ordered powers, where the authorities stand forever in authority, and the dominion of the dominions is unchangeable and abiding,
the thrones are firm, the principalities stand unenslaved, the powers bless God unceasingly, and
the flight of the seraphim does not cease, their standing does not change, and the cherubim hold that high and exalted throne, and this is their work forever; and those ministers
who do the deeds and listen to the words never cease from their service.
And since these authorities are ordered by God, and the ranks of those intelligible and heavenly powers stand forever unconfused, and no evil alters their order,

therefore the soul that imitates them accomplishes everything in good order and beautifully, and by this it gains such wonder as exists among those ordered powers, for the sense of "awe" is rendered as "astonishing."

And if someone understands awe as wonder, he would not be mistaken. But the word that follows leaves in doubt the persons by whom it was spoken and to whom it was spoken. That is: "Turn away your eyes from before me, for they have given me wings."
For some have supposed that these things were said to the King, or to the bride and pure soul. But I say that these words of theirs ascribe these sayings to him, and what has come to my heart
I will tell you briefly. For I have many times heard from the divinely inspired books the name of divine wings, for at one time it says:
"In the shelter of your wings shelter me," and: "In the shade of his wings you shall hope."
And again Moses, in that great song of his, signifies the same figure and says: "He spread out his wings and received them." And there is what was said by the Lord concerning Jerusalem:
"How many times have I wished to gather your children, in the way a bird gathers its chicks under its wings." And if someone understands the fitting together of the meaning,
let him not consider this statement to be out of keeping with what follows.
And if, by some ineffable understanding, Holy Scripture ascribes wings to the divine nature, and since our first creation was made in the image of God, as our nature confirms, this is also clear,
for that is called an image which falls short in nothing of its original archetype; and if that archetype were winged, human nature too would surely have been winged,
so that it might have the divine likeness in its wings as well.
But it is clear that the name "wings" must, by some figurative and parabolic manner of speech, be transposed so as to be understood in a way befitting God,
that is, as power and blessedness and incorruptibility, for such divine glories as these have been called by the name of wings.
And all this was seen in man as long as he remained in the divine image, but after that, the inclination toward evil stole such wings from us,
for since we came to be outside the shelter of the divine wings, we were stripped of our own wings as well.
And for this reason the grace of God appeared to enlighten us, so that we might renounce all ungodliness and fleshly desires and, through holiness and righteousness, become winged again.
And if this is not foreign to the truth, it would indeed be fitting for the bride to confess the grace wrought upon her, poured out by the divine regard,
for as God has looked upon us with the eye of his love for humankind, we too may become winged toward that first grace,
and for this reason David prayed and said: "And let your eyes behold my uprightness,
for you have tested my heart and examined it by night,
"You have tested me, and no falsehood was found in me." And these two sayings are one, namely:
"Let your eyes behold uprightness," and:

"Turn your eyes away from before me." For whoever looks at what is upright will not see what is crooked, and whoever does not see what is crooked will certainly see what is upright. The removal of the opposite side shows that those divine eyes see what is good. Through these eyes the soul becomes winged, in respect of [?] the disobedience of the first-created man.
had been made a stranger to its wings, for when the divine eyes look upon us, our eyes no longer see any opposing and unseemly deeds.
And thus we become winged again, and through the virtues we take up wings like those of a dove, and we fly up and rest in that rest
with which God rested from his works.
And again, after this, the praise of the bride's beauty begins to come in, which the discourse sets forth item by item through a certain figurative likeness,
for it praises the beauty of her hair and the orderly array of her teeth and the bloom of her lips and the sweetness of her voice and the coloring of her cheeks.

And each praise is completed by a certain fitting correspondence, for the hair is likened to a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead; and the flocks of newly shorn sheep, come up from the washing and rejoicing in bearing twins, complete the praise of the teeth by their likeness; and the lips resemble a scarlet cord; and the coloring of the pomegranate adorns the cheeks. And the words are spoken thus, for it says:
"Your hair is like flocks of goats that have appeared from Gilead;
your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and there is no barren one among them.
Your lips are like a scarlet cord, and your speech is beautiful; your cheeks are like a slice of pomegranate, apart from that silence of yours."
We have set forth the interpretation of all these things above, and I think it is superfluous to set forth the same words again and for the discourse to become tiresome.

But if anyone should be wearied by our setting forth the same words, for the sake of those who did not happen to hear the earlier ones, let us not refrain from setting them forth very briefly. Hair holds a rank set apart from the whole body.
For every body is governed by some sensation, without which life is impossible,
for the life of the flesh is sensation, and we see that hair alone,
though they are parts of the body, are also foreign to sensation, and they make this known in that neither burning nor shaving pains them as it does the other members.
And since, according to the word of Paul, "The glory of a woman is her hair, and by braiding it she adorns her head,"
we learn from this praise of the bride's hair that it is fitting for those who are seen on the bride's head,
by whom the Church is glorified, to be above the perception of the senses and to cover perception with wisdom, as is written in Proverbs:
"The wise will conceal perception"; for them the organs of sight do not become judges of the good,
nor is the good distinguished by taste, nor by the organs of smell, nor by touch, nor is the discernment of the good entrusted to any other sense,
but they mortify all the senses, and by the spirit alone and the mind they touch those visible goods and desire them.

And thus they become the glory of the Church, which is figured in the form of a woman. They neither grow arrogant because of honors nor are they constricted by faintheartedness because of afflictions, but even if it should be necessary to be cut for the faith of Christ,
or to be thrown to the fire or to the beasts, or to endure any other sufferings, they display the insensibility of hair.
Such was Elijah, who appeared from Gilead, covered with a shaggy [?] and dried-up body and with goatskin, who stood unshaken by all the threats of tyrants; and such are all
those who, in the likeness of that prophetic fortitude, separated themselves from all worldly affairs and lived destitute, afflicted and ill-treated in mountains and caves and holes of the earth,
of whom this world was not worthy. Such as these are seen like a flock on the head of all, and they become the adornment of the Church and are lifted up to heavenly joy with that Gileadite.
And as for the goat having been assigned as the animal for the praise of the hair, perhaps it is also for this reason:
because the nature of this animal is suited to growing hair, so that for this reason too it might become a figure for the adornment
of hair; and further, because it walks without stumbling on rocks, dwells on the summits of mountains, and boldly walks in rugged places that are hard to traverse.

And all these things are well suited to those who pursue that strenuous course of the virtues; and perhaps also for this reason, that in the service of the law this animal was brought in by the lawgiver as needful for many services, and so that through this too it might be worthy to be the praise of the head.

And again, I know that in the Proverbs too, among the four things that go forward well, this one is counted, that is, the he-goat, leader of the goats. And what we may understand by this is as follows:
Every undertaking, begun by one person, spreads out to many;
just as the book called Tubal the inventor of smithcraft, and traces back to him the art of all who came after him and who practice ironwork,
so also Abel became the leader of shepherding, and Cain of tilling the ground, and Nimrod of hunting, and Noah of vine-growing, and Enosh of hope in God.
And many such things are learned from the holy Scriptures, of which some one person became the inventor, and in this way the practice came into this life.
And since Elijah, more than all others, became the leader of divine zeal and was called zealous, all

who after him followed in his footsteps and became like him in his zeal became the flock of that leader of such a life; and such people appeared as the glory and praise of the church and were set as the adornment of the head in place of hair.

In the same way it completes the praise of the teeth, which nourish the body of the Church. These teeth ought to be always washed and to appear pure, and to have nothing superfluous, like newly shorn ewes.

They ought also to bear twins in giving birth to the virtues and to become the father of a twofold purity, which is seen in soul and in body. And all barrenness in good things should be driven away from such teeth.
And the scarlet cord, taken as a figure of the lips, signifies a measured and orderly ministry of the word, which the prophet named a balance and a firm door,

so that the door of the word may be opened at the proper time and shut at the proper time. And that the cord is called by the name of a measure we have learned from the prophecy of Zechariah, for a cord, a measure of the land,
was held by the angel who was talking with him;
and it becomes a measure of the word most of all when it is dyed with scarlet, which is a figure of the blood of our Savior.
And if anyone, like Paul, has Christ speaking within himself, Christ who redeemed us with his own blood, that person has in his mouth the cord that measures the earth, adorned with scarlet colour.

The next saying is the interpretation of this figure, for it calls the scarlet cord "beautiful speech." By this it again signifies purity and orderliness, for speech appears precisely beautiful when it reaches its full growth and is not without limit.
nor outside the limits, but in times and order and constitution is altogether complete and without lack;
and the adornment of the cheeks, by their likeness to the rind of a pomegranate, bears witness to a certain great perfection of good things in the bride,
For it signifies that she has not gathered her wealth from anywhere else, but is herself her own treasure, and contains within herself the provision of all good things.
For just as the rind of the pomegranate encloses the edible part, so she too, by that visible goodness of her life, has gathered her treasure within herself.
And this is that hidden treasure of hopes and the proper fruit of the spirit, which is secured by a virtuous life, as by the peel of a pomegranate.
But this saying, "apart from your silence," signifies something of this sort: your praise does not come so much from the things that are visible and evident, as much as the word indicates,
but rather from as much as is hidden by silence and flees from being revealed by speech;
for just as silence is indicated as being apart from speech, so too whoever understands speech as being apart from silence will not err,

For we keep silent about what we are unable to express in words. And if silence is understood as lying outside speech, then certainly speech is signified as lying outside silence. Therefore the one who said:
"Apart from that silence of yours" makes clear by this word that all the things outside silence are great and lofty, and they can be revealed even in words.
but the things that are beyond speech, hidden by silence, inexpressible and unrevealed, are greater and higher than those that are uttered.
Let us then hear also the meaning of the praise that follows, the understanding of which is like that well
whose mouth a heavy stone had blocked, making the sharing of its water beyond the reach of those shepherd girls,

but Jacob came and moved that stone and rolled it away from the mouth of the well, and he filled the drinking troughs with water and watered the sheep, and he gave the shepherds authority to drink of that water as they wished. And what is this, then, that we liken to such a well? It is this:
"There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number.
One is my dove, my perfect one. She is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her." Who then might roll away for us the hiddenness of this saying,
Who could draw up for us the water of understanding that lies in such depths and cannot be touched by our words? But, as I think,
it is good for us to testify to our hearers that the knowledge of this belongs only to those to whom the apostle says: "In everything you were enriched,"
in all speech and all knowledge," whereas our poverty is unable to lay hold of the treasures of this present saying,
but so that we may escape the judgment for sloth and idleness from him who commanded us to search the Scriptures, for these reasons let us not be reluctant to shed a little sweat.

This, then, is what we say: by these words, the saying from those praises of the bride sets before us a certain teaching and lofty philosophy, and that teaching is this: not by one sequence and order were created beings created and renewed,

For when in the beginning he prepared the nature of beings by divine power, the beginning and the perfection of each being were established together, and all things came from non-being into being and received perfection together with their beginning.

Now human nature too is one of the creatures, but it did not receive its order of perfection like those other creatures, nor the same essence of creation, but one far higher and more glorious than all, as it is written:
"Man was made in the image and likeness of God,"
which shows the height and summit of good things, for what could be an imitator of the likeness of God?
And in that first creation the end was not separated from the beginning, and our nature took its start from perfection.
But since by its inclination toward evil it made death its own and fell away from that good life,
it no longer receives perfection at once, in the manner of the first creation,

but by a certain way and journey, advancing little by little toward perfection, in sequence and in order, it is raised to the summit of the virtues, when it casts off every improper love and all fellowship with adverse deeds.

For in that first creation nothing hindered the perfection of nature, since evil did not exist; but in this second renewal, length of time, a multitude of labors and virtues of various kinds became necessary for those who wish to ascend to that original restoration of good things,

since our mind has been bound by wickedness to material loves, and little by little, through a life of struggle, we cast off that multitude of evils that has come upon us, as if it were some rind and peel wrapped around us.

And for this reason we have learned that "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places," and in accordance with each person's making good things his own and hating evil things, the recompense for labors and the reward for struggles is prepared for all.

for one person has only learned to do good, and now, as if from a depth, has swum up out of an evil life to share in the truth. Another has grown further through desire for good things, and another has become higher through struggle,
and another has reached the midpoint of the lofty ascents, and another has gone even beyond the midpoint. And there are some
who have surpassed even these, and others who have advanced beyond them too, and after these, still others who strive more vigorously along the heavenly racecourse.

And so, in every way, according to the many kinds of difference and division in their wills, God receives all of them into his own dwellings and joins them to his own possessions. He gives all of them a good reward: to those who advance he adds more of his gifts, to those who fall short he generously supplies what they lack, and he repays each one according to his own works. This, then, is what that saying wisely teaches,
as we understand, that in the distinction of the souls who see the Bridegroom,
it teaches us through these sayings, and it ranks some as virgins, exceeding in multitude the measure of number, others as concubines, and others as queens.
Thus it recorded the names of the concubines as eighty and those of the queens as sixty,
but it exalts above all that one dove, seen in her solitude, the perfect one, the only one of her mother and the chosen one of her who bore her.

And these divine words give us to understand that those who have only now come forth, as if from a womb, out of the depth of error, are like certain newborns: they have not yet established word and reason within themselves, they are allotted to the faith in a childlike way, they are countless in number, and they believe
that the word of the mystery is saving and is life, yet they have not established the truth within themselves through instruction and through the heart's full assurance in the word.
These are called maidens in this place because of the childishness of their spiritual age: they were born by the word of faith, yet through proper upbringing they have not yet become such
that they might come to the state of marriage and become full-grown men, complete in the measure of marriageable age,
so that through the fear of the Lord they might be able to conceive and give birth to the spirit of salvation,

but they are still being saved with a childish and incomplete mind, without reason. Yet these too are among those who are to be saved, as the prophet says: "Man and beast you save, O Lord," and he classes as irrational beasts that part of the saved which is incomplete in reason.
But among those who have grown in mind through due labor and have left childishness behind, we are taught a twofold division,

for the souls of both these and those become one body with the Word, but the former are joined to the Lord by a kind of passionate longing and boundless love, as was the soul of David and the soul of Paul. For the one said:
"But for me, drawing near to God is good," and the other in turn: "No one shall separate us from the love of God
which is through Christ Jesus, neither life, nor death, nor this world, nor the one to come, nor anything else among existing things at all." But the others flee fornication out of fear of torments;
these too, then, remain in incorruption and purity, but, schooled by fear rather than by love, they become strangers to evil and do not admit passion.

But those lofty souls who, with perfect desire and love of incorruption, are mingled with the divine purity are called queens because of their communion with the King. And those who become workers of the virtues through threats and the terror of what has been said,
the Word names concubines, for none of them has yet become mother of the king, nor are they able to share in that royal honor.
And how could one be able to, who has not yet become free and master of himself and self-governing in a virtuous mind and in prudence,

but who withdraws from communion with evil things out of slavish fear? And the sign of what has been said is this: for the queens, being counted worthy to stand at the right hand, those to whom the King says:
"Come, you blessed of my Father, and inherit the kingdom prepared for you." But of that lesser, second part, those to whom the Lord says:
"Fear him who, after killing, has authority to cast you into the fire of Gehenna."

And I suppose that this division, the separation of the two orders, is expressed figuratively by means of number, that is to say: six are the commandments on account of which the kingdom is prepared for those on the right,
Let us understand these as royal talents, each of which the wise and faithful servant ought to multiply tenfold by increase,
so that in this way he may enter into the joy of his Lord, and, because he was faithful over a little, be set over much,

Hence these six commandments, which are "I was hungry" and those that follow, through which the soul becomes a sharer in the kingdom, and the full increase of each of them is a tenfold multiplication,
just as that good servant said to his lord: "Your talent has gained ten others."
As a consequence of this, then, we find one queen, expanded to sixty through the tenfold multiplication of each of those six commandments, and received into a share of the kingdom.
For when one commandment is divided into many parts, it thus multiplies itself and is distinguished and given form by each of the virtues.
In this way, then, it is divided into sixty queens,

each one apportioned and counted according to those various commandments; and she becomes a bride sharing in the divine kingdom, and the one is transformed into a choir of queens and is reckoned with the honor of just so many commandments.
Now if we have understood, not beyond what is fitting, that the soul which multiplies each of the set of six commandments tenfold is figuratively signified by the sixty queens, it is fitting

that concerning the eighty concubines, who are counted as eight tens, we should understand the mystery figuratively from the inscription of the eighth of the Psalms, to which those instructed by fear look, and so depart from evil things,
whose words are suited to scourgings, and which through fear of torments bend that terrible Judge to mercy, for it says:
"O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your wrath. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled."
And whatever else the sequel adds after the entreaty to that terrible Judge, in which he laments for this reason, that there is no remembrance of God in death.

And how could those condemned to weeping and gnashing of teeth attain the joy of the remembrance of God, as it says in another place: "The remembrance of God brings joy"? And it sets forth many other such things.
Now then, whoever fears because of the eighth seeks a share in the mercy of God and is made worthy of it, as it says: "He has heard the voice of my weeping."
And since the holy Scriptures announce to us many who are blessed because of fear, let there be for these too, in the same way, a tenfold growth from those six commandments.
And if that fear of the Lord taught in the Psalms somehow makes progress, which is turning away from evil and doing good,
and is made tenfold like some mina or talent through the increase of fear, so that in this way the soul that comes next after the queens, by fear and not by love, may add to the good
and may extend to that number of eighty, and may display in its own life each form of the virtues of fear, unmingled and distinct,

so that in this way the tenfold increase of the eighth may be magnified tenfold more, and so that she may thus become one who has drawn near to the good through a slave's fear and not through a bride's love, and a concubine instead of a queen, because of fear of the eighth, which she increased tenfold through the virtues in imitation of the number eighty, which the word of the testimonies also commands,
so that the slave woman may not become an heir with the queen, nor the son born of a concubine with the free-born son. For it says:
"Cast out this slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman."

But if anyone finds the way the numbers mentioned above have been fitted together harsh or forced, let him remember that at the very beginning of the discourse we admitted that we cannot truly reach their meaning. We have touched on it only this far, so that the parable would not be passed over entirely unexamined.
But since perfect love casts out fear, as it is written, and when fear is changed into love,
then the dwellings of those who are saved are found in the sharing of the one and only good, when all are united with one another by likeness to that perfect dove.
For some such meaning is seen in the present passage, for it says: "One is my dove, my perfect one.
She is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her."

And the meaning of these words is clearly taught to us in the Gospel by the words of God: when he had granted to his disciples the whole abundance of the graces of his teaching, and by speaking to the Father had bestowed those countless good things on those worthy of him,
he also fittingly added the chief point: that they should no longer be scattered in many directions or divided by any division of wills,

but that all should be one, united to the one and only good, and made firm by the unity of the Holy Spirit, as the apostle says, and joined together by the bond of peace, one in soul and one in body, and in the one hope to which they were appointed. And I think it good that we recall the very words of the Gospel, for it says:
"That all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they may be in us."
And what binds this unity together is glory, and the Holy Spirit is called glory.
For this reason he says, "The glory that you gave me I have given to them." And he truly gave them such glory when he said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit." And he received this glory,
which he always had before the creation of the world,
he who put on human nature, which, once it had been glorified by the Holy Spirit, began from the disciples and spread out to all; whence he says:
"The glory which you gave me I have given to them, that they may be one, as we are one.
I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfectly one."

Now then, whoever grows from infancy to the fullness of manhood and reaches the full, spiritual stature of the fullness of Christ, and who gains the honor of royalty in place of slavery and concubinage, and becomes a receiver of the Father's glory through freedom from passion and through purity, that one is the perfect dove whom the bride looks at and says:
"My dove is one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her." But surely there is no one who would not know the mother of the dove, since the tree is known by its fruit?

For just as when we see a man we are in no doubt that he was born of a man, so those who seek the mother of that chosen dove can understand nothing else than a dove as well, because a child is undoubtedly seen to have the nature of its parent.
And since that which is born of the Spirit is spirit, and the child is a dove,
the mother of the child must also undoubtedly be a dove: the one that came down from heaven at the Jordan, as John testifies.
Her the virgins call blessed, her the concubines and queens praise, for out of all ranks and all souls a common gathering is formed for such blessedness. Hence it says:
"The daughters saw her and called her blessed; queens and maidservants praised her,"
for all have by nature a growth of their desire and longing toward what is blessed and praised.
And since the daughters call that dove blessed, they undoubtedly desire to become doves themselves as well, and the praise of the dove by the maidservants and queens is a sign
that they too have zeal toward the one who is praised,

until all become one in contemplating and longing for that goal set before them, and no evil whatsoever remains, but God is all in all in those who through unity have become one and have been joined to one another by sharing in the good, through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen!
